title: Donkey Kong jump: the envelope lid dips 0.21 V too shallow, so the square clears it by too little
description:
Last gap in the jump chain after the rebuild. Everything else lands: level exact, decay 0.419 s against 0.495, the wobble's period 0.109 s against 0.110 and its pitch range 320-485 Hz against 325-485. What is left is the band split — 150-400 Hz holds 51.6 % against the reference's 69.0 %, and 400-1000 Hz 45.5 % against 27.1 %.

It is a waveform SHAPE difference, not a pitch one. Plotted cycle against cycle, our output has a genuinely FLAT top where the board's is rounded throughout: the emitter follower (JUMP_INT, core NodeKind::RcIntegrate) charges with tau = 150 us, reaches its target part-way through the square's ~2 ms high phase, and then sits there. A flat top with a sharp corner carries harmonics a rounded one does not, and that is the excess above 400 Hz.

So the follower's rise is missing something. Candidates, in the order worth testing:
  - the transistor's own response — the base node is not a perfect square and the emitter does not track it instantly;
  - the discharge threshold. Ours switches to discharge when (in - Vbe) < Vcap; the board's divider makes it (in - Vbe) < Vcap * Re/(Re+Rload) = 0.95 * Vcap, so it holds on slightly longer;
  - the 555's edges. Ours are hard at sample boundaries where the board's are not, which also shows as 3x the reference's energy in 1000-3000 Hz (0.72 % against 0.26 %).

DO NOT close this by putting a low-pass at a fitted corner in front of the divider. That would measure better and model nothing, which is the failure mode docs/designs/discrete-sound-fidelity.md records under 'What the first board taught'. The rounding has a mechanism; find it.

Node-level comparison (…-discrete-node-compare-2b7f) would settle it in one measurement, since JUMP_INT is exactly the node in question.
notes:
DIAGNOSIS CORRECTED by the node dump. It is NOT the emitter follower.

Built MAME 0.287 with DISCRETE_CSVLOG5 on the jump chain (NODE_28/29/35/38/39)
and compared stage by stage against our probes.

WHAT THE FOLLOWER ACTUALLY DOES. Through the square's high phase MAME's NODE_39
creeps 3.0097 -> 3.0248 with tau ~160 us, against our modelled 150 us. It is
just as flat-topped as ours. The 'flat top vs rounded' reading taken from the
final output was real but its cause was upstream.

THE 555 IS RIGHT TOO: ours high 1.722 ms / low 0.892 ms / duty 65.9 %, MAME
1.663 / 0.880 / 65.4 %.

WHERE IT ACTUALLY IS — the envelope lid dips too shallow:

  t(s)     ours     MAME    diff
  1.99   4.8935   4.8935   0.0000   (at rest, identical)
  2.05   2.9157   2.7064   +0.209   (the dip floor)
  2.20   3.4407   3.2841   +0.157
  2.50   4.1272   4.0395   +0.088

A lid sitting 0.21 V high is a pedestal 0.21 V high, so the square clears it by
less. That is the whole of the amplitude difference: the follower swings 0.878 V
p-p in MAME against 0.576 V here, and only 19 % of MAME's samples sit within 2 %
of peak against our 54 %. Less clearance is a smaller, flatter-topped wave with
proportionally more harmonic content — the 150-400/400-1000 split.

CAUSE: the conditioned trigger is short. Working back from the dip floor,
4.8955 * exp(-T/47ms) = 2.70 gives T = 28.0 ms; JUMP_TRIG_S is 26 ms, derived
as 20 ms * ln(2.2/0.6) = 25.99. So the derivation is ~7 % short somewhere —
either the differentiator's start value is above 2.2 V or its relaxation is
slower than the 20 ms that (R1+R2) and (R4) with 1 uF imply.

DO NOT simply set JUMP_TRIG_S to 28 ms. The 26 ms is a derivation and the fix is
to find which term in it is wrong; log NODE_33 and NODE_34 in the same way and
the answer is immediate.

NOTE the dump also shows a ~13 ms timing offset: the Lua driver asserts on the
frame boundary at ~2.013 s where the sndcmp scenario asserts at exactly 2.000 s.
That is the 'onset +0.020 s' every jump audiodiff has reported. Harmless for
spectra, but it should be aligned before any fine time-domain comparison.

STOMP: its residual has the same shape and its lid is the same structure with
different values (3.3 uF, 33 ms / 363 ms) driven by the SAME trigger pulse, so
this likely explains both — but that is now a prediction to test rather than the
established fact the earlier note implied.
close_reason:
Fixed for jump, and the node dump closed the question it was retitled around.

THE ENVELOPE WAS DIPPING SHALLOW because the trigger was 2 ms short, and the trigger was short because one term in its derivation was wrong. Logging the differentiator and its comparator settled which:

                        model      board
  relaxation tau      20.00 ms   20.00 ms
  comparator ref        0.60 V    0.5994 V
  spike start           2.20 V    2.4974 V

The capacitor sits DISCHARGED while the latch is idle, not at the 0.6 V clamp the derivation assumed. 20 ms * ln(2.5/0.6) = 28.5 ms against the board's 28.52. Both triggers are now built from the network rather than asserted, so the width is a consequence — including that it depends on where the capacitor sits when the edge arrives, which the fixed-width one-shot could not express.

Jump now: T40 0.514 s against 0.500, fundamental 347.2 Hz against 347.8, level exact, STFT 3.190.

STOMP, which this issue speculated shared a cause: it does not, and everything upstream of its output matches the board.
  envelope        within 5 mV at every timepoint checked, 0 to 1 s
  trigger         28.52 ms, the same shared network
  rumble          126.0 Hz against 125.0
  follower bands  99.03 / 0.89 % against 99.52 / 0.43 %

What is left is that 0.89 against 0.43 — twice the board's harmonic content, but under 1 % of the voice's energy. The output high-pass strips the 99 % DC bulk they share and magnifies the remainder into the 18 % against 10 % visible at the final mix.

The most likely cause is edge quantisation rather than a wrong value: our divider toggles on noise edges landing on 44.1 kHz sample boundaries, where the board's counter output carries sub-sample timing. That is a framework-wide question about how squares are generated, not a stomp constant, and it is small enough not to be worth chasing on its own. If it is ever picked up, it plausibly also explains walk's remaining 150-400 Hz deficit (…-4q42), which has the same shape and survived every other explanation.

title: Fix Joust graphical bug
description: Joust has a graphical rendering bug that needs investigation and fixing.
close_reason: Root cause: M6809 TST <memory> (0x0D/0x6D/0x7D) erroneously wrote the operand back through the RMW helper. On real hardware TST reads + does dummy VMA cycles, no store (confirmed vs MAME TST8 microcode). Under Williams ROM banking a read returns ROM but the write lands in VRAM, so the boot text-print loop (TST ,U+ over a ROM message table) smeared ROM bytes into video RAM — the frame-447 vertical strip. Fixed: TST's final RMW cycle now does a dummy VMA read instead of a write. Verified full VRAM byte-identical to MAME 0.287 at frame 447. Added regression tests.

title: Concrete bus dispatch: TKG-04 (Donkey Kong, DK Jr, Mario Bros)
description:
Convert the TKG-04 board (Z80 + I8035 sound + DMA) to concrete bus dispatch per docs/designs/concrete-bus-dispatch.md. Three machines on one board and no reset-vector CPU, so this is the highest-value unblocked step after the prototypes.

Move cpu/sound_cpu out of Tkg04Board into the game wrappers, decide per game whether the board can be the bus outright or needs a view, split once per frame, and check the DMA path's bus master handling. Measure dkong before/after with phosphor-bench; run golden frames.
close_reason:
Done in 1372bb6.

Correction to the issue premise: Mario Bros is NOT on the TKG-04 board. It has its own MarioBrosBoard with a Z80 DMA and shares only the palette/monitor model with tkg04.rs. Converted it alongside DK and DK Jr anyway since the issue named it.

Numbers (phosphor-bench, release, 400f x 5 reps, best of 6 alternating runs, idle host):
  dkong     1.161 -> 0.966 ms/f  -16.8%
  mariobros 1.238 -> 1.017       -17.8%
The largest gains of the rollout so far -- 3.072 MHz boards at 50,688 cycles/frame, so almost all of the frame is CPU cycles and bus accesses. (DK Jr not benchmarked: the reference ROM collection has no revision it can boot -- the same reason it carries an [[unpinned]] golden-frame entry.)

Shapes used, one of each:
- Mario Bros: the board IS the bus (impl Bus for MarioBrosBoard), CPUs on the machine, tick takes them directly -- no trait, no view, since only one machine uses that board.
- DK / DK Jr: a newtype view over the shared board (struct DkongBus<'a>(&'a mut Tkg04Board)), because their address decoding differs while the state behind it is all board. Single pointer, hoisted per frame -- none of the multi-pointer view cost the Galaga prototype found.

Neither board's DMA is a bus master in the trait sense: TKG-04's sprite DMA and Mario's Z80Dma both move bytes through the address space directly (main_map), not through Bus, so no lift was needed (unlike Williams' blitter).

New wrinkle worth recording for the remaining conversions: the sound CPU's *ports* are bus-visible. The I8035 reads its own P1/P2 back through io_read, and DK's main CPU reads P2 bit 4 as a sound-busy bit -- so with the CPU outside the bus, the board keeps a cycle-fresh mirror (sound_p1/sound_p2), latched in begin_cycle_inner before either CPU steps. Faithful because only the sound CPU writes those ports and it steps later in the same cycle. Derived state, not saved.

Also inverted both boards' frame loops to scanline-outer / cycle-inner, and renamed MarioBrosBoard::check_interrupts to interrupt_state so the Bus method of the same name can call it without recursing (the compiler caught this as 'function cannot return without recursing').

Golden frames unchanged for all pinned machines; machine, harness and ROM-gated suites pass; clippy and fmt clean.

title: Q*Bert speech too slow: Votrax clock hardcoded to 720 kHz, speech-clock DAC unimplemented
description:
Q*Bert's Votrax SC-01 speech plays back noticeably slower than on real hardware.

## Root cause

The Gottlieb Rev 1 sound/speech board drives the Votrax SC-01's master clock with
a writable VCO controlled by a "speech clock DAC" mapped at 0x3000 on the sound
CPU. The game writes this DAC to set (and dynamically vary) the speech rate/pitch.

In phosphor this is unimplemented in two places:

- machines/src/gottlieb.rs:290-291 — the DAC write is a no-op stub:
      // Speech clock DAC: 0x3000-0x3FFF (stub — adjusts Votrax VCO)
      0x3000..=0x3FFF => {}
- machines/src/gottlieb.rs:92 — the Votrax master clock is hardcoded:
      const VOTRAX_CLOCK_HZ: u64 = 720_000;
  with a fixed divider 18/125 (gottlieb.rs:94-95, used at :144, :434, :889).

Because the DAC is ignored, the Votrax always runs at a fixed 720 kHz instead of
the rate the game requests, and the speech rate never varies.

## What MAME does

src/mame/shared/gottlieb_a.cpp:
- :419  convert_speech_clock(data) = 950000 + (data - 0xa0) * 5500
- :426  speech_clock_dac_w() -> m_votrax->set_unscaled_clock(convert_speech_clock(data))
- :438  the 0x3000 (mirror 0x0fff) write maps to speech_clock_dac_w
- :471  device is created with convert_speech_clock(0) as the initial clock

So the nominal clock (data=0xa0) is 950 kHz and the game adjusts it from there.
phosphor's fixed 720 kHz is ~76% of the 950 kHz nominal, i.e. speech runs roughly
24% too slow — consistent with the reported symptom — and the game's intended
pitch/rate variation is lost entirely.

## Fix sketch

1. Implement the 0x3000-0x3FFF write: compute clock = 950000 + (data - 0xa0)*5500
   and push it to the Votrax (add a set_clock/set_unscaled_clock on VotraxSc01 in
   core/src/device/votrax_sc01.rs that recomputes sclock/cclock from the new clock).
2. Make the gottlieb sound-board <-> votrax clock divider track the current Votrax
   clock instead of the fixed VOTRAX_CLOCK_NUM/DEN (18/125), since the divider
   ratio against the 5 MHz timebase changes with the DAC value.
3. Initialize the Votrax clock from convert_speech_clock(0) to match MAME's
   construction default.

## Verification

After the fix, compare Q*Bert speech rate against MAME (gottlieb1_votrax /
GOTTLIEB_SOUND_SPEECH_REV1A) — durations should match and pitch should vary as
the game writes the DAC.
close_reason: Implemented the speech-clock DAC (sound CPU 0x3000): it now retunes the Votrax SC-01 VCO via convert_speech_clock (950 kHz nominal at 0xA0, ±5.5 kHz/step), matching MAME. The board re-derives the Votrax tick divider and the device's internal sclock/cclock + resampler rate whenever the DAC changes (and after state load). Default clock raised from the incorrect fixed 720 kHz to the 950 kHz nominal, fixing the too-slow speech.

title: MCR II declares a 36.93 Hz frame rate; the reference says 30 Hz
description:
Satan's Hollow reports a 36.93 Hz frame rate. MAME declares 30 Hz for the same
board. Neither our figure nor a plausible field rate of 60 Hz comes out of our
constants, so something in the vertical timing is wrong.

WHERE IT COMES FROM. mcr2.rs:32-41 declares cpu_clock_hz 2_496_000,
cycles_per_scanline 256 and total_scanlines 264. TimingConfig::frame_rate_hz
(core/src/core/machine.rs:69) is cpu_clock / (scanline * lines), so
2_496_000 / 67_584 = 36.93 Hz, and machine_core_metadata! hands that straight to
the frontend (satans_hollow.rs:466).

WHAT THE REFERENCE SAYS. mcr.cpp:1821 sets refresh to 30 Hz for mcr_90009, which
mcr_90010 (Satan's Hollow) inherits, with no raw pixel timing anywhere in the
MCR drivers: set_size(32*16, 30*16) and nothing else. So MAME does not settle the
true HTOTAL or VTOTAL either. The clock tree is not in doubt: one 19.968 MHz
oscillator, Z80 at /8 = 2.496 MHz, pixel clock at /4 = 4.992 MHz
(mcr2.rs:43-65), and MAIN_OSC_MCR_I at mcr.h:32 agrees.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY UNKNOWN. The 512 dots per line and 264 lines per field in
mcr2.rs are ours. 512 x 264 dots at 4.992 MHz is 27.1 ms, which is neither
1/30 nor 1/60 s. Any pair that divides 4.992 MHz into 30 Hz or 60 fields is a
candidate and the schematic decides which. Do not fit a pair to make the number
come out; read the horizontal and vertical divider chain.

WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT. Nothing in the tree asserts a frame rate against anything
external. The golden frame is a hash at a fixed frame count, so a wrong frame
period moves the attract loop by the same amount in both the capture and the
comparison and cancels. Audio sanity measures spectrum, not rate.

SURFACED BY phosphor-emulator-conformance-rom-programme-hl4t.1 while surveying
what each board's CPU can see of the beam. It matters to that programme because
mcr2's Z80 CTC can be programmed as an exact scanline counter (256 CPU cycles
per line), and an expectation stated in frames would be standing on this.

Fixing it will move the mcr2 golden frame and the audio capture.
close_reason: Derived from the Satan's Hollow schematic and fixed. The dot clock is master/2 (9.984 MHz), not master/4, and HTOTAL is the 634 the decode net names, giving a 15,747.6 Hz line rate: NTSC's to within 0.09%. VTOTAL 512 makes the frame 81,152 CPU cycles at 30.757 Hz. 634 dots is 158.5 CPU cycles, so the board steps in line pairs of 317, which is exact and safe here only because the renderer never consults a scanline index. Correcting my own earlier comment: the game was running 20% too FAST with an uneven field cadence, not 40% slow. Golden frame recaptured after comparing both images by eye; both render cleanly and the difference is attract-loop state. VTOTAL and HTOTAL remain inferences from the decode net names, since the terminal counts are inside Midway custom parts.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
Derived from the schematic (Satan's Hollow Parts and Operating Manual, Oct 1982,
sheet 9-6 "Schematic Drwg Super CPU" A082-90010-E000, 9/7/82). The frame rate is
wrong, and it is wrong for a different reason than the issue guessed: the dot
clock is out by a factor of two AND the line is 634 dots, not 512.

THE CLOCK TREE, READ OFF THE PAGE. All on the Super CPU board, top-left of 9-6:

  X-TAL 19.968 MHz -> A11 (S04) oscillator
    -> A10 S74 half 1, D tied to its own Q-, so divide by 2 -> HCLK
    -> HCLK- clocks A9 S74 half 1, whose Q clocks A9 S74 half 2, each wired D
       from Q-, so divide by 4 -> C10 S04 -> Q101 -> the Z80 clock

  HCLK  = 19.968 / 2 = 9.984 MHz
  Z80   = 19.968 / 8 = 2.496 MHz

The Z80 rate matches what we already have. HCLK does not: clock_tree() in
mcr2.rs declares the pixel clock as master/4 = 4.992 MHz. It is master/2.

THE COUNTERS. Bottom middle of 9-6, four Midway custom parts:

  A12 = MMC01   outputs H2..H9          (with B12 = MMC03 supplying H0, H1,
                                         *H0..*H3 and HBLNK)
  G12 = MMC02   outputs DV0..DV8, VBLNK
  G11 = MMC06   takes DV0..DV6, outputs DV7, DV8, AV3, 493, VBLNK

So the horizontal counter is 10 bits and the vertical counter is 9 bits. Four
decode nets are distributed to all of them: 634, 317, 511 and V00. A fifth, 493,
comes out of MMC06 and is the signal MAME already names as the CTC's channel-3
trigger.

Midway names a decode net after the count it decodes, the way Atari names one
after its divider tap. That gives:

  HTOTAL = 634 HCLKs           (10-bit counter, 634 fits, 512 does not explain
                                a net called 634)
  317    = 634 / 2, the half-line an interlaced sync generator needs for its
           equalizing pulses
  VTOTAL = 512 lines           (9-bit counter, terminal count 511)
  493    = a line inside vertical blanking, once per frame

WHAT FOLLOWS, AND IT IS ARITHMETIC FROM HERE.

  line rate   = 9.984 MHz / 634       = 15,747.6 Hz
  frame       = 15,747.6 / 512        = 30.76 Hz
  field       = 15,747.6 / 256        = 61.51 Hz
  CPU / frame = 2 x 634 x 512 / 8     = 81,152 cycles exactly
  CPU / line  = 81,152 / 512          = 158.5 cycles

15,747.6 Hz is the NTSC line rate to within 0.09%, which is the corroboration
that matters most: the number falls out of the crystal and the decode, and it
lands on a real monitor's scan rate rather than near one.

FOUR THINGS AGREE AT ONCE. VBLANK decoded ignoring the counter's top bit fires
twice per 512-line frame, which is MAME's "CTC line 2 is connected to VBLANK,
which is once every 1/2 frame"; 493 lies in 480..511, so it fires once per frame,
which is MAME's "CTC line 3 is connected to 493, signalled once every frame at
30Hz"; 480 visible of 512 leaves 32 blanked lines, a normal proportion; and the
CPU frame comes out as an exact integer only for VTOTAL = 512, not 511.

WHAT WE HAVE, AND WHAT IT COSTS.

                        ours          hardware
  pixel clock        4.992 MHz       9.984 MHz
  HTOTAL             512 dots        634 dots
  CPU per line       256             158.5
  lines per field    264             256
  CPU per field      67,584          40,576
  field rate         36.93 Hz        61.51 Hz

The CPU clock is right, so instructions run at the correct rate. What is wrong is
how much CPU time passes between VBLANKs: 67,584 cycles where the hardware gives
40,576. Satan's Hollow's animation, its attract loop and everything its CTC
drives therefore run about 40% slow, and the machine reports 36.93 Hz to the
frontend. That is the real defect; the frame-rate number in the issue title was
the symptom.

WHAT I COULD NOT READ, STATED PLAINLY. The terminal counts live inside MMC01,
MMC02 and MMC06, which are Midway custom parts, so their internals are not on
the sheet. HTOTAL = 634 and VTOTAL = 512 rest on the net names, the counter
widths, the resulting line rate being NTSC's, and the CPU frame being an integer.
That is four independent agreements and it is still not the same as reading the
number off the page. If someone turns up a Midway video timing chart, it should
be checked against this.

WHY I HAVE NOT CHANGED ANYTHING YET, AND THE DECISION IT NEEDS.

158.5 CPU cycles per scanline is not an integer, and TimingConfig::
cycles_per_scanline is a u64 that every machine and the whole run_scanlines
contract are built on (core/src/core/machine.rs:65-71). There is no way to
express this board honestly in the current shape. The options I can see, none of
which I should pick alone:

1. Keep the integer field and step two lines at a time: 317 cycles per pair, 128
   pairs per field. Exact, no contract change, but halves the per-scanline
   rendering granularity on a board whose open W1 issue is about per-scanline
   palette.
2. Carry cycles_per_frame as the primitive and derive scanline boundaries by
   division, letting them fall mid-cycle. Honest for every machine, and a change
   to a contract 30-odd machines share.
3. Count in master-clock units rather than CPU cycles, which is what the hardware
   does and what ClockTree already half expresses.

Whichever it is, landing it will move the shollow golden frame and its audio
capture, because the machine will start running at the right speed for the first
time. It also interacts with phosphor-emulator-d4d5 (the missing CTC cascade)
and with raster-sampling-6kae.1 (W1, per-scanline palette on mcr2), so the order
matters.

Recorded and left open for that decision. Nothing in the tree was changed.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
Fixed. First, a correction to the comment above, because it got the direction of
the error backwards.

I wrote that the game "runs about 40% slow", from comparing the reported 36.93 Hz
against the true 61.51 Hz field rate. Those are not the same quantity and the
comparison was meaningless. What reaches the game is the CTC cadence, and the old
code fired channel 2 at scanlines 0 and 240 of a 264-line unit and channel 3 at
scanline 0, which is two and one per run_frame either way. The count was never
wrong; the duration was.

                        trg2 (VBLANK)                  trg3 (the 493 decode)
  before      73.86 Hz, unevenly spaced                     36.93 Hz
              (61,440 cycles, then 6,144)
  after       61.51 Hz, even                                30.757 Hz
  hardware    61.51 Hz                                      30.757 Hz

So Satan's Hollow was running 20% too FAST, with a lopsided field cadence, not
40% slow. The Z80 clock was right the whole time; only the spacing of the
interrupts against it was wrong. Everything else in the previous comment stands.

WHAT LANDED. TIMING now declares 317 cycles per scanline and 256 scanlines, and
the file says in a header comment that a scanline here is a LINE PAIR and why:
634 dot clocks is 158.5 CPU cycles, which no integer cycles_per_scanline can
hold, and two lines is 317 exactly. That trick is available only because this
board's renderer is a dirty-gated per-tile compositor that runs at the frame
boundary and never consults a scanline index; the only consumer of one is the CTC
trigger. The comment says that too, so nobody carries the trick to a board that
renders per scanline.

clock_tree() declares the dot clock as master/2 rather than master/4, and
set_raster as 2 * HTOTAL_DOTS = 1268. That last part matters more than it looks:
machines/tests/clock_tree_test.rs::declared_raster_reproduces_cycles_per_scanline
is registry-driven and re-derives cycles_per_scanline from the declared dot clock
and htotal, so the 317 is now checked against the crystal rather than asserted.
It comes out at 0 ppm, and declared_tolerance_is_tight makes the board declare
that 0 rather than a loose bound.

begin_scanline triggers channel 2 every PAIRS_PER_FIELD = 128 and channel 3 at 0.

THREE TESTS, EACH MUTATED UNTIL IT FAILED.

  the_line_rate_is_the_ntsc_line_rate is the one that anchors the derivation to
  something outside our own constants: 9.984 MHz over 634 has to land within 0.1%
  of NTSC's 15,734.264 Hz. Against the old geometry: "634 dot clocks at 4992000
  Hz is a 7873.8 Hz line rate, 49.96% off NTSC".

  a_frame_is_512_lines_at_about_30_hz pins 81,152 cycles and bounds the rate to
  30..31 Hz, which fails both for the old 36.93 and for the 61.5 a field-shaped
  run_frame would report. Against the old geometry: left 528, right 512.

  the_ctc_sees_vblank_twice_a_frame_and_the_493_decode_once counts edges through
  the device by putting both channels in counter mode and reading the down
  counters back.

The third one is worth a note, because my first draft of its doc comment claimed
it would fail against the old geometry and that was false: the counts per
run_frame were 2 and 1 before and after, so it passed under that mutation. The
comment now says what it actually guards, which is the field split and the
trigger conditions, and it was made to fail by setting PAIRS_PER_FIELD to 64
(left 4, right 2). The frame-length tests are what catch the defect this change
was for.

THE GOLDEN FRAME MOVED AND WAS RECAPTURED AFTER LOOKING AT BOTH IMAGES. The pin
was the SATAN'S HOLLOW title screen; at the same 1800-frame count the machine now
shows the SHIELD instruction screen. Both render cleanly, with correct glyphs,
colours, geometry and sprite, so this is a state difference and not a rendering
one: a 20% speed correction puts the attract loop somewhere else at a fixed frame
count. The frames.toml `shows` description was rewritten to match, since it
described the old screen. This is exactly the confusion
phosphor-emulator-conformance-rom-programme-hl4t exists to remove, and it had to
be checked by eye because nothing else can tell those two apart.

WHAT IS STILL OPEN. VTOTAL = 512 and HTOTAL = 634 remain inferences from the
decode net names plus four agreements (the NTSC line rate, the CTC cadences MAME
describes, 480 of 512 visible being a normal blanking proportion, and only 512
making the CPU frame an integer). The terminal counts are inside MMC01, MMC02 and
MMC06 and are not on the sheet. Also untouched: whether the two fields should
render different line sets, which is what interlace actually does and which this
board does not model either before or after.

Verified: clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -D warnings clean with
mcr2.rs touched first; cargo test --workspace green; cargo fmt clean; ROM-gated
boot_check 7/7, save_state_rom 7/7, audio_sanity 13/13, golden_frame 11/11 plus
the shollow comparison forced past the #[ignore] that is phosphor-emulator-gn5w.

title: Generalize display aspect-ratio handling (Renderable hint + frontend presentation)
description:
Aspect-ratio handling is currently ad-hoc per machine: Star Wars bakes a horizontal stretch into display_width + render (anamorphic); Burgertime bakes a vertical stretch into display_size (240x320) with a per-frame CPU nearest-neighbor upscale in render_frame. Most raster machines report their native raster and rely on it approximating the tube aspect, so any machine whose raster isn't its tube aspect (e.g. a 256x256 game on a 4:3 tube) is subtly wrong (square pixels).

Proposal: keep Renderable::display_size() as the true render resolution (native raster) and add a display-aspect hint (e.g. display_aspect_ratio() -> f32, default = native square, or an Option<(w,h)>). The frontend does aspect correction once at presentation time (size the window to the aspect, letterbox, let the GPU sample the texture). Machines like Burgertime/Star Wars set the hint instead of baking a lossy upscale into render_frame.

Benefits: correctness for every non-square-pixel machine; crisper output (one GPU stretch vs CPU nearest-neighbor + integer scale); native-resolution renders stay testable in native coords; removes per-machine bake duplication.

Scope/risks: touches core Renderable trait; frontend window-sizing / scale / egui side-panel layout (all keyed off display_size today, see frontend/src/emulator.rs and video.rs); needs a visual re-verification pass across machines to set correct aspects and catch regressions.

Migration: after the mechanism lands, migrate Burgertime (drop the 240x320 stretch in machines/src/btime.rs render_frame, set 3:4 hint) and Star Wars (drop the display_width=400 anamorphic bake) to the hint, and audit other raster machines for correct aspect.
close_reason: Generalized display aspect handling: display_aspect hint on TimingConfig/Renderable, presentation-time correction in the frontend (window sizing, unified letterbox, vector viewport), migrated Burgertime (3:4) and Star Wars (true 4:3) off their bakes, and set 4:3/3:4 hints across all raster + vector machines. Visually verified.

title: Food Fight IRQ1 fires on 0/64/128/192; the hardware is 32V
description:
Food Fight's IRQ1 is documented as 32V, which puts it on scanlines 32, 96, 160
and 224. We fire it on 0, 64, 128 and 192, copying MAME, which says in its own
source that this is wrong and that it has not worked out why it has to be
(foodf.cpp:326-329):

  /* WARNING: the timing of this is not perfectly accurate; it should fire on
     32V (i.e., on scanlines 32, 96, 160, and 224). However, due to the
     interrupt structure, it cannot fire at the same time as VBLANK. I have not
     solved this mystery yet */

Ours is foodf.rs:778-781, matching MAME's fallback exactly. The header comment in
the same MAME file states the hardware plainly at foodf.cpp:70: "IRQ1 = 32V".

WHY IT IS FILED NOW. phosphor-emulator-conformance-rom-programme-hl4t.1 graded
foodf as a board where a conformance ROM is possible: four beam-locked
interrupts a frame at 64-line spacing is enough to place a mid-frame write
without counting cycles. But every expectation such a ROM could carry about
where IRQ1 fires would be pinning MAME's acknowledged approximation. The
instrument would then make the approximation permanent, which is the exact
failure mode williams-video-conformance.md risk 1 warns about.

THE MYSTERY IS PROBABLY THE INTERRUPT ENCODING. IRQ1 is 32V, IRQ2 is VBLANK, and
the 68000 sees IRQ3 when both latches are set at once (foodf.cpp:314-319,
foodf.rs:759-767). VBLANK is at 224 and 32V would also be high at 224, so with
the real positions the two coincide once a frame and the CPU takes a level 3
autovector instead of separate 1 and 2. Whether the game's IRQ3 handler copes is
the question to answer, and it is answerable by reading the game's vector table
and handlers with the disassembler rather than by guessing.

WHAT TO DO. Read the 68000 vector table and the three handlers in the Food Fight
ROM (cargo run -p phosphor-disasm), work out what the program expects at each
level, then decide whether 32/96/160/224 with a real level-3 case is correct. If
it is, our board should implement it and say so, and MAME's mystery is solved
rather than inherited. If the game genuinely cannot cope, that is evidence the
hardware does something else at the coincidence, and that needs the schematic.

See docs/designs/conformance-rom-board-survey.md.
close_reason: Settled from the SP-229 schematic, not inferred. Sheet 5A: 32V clocks a 74LS74 (D grounded, preset from INT3RST-), so the request is set on 32V's RISING edge, i.e. lines 32/96/160/224; we were on the falling edges. Sheet 4B: IL3- to IPL0-, IL4- to IPL1-, IPL2- pulled up, so 32V=level 1, VBLANK=level 2, both=level 3 and our level encoding was already right. The ROM's vector table confirms it: level 1 acks bit 2 (the 32V latch), levels 2/3/4 share a handler that acks bit 3, so the line-224 coincidence is serviced as level 3 then level 1 with nothing lost. The reference's mystery was a problem this game does not have. Golden frame byte-identical; level 2 becomes correctly unreachable. Also added the foodf DisasmRegion the investigation needed.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
Settled from the schematic. IRQ1 fires on 32, 96, 160 and 224, and the reason
the reference could not use those is not a reason.

THE SCHEMATIC (SP-229 2nd printing, sheets 5A, 6B and 4B; the PDF the issue was
worked from is on arcarc). Three sheets answer the whole thing.

Sheet 6B, Sync: a 12.096 MHz crystal feeds three LS163s for the horizontal chain
and two more (2M, 2N) clocked by 256H- for the vertical chain, giving the taps
1V, 2V, 4V, 8V, 16V, 32V, 64V, 128V. VBLANK, VSYNC and VPRESET come out of a
136020-112 PROM addressed by VBLANK/64V/32V/16V/8V/4V/2V/1V and latched in an
LS175 clocked by 256H-.

Sheet 5A, Reset and Digital I/O, is the one that matters. Two halves of a 74LS74
at 10F, each with D tied to ground and CLR- tied to +5V:

  32V     -> pin 3  (CLK), preset from INT3RST-, outputs IL3- (Q) and IL3 (Q-)
  VBLANK  -> pin 11 (CLK), preset from INT4RST-, output  IL4- (Q)

An LS74 is positive-edge triggered, so each request is SET by its timing
signal's RISING edge and cleared only when the program pulses the matching
preset. The presets come from an LS273 at 11C/D holding the digital-output byte:
BD2 -> INT3RST-, BD3 -> INT4RST-. Those are the same two bits the reference calls
"INT1 reset" and "INT2 reset", so the bit mapping was already right and only the
names differ.

32V is high for lines 32-63, 96-127, 160-191 and 224-255. Its rising edges are
therefore 32, 96, 160 and 224. We were firing on 0, 64, 128 and 192, which are
the falling edges: the same four events, one tap-width early.

Sheet 4B, CPU, kills the remaining ambiguity about what "IL3" means. On the
68000L6:

  IL3-   pin 25  IPL0-
  IL4-   pin 24  IPL1-
  P,R19  pin 23  IPL2-   (pull-up, never asserted)

So 32V alone is level 1, VBLANK alone is level 2, both together are level 3, and
levels 4 through 7 are unreachable. The IL3/IL4 names are net names, not 68000
levels; our interrupt_level() encoding was already exactly right.

THE GAME AGREES, AND ITS VECTOR TABLE IS THE PROOF. I added a DisasmRegion for
foodf (it had none) and read the ROM. Autovectors:

  0x64  level 1 -> 0x000112
  0x68  level 2 -> 0x000148
  0x6C  level 3 -> 0x000148
  0x70  level 4 -> 0x000148
  0x74+ levels 5-7 -> 0x00008C, the catch-all everything else points at

0x000112 pulses digital-output bit 2 low and back (AND with $FFFB against the
shadow copy at $0001861E, store, restore), i.e. it acks INT3RST-, the 32V latch.
0x000148 does the same with bit 3, acking INT4RST-, the VBLANK latch. So the
level-1 handler clears the 32V request and the level-2/3/4 handler clears the
VBLANK one, each clearing only its own.

That is what makes the coincidence harmless, and it is deliberate. 32V's fourth
rising edge is line 224, which is also where VBLANK rises, so the CPU sees level
3. It vectors to 0x148, does the VBLANK work, acks bit 3 only, and RTEs; the 32V
request is still latched, so the next instruction boundary takes level 1 and runs
0x112. Nothing is lost and nothing runs twice. Pointing levels 2, 3 and 4 at one
handler is exactly what you write if you know VBLANK can arrive as either 2 or 3.

So the reference's "it cannot fire at the same time as VBLANK, I have not solved
this mystery yet" describes a problem the game does not have. There was nothing
to dodge.

WHAT CHANGED AND WHAT IT COST. SCANLINE_INT_LINES is now [32, 96, 160,
VBLANK_SCANLINE], with the derivation and the two-step service sequence in the
doc comment. Nothing else moved: the level encoding, the ack bits and the
handlers were all already right.

Measured over a 1800-frame boot from real ROMs, counting cycles in which each
level was presented to the CPU:

              level 1    level 2    level 3     (cycles per frame)
  before       1721.8      282.3     2190.9
  after        1968.1        0.0     2473.2

Level 2 becomes unreachable, and that is correct rather than alarming: IL4- can
now never be asserted without IL3-, because the two latches clock on the same
line, so VBLANK always presents as level 3 and drops to level 1 when its handler
acks. The game's level-2 vector is vestigial on real hardware. The old positions
made it reachable for ~282 cycles a frame, which is the artefact.

The Food Fight golden frame is byte-identical before and after. That is not the
change being inert: the unit tests below fail against the old positions, so the
board's behaviour did move. The picture does not, because the level-1 handler's
work ($102A, $8048) is game logic with nothing beam-relative in it, and both edge
choices deliver four requests per frame. The level-3 path was already being taken
heavily before this change (2191 cycles a frame), because the game is slow enough
to ack that the two latches overlapped anyway, so no new path is being exercised
for the first time by a real ROM.

THE CHECKS WERE MADE TO FAIL FIRST. Two tests in machines/src/foodf.rs:

  the_scanline_interrupt_fires_on_the_rising_edges_of_32v sweeps a whole frame
  and asserts the full set [32, 96, 160, 224] rather than a count, because a
  count cannot tell a rising edge from a falling one.
  the_fourth_32v_edge_coincides_with_vblank_and_reads_as_level_3 walks the
  service sequence in the order the ROM performs it: level 3, ack bit 3 only,
  level 1 survives, ack bit 2, level 0.

Reverting SCANLINE_INT_LINES to [0, 64, 128, 192] fails both, the first with
left [0, 64, 128, 192] against right [32, 96, 160, 224].

ALSO LANDED, because the investigation needed it. foodf had no DisasmRegion, so
`disasm machine --machine foodf` could not read the ROM this issue is about. The
even/odd de-interleave was inline in load_rom_set; it is now
load_program_image(), shared by the board and the new region. Reading the raw
concatenation instead would put each word's halves 8 KB apart, so the two have to
agree and now cannot drift.

WHAT I DID NOT DO. The VBLANK line itself is unchanged at 224 and I did not
re-derive it from the 136020-112 PROM, which would need the PROM dump rather than
the schematic. Nothing here touches the horizontal chain or the 259/384 frame
geometry.

VERIFICATION. clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -D warnings clean
with foodf.rs touched first; cargo test --workspace --all-features green; cargo
fmt clean. ROM-gated, individually: boot_check 7/7, save_state_rom 7/7,
audio_sanity 13/13, and the foodf golden frame compared (forced past the
#[ignore] that is phosphor-emulator-gn5w) and matching.

title: Epic: CRT rendering for the raster machines
description:
The vector machines model a beam: spot size from the tube, brightness from dwell, bright vertices from the stationary beam, halation from the faceplate. The roughly 35 raster machines draw flat pixel grids. They ran on the same family of tube, and the figures to do the same for them are already in the tree.

THE FINDING THAT SHAPES THIS. Two numbers decide what is worth building, and both come from BEAM_SPOT_MM (0.7) and TUBE_LONG_AXIS_MM (360) in phosphor_core::device::dvg plus each machine line count.

Scanlines dominate, and only on some machines. A 19 inch viewable height is about 270 mm. A 224-line machine has a line pitch of 1.21 mm against a 0.7 mm spot, so the beam covers 58 percent of the pitch and the gaps between lines are real. MCR2 runs 480 lines: pitch 0.56 mm against the same spot, so the lines overlap and there are no visible scanlines at all. Scanline visibility is derivable per machine, and a shader that applies them uniformly is wrong for the high-resolution boards.

The shadow mask is finer than the pixel grid. Mask pitch is about 0.6 mm. Pac-Man 288 pixels across 360 mm makes one emulated pixel 1.25 mm, so a pixel spans about two triads. The RGB stripe look people associate with CRT shaders comes from PC monitors at 640x480 and up, where a pixel is roughly one triad. At arcade resolutions the mask sits BELOW the pixel grid and reads as slight softening, not stripes. Building visible stripes would be building a look these cabinets never had.

That inverts the usual priority: spot profile and scanlines first, mask last and possibly never.

WHAT ALREADY EXISTS. core::display::DisplaySettings (brightness, focus, halation), read at the edge, persisted diff-only per machine, live on a panel at Shift+backtick. Its module doc already states that these are properties of the tube rather than of the vector generator and that raster-only knobs belong beside them. halation_sigma_units() is derived from the faceplate critical angle and applies unchanged to a raster tube. machines/src/atari_dvg.rs::rasterize_vectors is the worked example of deriving a renderer from the tube instead of tuning it.

THE ARCHITECTURAL PROBLEM. The vector path owns a GL program and draws to the window. The raster path uploads the framebuffer as a texture and hands it to egui (ui.image at frontend/src/video.rs:132). There is no shader stage of ours on that path. The real cost of this epic is not the physics, it is inserting a render stage into a presentation path that delegates to egui, without breaking the debug panels that lay out around that texture.

BLOCKED ON phosphor-emulator-gr27. Every raster machine is pinned on a frame hash, so any CRT effect changes all 35 at once. The vector work got away with churning pins because there were three machines and a human could eyeball them; 35 is a different problem. gr27 is already open on what that test is for and must be settled first.

DECISIONS TO MAKE WITH THE REQUESTER, NOT TO ASSUME.

1. Which renderer. This is the same fork the vector work hit, and it resolved as: expensive effects on the GPU, CPU path stays cheap and serves screenshots and the debug panel. The question underneath is whether a screenshot should match what ships.
2. Upscale factor, and whether it is per machine or global.
3. Whether the CPU path gets anything at all, given what the cost measurement says.

COST, from the vector work. The CPU rasterizer went from 0.043 to about 1.4 ms per frame when it grew a beam model. A raster CRT effect touches every pixel of every machine every frame, so a CPU implementation would be worse across the whole library. That is the strongest argument for settling the renderer fork up front rather than discovering it, which is how it went with halation: it read as a 4 ms problem on a 580x570 field and was 13.5 ms on 1024 by 1024, because the cost is O(pixels).

TRAPS SPECIFIC TO RASTER.

Scanlines must be applied in tube space, not pixel space. Arcade pixels are not square and display_aspect corrects at presentation; applying scanlines before that correction puts the spacing wrong on every non-square-pixel machine.

Scanline direction follows the tube, not the image. On a rotated cabinet the beam horizontal is the screen vertical. A double-applied rotation on Tempest was open from August until this session (phosphor-emulator-iitc); this is the same class of error waiting in a new place.

Measure on the largest raster machine, not the convenient one, and pass --machine explicitly, because phosphor-bench default set is not representative.

Expect exactly one figure you cannot derive, as the halation fraction was. Label it as underived in the source and put it on the slider. Two such figures means a missing mechanism.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
Filed .7, .8 and .9 for the CPU path performance question, in that order deliberately.

The short version, so it is not re-litigated from first principles: the per-pixel loops look arithmetic-bound and are not. Optimising the vector rasterizer this session, removing about 2.2 million exp() calls bought 0.19 ms and removing a 4 MB per-frame allocation bought nothing measurable, while the two algorithmic changes (windowing rows to the segment stadium, precomputing bilinear taps) bought 3.4 ms and 3.9 ms. Asteroids accumulator is 12.6 MB and a frame traverses it two to three times. That is a memory-traffic problem.

So the order is: shrink the accumulator (.7), fuse the traversals (.8), and only then consider SIMD (.9), which also depends on .8 having linearised the gather-shaped halation composite that SSE2 cannot load contiguously anyway. SIMD additionally costs a NEON path, since aarch64-apple-darwin is a supported target and std::simd is nightly.

All three are conditional on fork 1 in the description. If the GPU owns the effects and screenshots are allowed not to match what ships, the CPU rasterizer serves only screenshots and the debug panel and none of this is needed. Decide that first.

One caveat carried on each of them: memory-bound is inferred from those measurements and from the buffer size, not from a profiler. Confirm it before building on it, because if it is wrong all three are wrong together.

title: Confirm the scanline prediction before building anything
description:
The cheapest thing in the epic and the one that decides its shape. No code.

Claim to check: scanline visibility is derivable per machine from line pitch against spot size, and it goes to zero on the high-resolution boards. A 19 inch viewable height is about 270 mm and the focused spot about 0.7 mm, so a 224-line machine has a 1.21 mm pitch (spot covers 58 percent, gaps visible) and a 480-line machine has a 0.56 mm pitch (spot covers 125 percent, lines overlap, no gaps).

Take one low-line-count machine and one high-line-count machine, work the ratio for each from TimingConfig and the tube figures, and say plainly whether the prediction holds. If it does, stage 2 renders scanlines derived per machine rather than uniformly, and stage 4 is probably dead. If it does not, the whole epic needs rethinking before any rendering code exists.

Verify both halves. It is not enough that the low-resolution machine predicts visible lines; the high-resolution one has to predict none, or the model is not discriminating and is just a knob with extra steps.

title: Separate native raster from output resolution
description:
A 288x224 framebuffer has nowhere to put a scanline. Before any effect can exist there has to be a distinction between the raster a machine produces and the pixels it is drawn into.

This is the raster analogue of what Renderable::vector_field_size did for the vector machines, where display_size was doing two jobs at once: the coordinate extent the generator works in and the pixel count to rasterize into. Conflating them capped a machine rendered detail at whatever numeric range its data happened to use, and Star Wars was rendering at 320x330 because of it. The raster machines conflate the same two things, for the same reason, and the fix should look like the same fix.

Read the vector_field_size commit before designing this. Note in particular that enlarging the output alone does not work if something else is derived from the same number: for the vector machines xcenter moved with it and the picture shrank into the middle. Check what else reads display_size on a raster board before changing what it means.

title: Beam profile and scanlines, derived per machine
description:
The dominant visible effect, and the one with a real derivation behind it.

The beam is the same round spot the vector work models: 0.7 mm on a 19 inch tube. Sweeping it along a line and stepping down by the line pitch gives the scanline structure directly, with the gap falling out of pitch against spot rather than being dialled in. Machines whose pitch is finer than the spot get no gaps, which is a result rather than a special case.

Depends on the resolution split, since there is nowhere to draw this otherwise, and on the prediction check, which decides whether it is per machine or uniform.

The profile itself already exists in a tested form: machines/src/atari_dvg.rs works out a Gaussian from the tube, floors sigma where the output grid cannot represent it (the ripple from sampling a Gaussian on a unit grid is about 2*exp(-2*pi^2*sigma^2), which is brightness varying with position), and normalises so a full-intensity line peaks at full white. Reuse the reasoning, and probably the constants, rather than reinventing either.

title: Halation for the raster machines
description:
A raster tube halates exactly as a vector one does, and the width is already derived: light past the critical angle cannot leave the faceplate, reflects, crosses the glass again and re-emerges at 2*t*tan(asin(1/n)), about 19 mm on an 11 mm faceplate at n = 1.54, or 5 percent of the tube long axis. halation_sigma_units() in phosphor_core::device::dvg computes it and needs no changes.

Composite it as light taken from the core rather than added to it, and raise the brightness gain to hold the peak, exactly as the vector path does. Note that those two facts mean total emitted light rises with the halation fraction: peak-at-full-white and total-light-conserved cannot both hold while the fraction varies, and a test asserting both shipped and had to be corrected.

GPU only, on measured evidence. On the CPU path a full-frame blur measured four to five times the beam sweep itself: Asteroids went from 2.7 to 13.5 ms per frame against 0.4 ms to emulate the machine. Every raster machine would pay that on every frame.

The fraction that halates is the one figure with no derivation behind it and is already on the display panel at 0.07, set by eye. Do not add a second underived figure here.

title: Is the shadow mask visible at arcade resolutions?
description:
A measurement that may well close as no, and is worth doing before anyone writes a mask shader.

Mask pitch on a 19 inch tube is about 0.6 mm. Pac-Man 288 pixels across a 360 mm axis makes one emulated pixel 1.25 mm, so a pixel spans about two mask triads. The visible RGB stripe look that CRT shaders usually reproduce comes from PC monitors at 640x480 and above, where a pixel is roughly one triad. Below the pixel grid the mask cannot produce stripes; it can only soften and add a faint luminance texture.

So the question is not how to render a mask, it is whether there is anything to render. Work out the triads per emulated pixel for the widest and narrowest raster machines in the registry, and decide from the numbers.

If the answer is no, close this and say so in the epic, because a future reader will otherwise assume it was forgotten rather than answered. If the answer is yes for the high-resolution boards only, it belongs behind the same per-machine derivation the scanlines use.

title: Raster knobs on the display panel
description:
The panel, the persistence and the resolution chain already exist: core::display::DisplaySettings carries brightness, focus and halation, resolves measured then config.toml then the game entry in state.toml diff-only, and draws at Shift+backtick. Its module doc already says raster-only knobs belong there beside the tube ones rather than in a parallel set.

So this is mostly a question of which knobs are worth having, and the answer should fall out of the earlier stages rather than being decided up front. Scanline depth is the obvious candidate if stage 2 shows it varies usefully; a mask knob only exists if the mask measurement says yes.

Each knob is documented as a deviation from what was measured, and 1.0 means the figure the tube gives rather than the middle of a slider. Do not add a preset that preserves the pre-effect look: the same idea was proposed for the vector work as a "flat" preset and dropped, because it would have preserved a defect rather than a baseline.

title: Shrink the rasterizer accumulator: f32 to fixed point
description:
The per-pixel work in the CPU rasterizer looks arithmetic-bound and is not. Shrinking the working set is the first lever, ahead of anything clever.

THE EVIDENCE, from optimising the vector rasterizer. Two changes that should have been large if the loops were ALU-bound were not:

  first cut                                          4.934 ms/frame (tempest)
  window each row to the segment stadium             1.509   (algorithmic)
  replace about 2.2M exp() calls with a lookup table 1.320   (-0.19)
  reuse the accumulator instead of a 4 MB alloc      1.362   (noise, no gain)

Removing 2.2 million transcendental calls bought 0.19 ms and removing a per-frame 4 MB allocation bought nothing measurable. That is the signature of waiting on memory rather than on the ALU.

The sizes agree. Asteroids accumulator is 1024 x 1024 x 3 f32 = 12.6 MB, and a frame clears it, sweeps into part of it, then reads all of it to convert: roughly 25 to 38 MB of traffic per frame, far past any cache.

CAVEAT TO CHECK FIRST. Memory-bound is inferred from those two measurements and from the buffer size, not from a profiler. Confirm it before building on it; if it is wrong, this issue and its two siblings are wrong together.

THE CHANGE. 8.8 fixed point in u16 halves the traffic. Do NOT go to u8: f32 was chosen deliberately because summing 8-bit steps loses every contribution under half a level, which is most of the beam skirt and all of a dim vector. 8.8 keeps the sub-level precision at half the bandwidth, which is the point.

Watch the existing tests, which pin real quantities and will notice a precision regression: a full-intensity vector peaks at full white, equal-length segments emit equal light at any angle, splitting a vector conserves its light, and halation puts light beyond the core reach without creating any. If one of those starts failing, the format is too narrow.

MAY BE MOOT. If fork 1 on the parent resolves as "the GPU does the effects and screenshots do not have to match", the CPU path stays cheap and none of this is needed. Read that decision before starting.

title: Fuse the sweep and the convert into one traversal
description:
The CPU rasterizer walks the accumulator more than once per frame: it clears it, sweeps geometry into it, then reads all of it again to quantise into the output buffer. On Asteroids that is an extra full read of 12.6 MB every frame for no reason other than how the passes are arranged.

Fusing the sweep and the convert removes one whole traversal. The dirty-row range already tracked by the sweep is most of the bookkeeping needed to know what has to be converted.

Same evidence and the same caveat as the accumulator-width issue: the loops look arithmetic-bound and are not, and that is inferred from measurements rather than from a profiler. Confirm before building.

Order matters. This and the accumulator width should land before any SIMD work, because both of them shrink and linearise the loops that SIMD would then be applied to. Doing SIMD first optimises code that is about to be replaced.

Halation complicates it: the composite reads a reduced-resolution field with per-column bilinear taps, so it cannot simply ride along with the sweep. Fuse what can be fused and say plainly what could not, rather than forcing the whole chain into one pass.

MAY BE MOOT. See the same note on the accumulator-width issue: if the GPU owns the effects, the CPU path does not need this.

title: SIMD the per-pixel loops, after the traversal work
description:
Explicit vectorisation of the rasterizer per-pixel loops. Deliberately last of the three performance issues, and possibly not worth doing at all.

WHY IT IS NOT FIRST. The loops look arithmetic-bound and are not: removing 2.2 million exp() calls from the vector rasterizer bought 0.19 ms, and removing a 4 MB per-frame allocation bought nothing measurable. SSE2 widens the ALU, which is not the constraint. Shrinking the accumulator and fusing the traversals address the actual limit, and they also linearise the loops that vectorisation needs.

THE STRUCTURAL BLOCKER. The halation composite inner loop is a gather: four samples of the reduced field at column-dependent offsets per output pixel. SSE2 cannot load those contiguously, and AVX2 gather is slow enough to be a wash. Making the upsample separable (a vertical blend into a row buffer, then a horizontal pass along it) turns the reads linear, which is the precondition for vectorising rather than an alternative to it. That restructuring is the real work; the intrinsics are the easy part afterwards.

PORTABILITY, which is a real cost here. aarch64-apple-darwin is a supported target: .cargo/config.toml carries a Homebrew SDL2 path for it. SSE2 and SSE3 do not exist there, so explicit intrinsics need a NEON path beside them, and std::simd is nightly while the flake pins stable. Either take a portable-SIMD dependency or accept two implementations and the drift between them. Decide that before writing intrinsics, not after.

Also worth checking before writing anything: how much LLVM already does. x86-64 mandates SSE2, and the simple contiguous loops (the clear, the quantise) may well be vectorised already, in which case the only gains left are in the loops that are not, which are exactly the gather-shaped ones above.

MAY BE MOOT, twice over: if the GPU owns the effects the CPU path does not need to be fast, and if the two issues above land the remaining headroom may not be worth a portability problem. Measure before and after, on the largest raster machine, with --machine passed explicitly.

title: Congo Bongo: migrate to declarative ROT90 orientation
close_reason: Congo Bongo board emits native 256x224 RGB and declares Orientation::ROT90 (forwarded via board-delegation macro); frontend rotates centrally. TIMING reports native dims.

title: Concrete bus dispatch: Atari System 1 and Gottlieb System 80
description:
Convert Marble Madness and Road Runner (M68000, the bus_split! 'u32 word' arm and impl_board_delegation's bus_addr option) and Q*bert (I8088 + M6502, the 'u32' arm), per docs/designs/concrete-bus-dispatch.md. Blocked by the generic Cpu::reset task.

Nothing about the conversion is width-specific: the bus_split! arms exist only to name the trait object's type parameters and disappear with it. Marble is the slowest board in the bench set, so measure it carefully.
close_reason:
Done in 926a5af (marble + roadrunner on Atari System 1; qbert on Gottlieb System 80).

Numbers (phosphor-bench, release, 400f x 5 reps, best of 6 alternating runs, idle host):
  roadrunner 1.634 -> 1.387 ms/f  -15.1%
  marble     2.169 -> 1.902       -12.3%
  qbert      2.797 -> 2.777        -0.7%

Q*bert is the one board in the whole rollout that gained essentially nothing, and the cause is specific: its ~2.8 ms/frame is dominated by the Gottlieb sound board, which runs a second 6502 at 894 kHz plus Votrax SC-01 speech through its OWN bus_split! inside GottliebSoundBoard::tick. The main 8088 bus was never where Q*bert's time went. Filed as 61aj with the measurement.

Shapes: Atari System 1 kept the board and gave each game a view (Marble's trackball counters, Road Runner's joystick ADC), with the helpers that read them moving onto the views. Gottlieb's board became the bus outright, Q*bert being its only machine.

Both wide bus_split! arms are now unreferenced, and impl_board_delegation!'s bus_addr / 'bus_addr: u32 word' options are unused by any machine -- both get deleted with bus_split! itself in 642d. The design doc's prediction held again: nothing in either conversion was width-specific.

Also inverted the Atari System 1 frame loop (VBLANK IRQ4 + the motion-object scanline IRQ3 are the per-scanline work); Gottlieb needed no inversion, its only frame-position test being the end-of-frame render.

One test caught a real mistake in my rewrite: Road Runner's check_interrupts sets the IRQ2 line from the ADC before delegating to the board, so routing the test at the board directly reported irq_level 0. It goes through the view, like the CPU does.

Golden frames unchanged for all pinned machines; machine, harness and ROM-gated suites pass; clippy and fmt clean.

19 files still reference bus_split!, all in the 642d (standalone machines) bucket.

title: Williams machines never leave FACTORY SETTINGS RESTORED on a cold boot
description:
Captured while pinning golden frames (phosphor-emulator-frame-regression-w1pi.2). Booted from reset with no NVRAM, joust, robotron and sinistar print the CMOS-init message and stay on it: joust still shows 'FACTORY SETTINGS RESTORED' at 10000 frames (~166 emulated seconds). On hardware the message clears after a few seconds and the game drops into attract mode.

Loading a factory NVRAM works around it completely — with a dumped 1 KB CMOS image, joust reaches its title screen by frame 2400, robotron by 2400 and sinistar by 1800 — so the boards, blitter, palette and sound are fine. What is stuck is whatever the CMOS-init path waits on before continuing: a timer, an operator-switch read, or the post-init warm-start branch.

boot_check_test.rs does not catch it because the message itself is drawn pixels, which satisfies 'the machine drew something'.

Until it is fixed the three golden frames use committed NVRAM fixtures (harness/tests/golden/nvram/*.nv); once the cold boot reaches attract on its own, those entries can drop the fixture and be recaptured.
close_reason: Not a bug: this is the real board's behaviour. With blank battery RAM the Williams boards factory-reset, print FACTORY SETTINGS RESTORED and hold there until an operator presses the reset button. The golden frames keep their committed CMOS fixtures (harness/tests/golden/nvram/*.nv) permanently, not as a workaround; docs/designs/frame-regression.md, the nvram README, frames.toml and golden_frame_test.rs updated to say so.

title: Donkey Kong stomp: rebuild from the board — its low end is a counter dividing the noise, not a filter
description:
Stomp is the last Donkey Kong voice still built from fitted values rather than
from the board, and reading the netlist after the jump rebuild shows it is the
same chain jump is, with a different source.

WHAT THE BOARD DOES:
  24-bit LFSR clocked at 4 kHz (CLOCK_2VF = 61.44 MHz / 5 / 4 / 16 / 12 / 2)
    -> LS161 counter, clocked on the noise's rising edges, counting 0..7
    -> output is (count > 3) * 5 V, i.e. bit 3 — a divide-by-8, 50 % duty
    -> ~26 ms conditioned trigger (10 k + 10 k into 1 uF), same as jump's
    -> envelope lid: 3.3 uF, dip through 10 k (33 ms), recover through 110 k
       (363 ms) — jump's structure with jump's shape
    -> diode mixer against the divided noise, drops 0.4 V and 0.8 V
    -> emitter follower: 750 ohm into 1 uF, loaded by 4.7k || (2k + 5.1k) = 2.83k
    -> divider 5.1/7.1 into the board mixer

Every stage after the source is IDENTICAL IN FORM to jump's, and three of them
are identical in value. The primitives all exist now (rc_integrate,
diode_mixer_drops, rc_envelope, DkongEdgePulse), so this is mostly assembly.

WHAT WE DO INSTEAD: a one-shot LFSR burst with a fitted exponential envelope
(STOMP_TAU) into a fitted one-pole low-pass (STOMP_LP_HZ = 175) and a fitted
gain. None of the envelope, the mixer or the follower is present.

THE KEY FINDING. Stomp's low frequency comes from the COUNTER, not from a
filter. Dividing the noise's rising edges by 8 lands the rumble near 125 Hz on
its own — which is exactly the reference's measured centroid. STOMP_LP_HZ is a
filter corner standing in for that divider: a fitted scalar substituting for a
missing mechanism, the specific failure docs/designs/discrete-sound-fidelity.md
warns about under 'What the first board taught'.

It also explains the decay, which has never fit. The source comment already
says 'the reference falls faster than one pole allows, which points at a second
filter stage on the board'. There is no second filter — the shape is not coming
from a pole at all. Currently T20 measures 0.279 s against the reference's
0.545, the largest per-voice gap left.

WHAT IS MISSING FROM THE FRAMEWORK: an edge-clocked modulo-N counter. MAME has
DISCRETE_COUNTER and uses it widely, so this is a shared primitive rather than a
dkong custom component. It needs a clock source, a modulus, and an edge sense.

EXPECT the gain and any remaining shaping constants to be re-derived once the
structure is right, exactly as jump's were — and expect them to move a lot,
because they are currently absorbing the missing stages.
close_reason:
Done. Stomp is rebuilt from the board: 24-bit shift register at 4 kHz into a counter dividing its edges by eight, then jump's chain — the same ~28 ms conditioned trigger, a diode-mixed lid on 3.3 uF, the same emitter follower and divider. The divided source measures 124.7 Hz against the board's 125.0.

The decay was the thing that had never fit: 49 % short at T20 and 58 % long at T40, now 5 % and 3 % long. As predicted here, there was no 'second filter stage' — the decay was never a filter's.

One measurement bug caught on the way: the first pass ran at exactly twice the reference's pitch, and simulating both shift registers showed each produced 0.2500 rising edges per clock. The arithmetic was right and CLOCK_2VF was wrong — six divisions of the master, not five.

Remaining: 27 % of the energy sits in 150-400 Hz against the board's 10 %, tracked in …-0fbi. Two spin-offs filed: …-zg4w (lfsr_noise's tap numbering assumes the wrong shift direction) and the edge_divider primitive, which landed with this.

title: M6809: indexed indirect puts its don't-care cycles after the pointer read
description:
Found while doing phosphor-emulator-vy6l. Addresses are right, ORDER is not.

For an indirect indexed postbyte, the hardware forms the base address, spends
that mode's don't-care cycles, THEN reads the two pointer bytes, THEN spends one
final /VMA cycle:

    [base don't-cares]  ptr_hi  ptr_lo  $FFFF

`indexed_resolve` does it the other way round — states 10/11 read the pointer
first, and the whole don't-care countdown (state 20, plus the caller's base
don't-care) runs afterwards:

    ptr_hi  ptr_lo  [all don't-cares]

Cycle counts are identical, and every don't-care presents the address it should,
so nothing in cross-validation or the single-step vectors notices. What differs
is what an address-snooping device sees *between* the pointer read and the
don't-cares — and that ordering is exactly the kind of thing a slapstic decides
on. The chips on Atari System 1 (Marble Madness 103, Road Runner 108) are the
exposure; neither is verified against a reference here.

The fix is to split `indexed_resolve` so the base don't-cares are emitted before
the state-10 transition and exactly one /VMA remains after state 11. That also
lets the caller's base don't-care cycle (state 40 in every indexed op) fold back
into the resolver, which is where it belongs.

No known game depends on it, hence P3 — but it is a real difference from the
hardware, not a modelling choice.
close_reason: indexed_resolve now spends each mode's base don't-cares before the indirect pointer read, with exactly one trailing /VMA after it, and the caller's base don't-care (state 39/40 in every indexed op) folds back into the resolver. Cycle counts unchanged — rederived from the datasheet Table 2 '+' figures for all 24 modes, and confirmed by replaying the 266,000 single-step vectors: 10,549 traces reorder, none differ in registers, memory, cycle count, or read/write direction. Ordering pinned by 8 new cases in m6809_dont_care_cycle_test.rs. Commits a07ea73, 0804ee4.

title: Mario Bros: no sound — 8049 sound engine never enables timer/interrupts
description:
Mario Bros (mariobros) graphics, inputs, DMA, NVRAM all work, but there is no sound; the DAC path itself is dead (not just the deferred discrete circuit).

Findings (verified with the real mariog ROM):
- The 8049 sound CPU runs but is stuck in its sample-playback loop at PC 0x900-0x9FF, continuously writing DAC=0x00. Audio is a constant -32768 (3 distinct values over 2.2M samples).
- It NEVER enables timer/counter/TCNTI/interrupt across a full run (EVER all 0), though the sound ROM has STRT T / EN TCNTI / EN I at 0x062/0x070/0x379/0x04d.
- The main Z80 DOES request sounds (47 nonzero cmd writes to 0x7e00, 102 nonzero triggers to 0x7f00-0x7f07), so the Mario-side wiring is fine; the 8049 just never processes them (its timer-interrupt dispatch never starts).
- 8049 boot immediately CALLs ROM bank 1 (0x100) via SEL MB/DBF. Suspect a bug in the shared phosphor-core I8035 8049-mode execution: DBF/SEL-MBx (A11) addressing on CALL/JMP, interrupt vectoring (ext 0x003 / timer 0x007), or the P2/tune_r MOVX bank-select. I8035 changes need cross-validation.
- Still deferred regardless: discrete walk/skid analog sound (nl_mario.cpp) + the 0x7f07 skid trigger.

Repro: run mariobros, coin+start into gameplay; DAC stays 0x00.
close_reason: Fixed in cebacf6. Root cause: the M58715 sound CPU has an undumped internal-ROM bootstrap that runs before the external program; per MAME's audiocpu trace it does ANL P2,#$DF; SEL MB0; CALL $101, entering the external program at 0x101 (STRT T). We started at external 0x000, where the STRT T at 0x101 is swallowed as the JC operand at 0x100, so the sound engine's duration timer never started and every effect hung in its playback loop with a silent DAC. MarioBrosSystem::reset now replicates the bootstrap (P2=0xDF, MB0, PC=0x101). DAC output went from 3 distinct values to 20k+ across the full range — digitized SFX now play. Verified by diffing our 8049 PC trace against MAME -debugscript. Discrete walk/skid analog sound remains deferred (separate).

title: Gottlieb sound board: the sound 6502 still dispatches through bus_split!
description:
GottliebSoundBoard::tick (machines/src/gottlieb.rs:~212) still runs its M6502 through 'bus_split!(self, bus => ...)' -- the sound board is a self-contained bus (RIOT + DAC + Votrax SC-01 + 8KB ROM) whose CPU sits inside it, exactly the shape the rollout has been removing one level up.

Why it matters, measured: converting Q*bert's *main* 8088 bus (926a5af) moved its frame time by 0.7%, against 12-15% for the Atari System 1 boards in the same commit. Q*bert's emulation time is ~2.8 ms/frame and almost all of it is the sound board -- a second 6502 at 894 kHz plus Votrax speech synthesis, all dispatching through this remaining trait object. This is where Q*bert's win actually is.

Shape: give GottliebBoard a 'sound_cpu: M6502' field (or a small SoundCpu wrapper), have GottliebSoundBoard keep only the devices, and pass the CPU into tick -- 'sound.tick(&mut sound_cpu)'. The board is the bus; no view needed, since nothing is interposed. Follow docs/designs/concrete-bus-dispatch.md.

Watch: the sound board is saved as part of GottliebBoard's state, so moving the CPU field changes save layout unless the CPU is written in the same position (it is currently written by GottliebSoundBoard::save_state -- check the order before/after).

Measure qbert with phosphor-bench before and after; golden frames should be unchanged, but the Votrax/RIOT NMI edge timing is worth a careful look since the sound CPU's cycle boundaries are what drive it.
close_reason:
Done in 7fb70c2 -- but the hypothesis that motivated this issue was WRONG, and that is the main finding.

Measured (phosphor-bench, release, 400f x 5 reps, best of 6 alternating runs, idle host):
  qbert 2.780 -> 2.736 ms/f  -1.6%

This issue predicted the sound board was 'where Q*bert's win actually is', reasoning from the fact that its frame is dominated by sound-board work. That reasoning conflated 'the sound board dominates the frame' with 'the sound board's bus dispatch dominates the frame'. It does not. With BOTH CPUs now dispatching concretely, Q*bert has moved 2.3% in total across the two conversions, against 12-27% on boards where dispatch genuinely dominated.

So Q*bert's ~2.7 ms/frame is device simulation, not bus dispatch. The remaining candidates are the Votrax SC-01 speech synthesis (clocked ~950 kHz, doing filter work per tick) and the I8088 core itself, which executes a whole instruction per execute_cycle call. Apportioning that needs a profile rather than another guess, and it is not this epic's business -- I have not filed a follow-up, because filing one would repeat the mistake of guessing where the time goes.

The change stands on its own terms: the sound 6502 moved out of GottliebSoundBoard onto GottliebBoard, the board takes it as a separate borrow in tick(), and the last bus_split! in gottlieb.rs is gone. reset_sound resets the devices then the CPU against them (the 6502 fetches its reset vector through that bus). Save-state layout preserved -- the board writes the sound CPU immediately before the rest of the sound board, the order the sound board used when it owned it.

Golden frames unchanged; machine, harness and ROM-gated suites pass; clippy and fmt clean.

title: The two picture assertions, landed red as W3's acceptance test
description:
The two assertions that need the framebuffer, landed RED, as the acceptance test
W3 does not currently have.

READ THIS BEFORE DECIDING IT IS BROKEN. Road Runner is one of the nine
render-once machines in docs/designs/raster-sampling-fidelity.md: the compositor
runs at the frame boundary from whole-frame state. So a mid-frame palette write
affects the entire picture and a mid-frame playfield write shows up everywhere at
once. These two assertions therefore FAIL on landing and keep failing until W3
(phosphor-emulator-raster-sampling-6kae.3) converts the board to sample video
state at the rate the hardware samples it.

That is the point. W1, W2 and W3 have no acceptance test today beyond "golden
frames unchanged", which cannot tell a timing fix from an attract-loop shift.
These are that test, written in advance, in the machine's own instruction stream.

T6 - THE PALETTE SPLIT. Fill the playfield with one pen, set the palette entry to
one colour, and at a known scanline (placed by a motion-object timer entry, not
by counting cycles) write a different colour to that entry at B00000. On hardware
the rows above the write keep the old colour and the rows below take the new one.
Assert: a band of the old colour, a band of the new one, exactly one transition,
and the transition within a row or two of the line the interrupt named.

T7 - THE BEAM HAS ALREADY PASSED. The Joust bug class, restated for a tilemap.
At a known mid-frame line, write two playfield cells: one well above the beam and
one well below it. In the frame of the write, only the row below should change;
in the next frame, both. Get the render order wrong in either direction and one
of the two captures is wrong, which is what makes this discriminate rather than
merely observe.

HOW TO LAND SOMETHING RED WITHOUT IT ROTTING. A failing test that sits red is
indistinguishable from a broken one after a month. Options, and this needs a
decision rather than a default:

  a) #[ignore] with a message naming 6kae.3, the way golden_frame_test names its
     blocker. Honest, and it is the pattern the tree already uses, but
     phosphor-emulator-gn5w is what happens when nobody removes one.
  b) Assert the CURRENT whole-frame behaviour with a comment saying it is wrong
     and what it should become. The suite stays green and the test flips to the
     right expectation as part of W3. Risks reading as an endorsement of the
     defect.
  c) A ratchet like harness/tests/audio/expectations.toml's [[known_defect]],
     where the wrong behaviour is recorded and fixing it FAILS until the entry is
     deleted. Most work, and the only option where progress cannot regress and
     the test cannot rot.

(c) is what this repository already reached for when it had nine known-bad audio
outputs, and the same argument applies. Decide before writing.

WHATEVER IS CHOSEN, SAY IT OUT LOUD in the commit and in the source. A
conformance assertion that fails for a known reason is a specification; one that
fails for an unknown reason is a bug; and one that was quietly deleted because it
was red is how a suite stops meaning anything.

ACCEPTANCE. Both assertions exist, both are demonstrated to discriminate (mutate
the renderer to the model they reject and watch them behave differently), and the
way they are held is documented and linked from 6kae.3 so W3 knows it has an
acceptance test waiting.
