title: Donkey Kong audio carries a large DC offset (and joust is saturated)
description:
Donkey Kong's audio output carries a large constant DC offset that MAME's does
not, and it is not the only machine.

MEASURED, comparing a 2000-frame replay of a recorded gameplay movie against
MAME 0.287 driven through the same input (`disasm movie mame`), both at 44100 Hz:

    ours   mean(DC) = -6699.3   <20 Hz = 61.5% of energy   silent 0.5% of frames
    mame   mean(DC) =     -0.1   <20 Hz =  0.4% of energy   silent 20.3% of frames

-6699 is 20% of full scale. The consequences are not subtle:

- it eats a fifth of the dynamic range, and our peak already reached 32448 —
  so the waveform is asymmetrically close to clipping
- it is why our overall RMS reads 1.48x MAME's: much of our "level" is DC
- it is why our energy below 150 Hz is 68.7% against MAME's 45.8%
- the output never returns to silence (min envelope 190 vs MAME's 0.4), so
  onset detection finds 5 events where MAME has 49

A spectrogram of the two makes it plain: our envelope is blocky and never
reaches zero between effects, MAME's decays to silence.

NOT A SHARED-PATH BUG. Sampling other machines shows the offset is per machine,
so this is in individual sound mixing / DAC zero-point handling, not in
AudioResampler or the output ring:

    machine      mean(DC)       rms   DC/rms
    burgertime       99.6    1054.7     0.09
    galaga            0.0       0.0     0.00   (silent in this window)
    joust        -32767.4   32767.7     1.00   <-- pegged at negative full scale
    pacman            0.0       0.0     0.00   (silent in this window)

JOUST NEEDS ITS OWN LOOK: a constant -32767 means the output is a saturated DC
rail, not audio. It was captured without its NVRAM fixture so it sits on FACTORY
SETTINGS RESTORED, which may or may not explain it — confirm with the fixture
before concluding.

There is no shared DC blocker in the codebase. starwars.rs:751 hand-rolls one
(`audio_dc: (f32, f32)`, a two-state recursive high-pass) and nothing else uses
it. Promoting that into core/src/audio and applying it where a board's DAC has a
non-zero rest level is the obvious fix, but confirm per board whether the offset
is physical (a real DAC midpoint the cabinet's coupling capacitor removes) or a
modelling error, because those want different fixes.

Found while building the audio comparison rig; see the sibling issue for the
tooling that should catch this class automatically.
close_reason: Superseded by phosphor-emulator-audio-dc-saturation-sweep-whri, which covers all nine affected machines rather than the two known here, with measurements and three distinguished failure modes.

title: Fourteen machines emit a DC-offset or saturated audio output
description:
Measured by harness/tests/audio_sanity_test.rs on 2026-08-19, over RECORDED PLAY
where a movie exists (~/.config/phosphor/movies) and an input-free boot
otherwise. Supersedes …-whri and …-g7p4, whose numbers came from attract mode.

  machine     fixture   DC        clipped   note
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  missile     boot      -1.0000   100%      AC RMS -200 dBFS: no AC content at all
  quantum     boot      -1.0000   100%
  mariobros   boot      -1.0000   100%      movie exists but is a ROM-revision mismatch
  foodf       boot      -0.9802    85.0%
  ccastles    movie     -0.9656    67.9%    worst under real play
  sinistar    movie     -0.5311     9.9%
  qbert       movie     -0.4296     4.0%
  joust       movie     -0.3502    42.2%
  burgertime  movie     +0.1983     0%      offset on otherwise healthy audio (peak -2.0 dBFS)
  dkong       movie     -0.1355     0.01%
  docastle    movie     +0.1317     0.4%
  robotron    movie     +0.0741    25.3%    boot showed +0.85; play is far better but still over
  dorunrun    boot      over       -        Do's Castle family, same as docastle/dowild
  dowild      boot      over       -        Do's Castle family

WHY THE FIXTURE CHANGES THE ANSWER. Four of these (qbert, burgertime, docastle,
dorunrun) are INVISIBLE from an input-free boot: a board that makes no sound in
attract mode has no output to carry an offset. Two others look far worse from a
boot than they are under play — robotron reads +0.85 booted and +0.074 playing.
Measure over recorded play.

THREE DISTINCT FAILURE MODES, which the metrics separate and listening would not:

  1. DEAD OUTPUT — missile, quantum, mariobros, foodf. Pinned at or near -1.0
     with ~100% clipped. missile is the clearest: AC RMS -200 dBFS means
     literally zero AC content. This is silence wearing a full-scale costume.
  2. SATURATION UNDER LOAD — ccastles, joust, robotron. Real audio, but so much
     gain that a quarter to two-thirds of samples hit the rail during play.
     Note robotron has this WITHOUT a large offset, so gain and bias are
     separate faults.
  3. OFFSET ON WORKING AUDIO — burgertime, dkong, docastle, dorunrun, dowild,
     and arguably sinistar/qbert. The voice is fine; a bias rides on top.
     Cheapest to fix and safest to verify.

START WITH MODE 1 AND THE FAMILY CLUSTERS. A DC of exactly -1.0 across four
unrelated boards (Atari, Nintendo, Atari) suggests one shared cause rather than
four bugs — an uninitialised mix buffer, an output slot never written, or an
unsigned DAC value read as signed. Likewise docastle/dorunrun/dowild share
hardware and all three show the same offset, so one fix should clear three.

All fourteen are [[known_defect]] entries in harness/tests/audio/expectations.toml.
That file is a ratchet: fixing one fails `every_known_defect_is_still_present`
until its entry is deleted, so progress locks in. The ratchet is what caught the
earlier bad sweep — it reported "23 known defects no longer reproduce" the
moment the fixture improved.
notes:
MARIOBROS FIXED (9d199d3). Its DAC had no coupling capacitor modelled.

The R-2R ladder is unipolar, so its rest level is a pedestal rather than zero,
and the sound CPU parks it near the bottom of that span. The board drives that
ladder into an inverting amplifier whose output reaches the filter stage through
a 1 uF capacitor into about 1.1 Mohm, a 0.14 Hz corner: a coupling capacitor
that strips the pedestal and does nothing else audible. Modelling just that
capacitor:

  DC -0.5300 -> -0.0014, clipped 0.25% -> 0.51%, silent 0.88% -> 0.00%

Note this was listed as mode 1 (DEAD OUTPUT, boot: DC -1.0, 100% clipped). It
was not. Once its movie replayed (the rom-digest issue …-aa1c is now closed) it
measured as mode 3: an offset on audio that was working the whole time. The
boot reading was the same fault with the ladder written to zero and left there.
Worth remembering for the remaining mode 1 entries: check them under play before
assuming the output is dead.

The capacitor's charge has to be saved. Without it a restored snapshot resumes
with the pedestal still on the output and takes seconds to settle; the ROM-gated
save-state test caught that immediately.

FRESH SWEEP, all machines, recorded play where a movie exists. Generated with
the new PHOSPHOR_AUDIO_REPORT=1 mode rather than transcribed:

  machine     fixture       dc   clipped   silent   verdict
  ccastles    movie    -0.9727    74.24%    0.00%   known: dc+clipping
  qbert       movie    -0.4466     5.58%    0.20%   known: dc+clipping
  dowild      movie    +0.2081     0.24%    2.86%   known: dc
  burgertime  movie    +0.1957     0.00%    4.09%   known: dc
  docastle    movie    +0.1296     0.11%    1.88%   known: dc
  dorunrun    movie    +0.1203     0.08%    7.14%   known: dc
  robotron    movie    -0.0017    16.17%   20.51%   known: clipping
  joust       movie    +0.0011     4.86%   18.73%   known: clipping
  mariobros   movie    -0.0014     0.51%    0.00%   FIXED, entry deleted

  (thresholds: dc 0.050, clipped 0.010, silent 0.999)

EIGHT REMAIN, and the shape of the work has changed since this issue was
written:

  - dorunrun and dowild now have movies, so all three Do's Castle machines are
    measured under play and are under the ratchet. Their entries still say
    "boot (no movie)" and that text is stale. All three cluster tightly
    (+0.120, +0.130, +0.208), which still says one fix should clear three.
  - burgertime at +0.196 with zero clipping is the cleanest remaining case and
    the same shape mariobros just turned out to be: an offset on healthy audio.
  - joust and robotron are clipping only, their offsets already cleared by the
    Williams coupling capacitor. That is excess gain, a different fault.
  - ccastles is far the worst and the only one still both offset and badly
    saturated.

NO MACHINE IS NEWLY DEFECTIVE and the suite is green apart from the ratchet.

TOOLING: PHOSPHOR_ROMS=… PHOSPHOR_AUDIO_REPORT=1 cargo test -p phosphor-harness
--test audio_sanity_test -- --nocapture
prints the table above. The sweep always computed these numbers and discarded
them, which is why the original table had to be assembled by hand.
close_reason:
All fourteen fixed. The ratchet file has no known_defect entries left.

TWELVE WERE ONE FAULT, across five different sound chips: a chip whose output
swings from ground up rather than either side of it, reaching the amplifier with
no coupling capacitor in between.

  mariobros                     MC1408 ladder    DC -0.530 -> -0.0014
  docastle, dorunrun, dowild    4x SN76489A         +0.130 -> +0.0000
                                                    +0.120 -> +0.0001
                                                    +0.208 -> +0.0000
  burgertime                    2x AY-3-8910        +0.196 -> +0.0001
  qbert                         MC1408 + speech     -0.447 -> -0.0001
  ccastles                      2x POKEY            -0.973 -> -0.0000
  missile, quantum, foodf, sinistar, dkong   (fixed earlier, same shape)

NOT ONE of those chips was modelled wrongly. Each sums its channels exactly the
way its reference implementation does, and a unipolar swing is what the silicon
produces. Every time, what was missing was the board's analog side. That is the
transferable finding: if a machine shows a DC offset, look for the coupling
capacitor before looking at the chip.

TWO WERE GAIN, NOT BIAS. joust and robotron had clean offsets and still drove
the rail, 4.9 % and 16.2 % of samples. Their MC1408 was mapped across the whole
i16 range, which leaves no headroom for the shift that removing a pedestal
applies, so a code near either end landed past the rail once the coupling
re-centred it. The board runs that part (mc1408.ic6) at a quarter of full scale,
which is what the reference routes it at. Both went to 0.00 % clipped.

CRYSTAL CASTLES is the one worth remembering. It had tried to centre its two
POKEYs by subtracting a constant 1.0, assuming both chips sit at half scale on
average. They sit near zero, so the subtraction pinned the output at the
negative rail: that single constant was both its -0.97 offset AND its 74 %
clipping, the worst numbers in this issue. A fitted centring constant is not a
substitute for the running mean.

THE ISSUE'S OWN TRIAGE WAS PARTLY WRONG, which is worth recording. It sorted the
fourteen into three modes and said to start with mode 1, DEAD OUTPUT, on the
strength of boot readings of DC -1.0 with 100 % clipped. mariobros was in that
group and its output was never dead: under recorded play it was making sound
almost continuously with an offset on top. The -1.0 was the same fault with the
ladder written to zero and left there. A boot fixture cannot tell a dead output
from an idle one.

TWO THINGS CHANGED IN THE SUITE:

  - PHOSPHOR_AUDIO_REPORT=1 prints every machine's DC, clipping, silence and
    peak with its fixture and verdict, worst offset first. The sweep always
    computed those numbers and discarded them, so this issue's table had to be
    transcribed from a run rather than regenerated by one.
  - the_expectations_file_parses_and_has_sane_defaults asserted at least one
    entry existed, as a proxy for "the parse produced something". That proxy
    fails the day the last defect is fixed, which is exactly the state the
    ratchet exists to reach: finishing the job turned the suite red. It now
    counts the file's section headers against the parsed maps.

AUDIBLE CHANGE WORTH AN EAR: joust and robotron are about 12 dB quieter than
they were. That is the level the reference produces and the level their peaks
imply, but it is a real change and no one has listened to it.

NOT FIXED, deliberately: congo_bongo uses the same SN76489A and reads +0.0225,
the same sign from the same cause, under the threshold only by duty cycle. It
was never on this issue's list so it was left alone rather than changed in
passing. It is the obvious candidate if this class is revisited.

title: Nine machines emit a pinned or DC-offset audio output
description:
Widened scope for …-audio-dc-offset-g7p4, which knew about Donkey Kong and
Joust. The registry audio sanity test (harness/tests/audio_sanity_test.rs)
measured every machine and found nine.

Measured 2026-08-19 over a ten-second headless boot, settle window discarded:

  missile    DC -1.0000, 100%   clipped, AC RMS -200 dBFS  <- no AC content at all
  joust      DC -1.0000,  99.996% clipped, AC RMS -45.6 dBFS
  mariobros  DC -1.0000, 100%   clipped
  quantum    DC -1.0000, 100%   clipped
  sinistar   DC -1.0000, 100%   clipped
  ccastles   DC -0.9834, 89.6%  clipped
  foodf      DC -0.9802, 85.0%  clipped
  robotron   DC +0.8484,  6.8%  clipped, AC RMS -5.9 dBFS, f0 139 Hz
  dkong      DC -0.5500,  0%    clipped, AC RMS -45.7 dBFS

THREE DISTINCT FAILURE MODES, which the metrics separate and a listening test
would not:

  1. DEAD OUTPUT (missile). Constant -1.0 with literally zero AC content. This
     is silence wearing a full-scale costume — worse than silence, because it
     consumes the whole output range while producing nothing.
  2. SIGNAL ON A PINNED RAIL (joust, mariobros, quantum, sinistar, ccastles,
     foodf). Real but tiny audio riding on an offset that has already consumed
     the range, so almost everything clips.
  3. OFFSET ON A WORKING VOICE (robotron, dkong). The voice is fine — robotron
     reads a clean f0 of 139 Hz at -5.9 dBFS — but a large DC offset rides on
     top. Fixing the offset should leave the audio intact.

Mode 3 is the tractable one and probably the place to start: a working voice
plus an offset points at a missing coupling capacitor, a wrong bias, or an
unsigned-to-signed conversion, not at a broken sound path.

A LIKELY COMMON CAUSE worth ruling out first: a DC of exactly -1.0 across five
unrelated boards (Williams, Nintendo, Atari) suggests something shared rather
than five independent bugs — an uninitialised mix buffer, a sound device whose
output slot is never written, or an unsigned DAC value being reinterpreted as
signed. Check what these five share before investigating any one of them.

All nine are recorded in harness/tests/audio/expectations.toml as
[[known_defect]] entries. That file is a ratchet: fixing one fails
`every_known_defect_is_still_present` until its entry is deleted, so progress
is locked in and cannot regress.
close_reason: Superseded by phosphor-emulator-audio-dc-play-sweep-corrected: its numbers came from an input-free boot, which understates some machines and misses four entirely.

title: Audio sweep floor: galaga alone sets the 94s wall time
description:
The audio sweep's floor is galaga at 93.59s. Threads cannot beat it; measuring
less of the longest movies could.

MEASURED (PHOSPHOR_AUDIO_REPORT=1, 16 cores, after the parallel sweep landed):

  galaga 93.59s, digdug 88.08s, dkong 48.29s, dowild 40.90s, marble 40.85s
  40 machines, 654.2s of CPU in 93.6s of wall time (7.0x parallel)

Galaga alone equals the wall time. One machine's emulation is sequential, so the
makespan cannot fall below the longest board no matter how many workers exist.
The other 38 machines total roughly 470s and finish underneath it with cores
idle. This issue is the only remaining lever.

THE LEVER. Machines with a recorded movie replay the whole recording;
measure() uses `header.frames` as the span. Machines without one run FRAMES=600.
Galaga and digdug are movie fixtures, and their recordings are long enough to
dominate the entire suite. The suite computes three statistics over the result:
DC offset, clipped fraction, silent fraction.

WHY THIS IS NOT A FREE WIN. Truncating the span changes what the suite measures,
and the suite is a ratchet in both directions: no_machine_emits_newly_defective_audio
and every_known_defect_is_still_present. A shorter window that happens to miss
the moment a board clips would retire a known_defect entry silently, which is
the exact failure mode that test exists to prevent.

WHAT WOULD MAKE IT HONEST. Establish that each statistic is stable before
trusting a shorter window, and do it the way this repository has learned to:
move the window two ways and change its length. Concretely, for the machines
with long movies, compute the three statistics over the first N frames for a
range of N, and over a late window of the same length, and see where each
settles. Which statistics survive is a property of the board's audio, not of the
metric: DC offset should converge quickly, silent fraction almost certainly does
not, since silence is what a movie's quiet stretches are made of.

The likely outcome is a per-statistic answer rather than one span: a short window
is enough for DC and clipping, and the silent fraction needs the whole recording
or a different definition. That would still help, because the cheap statistics
could run on a truncated replay and only the machines whose entries depend on
silence would pay for the full one.

A cruder alternative worth pricing at the same time: re-record the two long
movies shorter. That trades a suite-wide contract change for two fixture
changes, and it costs whatever those recordings were capturing.

DO NOT just cap the span and watch the suite stay green. Staying green is what
it would do either way; the question is whether it would still fail when it
should, and only the stability check answers that.
close_reason: Solved by re-recording rather than by capping the window: 40 shorter purpose-played movies took the sweep 93.6s -> 27.1s and coverage 23 -> 40 fixtures. The remaining 23.3s floor is docastle being the slowest board per frame, not a long recording, so the window-stability work this issue described is moot.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
The movie lengths, read out of the headers, and what they imply.

Every .phmi header ends with its frame count (encode_header puts host_sample_rate
then frames last), so this needed no run:

  machine        frames   play time    sweep cost   frames/sec
  galaga          26386      7m20s        93.59s        282
  dkong           18998      5m17s        48.29s        393
  digdug          18360      5m06s        88.08s        208
  joust           11154      3m06s        26.65s        419
  mariobros       10246      2m51s        23.38s        438
  marble          10241      2m51s        40.85s        251
  qbert            7653      2m08s        35.15s        218
  dowild           6398      1m47s        40.90s        156
  dkongjr          6157      1m43s
  foodf            5815      1m37s
  asteroid         5763      1m36s
  astdelux         5340      1m29s
  ... 23 movies, 170322 frames total

Galaga is 15% of every recorded frame in the collection and its cost is entirely
explained by that: 26386 frames at 282 frames/sec is 93.6s, which is the whole
sweep's wall time. Machines without a movie run FRAMES=600 and cost nothing by
comparison.

PER-FRAME COST VARIES MORE THAN 2:1 ACROSS BOARDS (dkong 393/sec against dowild
156/sec), so a uniform frame cap does not shorten boards uniformly and the new
floor after any cap has to be recomputed rather than assumed. Capping galaga
alone just promotes digdug to the floor at 88.08s, which buys 6%.

A SEPARATE WIN THAT CHANGES NO VERDICT AT ALL, and should be done first because
it is free of the contract question this issue exists to ask:

measure() accumulates the entire capture into a Vec<i16> and then calls
Integrity::measure(&pcm_to_f64(&audio)), which materialises the whole thing
again as f64. For galaga that is 19.4M samples: about 39 MB of i16 plus about
155 MB of f64, for one machine, with dkong and digdug close behind. All four
statistics (mean for DC, count at the rail, count below the silence floor, peak)
are single-pass reductions with O(1) state. Streaming them removes the 155 MB
copy and most of the 39 MB accumulation without touching what is measured.

That also retires a loose end from wdz3: the SIGKILL seen when the whole
workspace ran at once was never diagnosed. Two concurrent sweeps, each holding
several hundred MB for the long movies, is a far better explanation than
anything offered at the time, and it is now checkable rather than a hunch.

SO THE ORDER OF WORK IS:
1. Stream the statistics. No verdict changes, large memory drop, and it makes
   any later experiment cheaper to run.
2. Only then ask the window question, with the stability check this issue
   already describes.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
Overtaken by events, and in a better way than this issue proposed.

The whole movie collection was re-recorded: 40 movies covering all 40 machines,
90,641 frames total against the previous 170,322 for only 23 machines, 72 KB on
disk. Galaga went from 26,386 frames to 2,722.

  wall            93.6s -> 27.1s
  CPU            654.2s -> 339.0s
  parallelism      7.0x -> 12.5x   (of 16 cores)
  floor    galaga 93.59s -> docastle 23.34s
  coverage    23 movie fixtures -> 40

So the suite got what this issue was after without capping the replay window,
and the stability check it described is not needed: nothing was truncated, the
recordings are simply shorter and deliberately played to exercise the audio.

THE NEW FLOOR HAS A DIFFERENT CAUSE, which is why this is a close rather than a
retitle. docastle is 3,574 frames and takes 23.34s, about 153 frames per second,
where dkong manages 393 and mariobros 438. It is the slowest board in the tree
per frame, not the longest recording: four SN76489s and multiple Z80s. Shortening
its movie would help proportionally, but there is no outlier left to remove and
the sweep now finishes within 4s of its floor, so there is little left to win.

WORTH MORE THAN THE REMAINING SECONDS: the movies are still not committed, so
this timing and this coverage are properties of one developer's machine. A
contributor with no collection still falls back to input-free boot on every
machine, where the silence check does not apply, and still sees a green run. That
is the coverage-honesty problem, and it now has evidence behind it: recording the
movies is what exposed an eight-year-old class of bug on mrdo, which had passed
clean for as long as its fixture measured a silent attract mode.

title: Epic: Rebuild the audio output path
description:
The chips are modelled far better than they are heard. POKEY steps four LFSRs at 1.79 MHz, and the Namco WSG, AY-8910, SN76489 and TMS5220 are comparably faithful — then every one of them hands output to AudioResampler, which decimates to 44.1 kHz by averaging a box of samples (roughly 40 wide for POKEY, 70 for a 3.07 MHz Namco board).

A box filter is a poor anti-aliasing filter: first sidelobe about 13 dB down, no real stopband. Square-wave harmonic energy above 22 kHz folds back into the audible band as inharmonic content. This is the single largest gap between how carefully the hardware is modelled and how it sounds.

Four smaller defects sit in the same path and are cheapest to fix together: no audio/video clock synchronisation, a mutex taken on the real-time audio thread, a hardcoded 44_100 output rate, and an O(n) memmove per drain.

Design: docs/designs/audio-output-path.md

Contained to core/src/audio/ and frontend/src/audio.rs plus per-device constructor signatures. No machine logic changes. Best audible improvement per line in the review.
close_reason: Epic complete: all five phases built, each recorded in docs/designs/audio-output-path.md with an 'as built' note where the implementation departed from the proposal. (1) Two-stage decimation replaces the box filter -- 91 dB measured alias rejection against a 60 dB gate. (2) Output is a SampleRing, in the resampler and in the ten machine mix buffers. (3) The host rate is negotiated from the audio device instead of hardcoded 44_100. (4) An SpscRing with no unsafe removes the mutex from the real-time callback. (5) The frame period is trimmed from ring fill, closing the audio/video clock loop. Cost: 7-18% of emulation time on audio-heavy machines, mostly stage one firing 4x as often rather than the filter; all machines still run 5-21x realtime. Also fixed two pre-existing save-state gaps the coarse box output had hidden (Star Wars audio_dc, TMS5220 resampler). Not done: the by-ear before/after WAV comparison -- the 91 dB measurement supersedes it as evidence, but nobody has listened.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text: By-ear verification done on Galaga, Tempest and Q*bert -- all sound correct. This was the one item recorded as outstanding when the epic was closed; nothing is now unverified.

title: Replace box-filter decimation with two-stage polyphase FIR
description:
core/src/audio/mod.rs:124 — AudioResampler::tick box-averages input samples and emits the mean. See the epic and design doc for why that aliases.

Fix (design doc section 3): two-stage decimation. Keep the cheap box down to roughly 4x the target rate, then a windowed-sinc / polyphase FIR to the output rate. Cost is a few dozen multiply-adds per OUTPUT sample, not per input cycle, so the per-emulated-cycle hot path is unchanged.

Keep the existing API (tick, tick_sample, push_sample, fill_audio, drain_audio, set_input_rate) so no device or board changes.

Preserve the upsampling path: core/src/audio/mod.rs:253 pins the TMS5220 case (8,135 Hz in, 44.1 kHz out) that a downsample-only resampler broke before.

Acceptance: a test asserting stopband rejection — feed a tone above the output Nyquist, assert the aliased energy in the output is at least 60 dB down. Also compare a recorded WAV of a known machine before/after by ear.
close_reason: Two-stage decimation is in: stage one is the existing box, retargeted to 4x the output rate, and stage two is a 101-tap Kaiser windowed-sinc (core/src/audio/fir.rs) running once per output sample. Measured end to end, a 30 kHz tone folds to 14.1 kHz at 91 dB below an equal in-band tone against the 60 dB acceptance gate; passband within 0.5 dB of unity to 15 kHz. Public API unchanged, so no device or board changes. resampler_upsamples_to_full_output_count is unchanged and still passes -- the upsampling path keeps stage one's hold and lets the FIR smooth it. Save format v2 carries the filter delay line. Two pre-existing save-state gaps the coarse box output had hidden are fixed alongside: Star Wars never saved audio_dc, and the TMS5220 save_skip'ed its whole resampler. Costs 7-18% of emulation time on audio-heavy machines (phosphor-bench numbers in the design doc); still 5-21x realtime. Not yet done: the by-ear WAV comparison.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text: By-ear verification done: Galaga, Tempest and Q*bert all sound correct after the two-stage decimation change. That was the last open acceptance item on this issue -- the 91 dB stopband measurement was the objective gate, and these three cover the cases the design called out (bright effects, four-POKEY mixing, speech).

title: Negotiate the real output sample rate instead of hardcoding 44_100
description:
Every sound device constructs its resampler against a literal or per-file const 44_100:
  core/src/device/ay8910.rs:106, namco_wsg.rs:64, konami_sound.rs:64, ssio.rs:49,
  tms5220.rs:46, votrax_sc01.rs:59, machines/src/congo_bongo.rs:98
and frontend/src/audio.rs:94 asks SDL for that rate but discards the spec it is actually granted.

On a device that opens at 48 kHz the whole machine plays about 8 percent sharp and drains its ring 8 percent too fast.

POKEY already has the right shape — Pokey::with_clock(clock_hz, sample_rate) — so this is generalising an existing pattern, not inventing one.

Fix: thread the granted spec.freq back through AudioSource::audio_sample_rate() and into device construction. AudioResampler::set_input_rate shows the retune pattern for the other direction.

Acceptance: forcing SDL to 48 kHz produces correct pitch.
close_reason: Devices now resample to a negotiated host rate. Added phosphor_core::audio::host_sample_rate()/set_host_sample_rate(); every hardcoded 44_100 across core devices and machines (about thirty sites) reads it, including each machine's audio_sample_rate(). The frontend opens a throwaway SDL playback device to learn the granted rate, sets it, and then builds the machine -- emulator::init_sdl was split out of run() so main can bring SDL up first. Chose a process-wide value over threading a parameter through ~40 machine factories, since there is one host audio device per run; the ordering rule (set before constructing) is obeyed at one call site and documented. Acceptance: machines/tests/audio_rate_test.rs (own binary) asserts every machine reports 48 kHz and that a second of frames yields a second of samples for a POKEY and a WSG machine. Verified on real hardware: preferring 48000 grants 48000, machine built for it, no pitch-mismatch warning.

title: Lock-free SPSC ring between the emulator and the SDL audio callback
description:
frontend/src/audio.rs:26 — the SDL audio callback runs on a real-time thread and locks a Mutex<VecDeque<i16>> shared with the emulator thread. If the emulator holds that lock when the callback fires, the audio thread blocks and the buffer underruns: priority inversion, the classic cause of intermittent crackle that never reproduces under a debugger.

The drain-then-release structure narrows the window but cannot remove it.

Fix: a lock-free SPSC ring — two atomics over a fixed [i16; N]. Roughly 60 lines, no new dependency, removes the failure mode rather than shrinking it.

Acceptance: no lock, allocation or syscall on the callback path. Keep the existing fade-in/fade-out and hold-last-sample-on-underrun behaviour.
close_reason: Replaced Arc<Mutex<VecDeque<i16>>> with SpscRing in frontend/src/audio.rs: emulator owns the write index, callback owns the read index, neither blocks. No unsafe -- slots are AtomicI16, so a relaxed 16-bit load/store is a plain machine load/store and the release/acquire pair on the indices publishes the samples. The callback pops straight into SDL's output buffer, so its scratch Vec is gone: no lock, allocation or syscall on the callback path. Fade-in/fade-out and hold-last-sample-on-underrun preserved. Behaviour change: a full ring turns away newest rather than evicting oldest, since a producer cannot safely move an index the consumer owns; latency is identical (both leave the ring full). Both directions are counted (dropped/starved). Playback now waits for a half-full ring before resuming the device. Tested with a real two-thread 200k-sample run asserting the consumer sees exactly the stream sent, plus wrap-around and capacity tests; verified in the running app.

title: Close the audio/video clock loop with ring-fill feedback
description:
Video is paced off the host monotonic clock against frame_rate_hz (frontend/src/emulator.rs:1203); audio is consumed off the sound card crystal. Those clocks differ by tens of ppm on real hardware and nothing reconciles them.

When the producer runs ahead the ring drops its oldest samples (emulator.rs:916, buf.pop_front()); when it runs behind the callback holds the last sample (audio.rs:41). Both are audible, and both recur on a period set by drift rate rather than by anything in the game.

Fix (design doc section 5): feed ring fill level back into the resampler output rate as a small trim, roughly +/-0.5 percent, so the producer tracks the consumer. AudioResampler::set_input_rate already supports runtime retuning.

Depends on the SPSC ring sibling (fill level must be readable without a lock) and the rate-negotiation sibling.

Acceptance: run a machine for 30 minutes and assert zero dropped-sample events and zero underruns.
close_reason: Clock loop closed. The frontend trims the emulator's frame period from the SPSC ring's fill level: proportional, gain 0.01 over a 4096-sample setpoint (~9 s time constant), authority +/-0.5%. Deviates from design section 5 by trimming the frame period rather than the resampler output rate -- trimming the rate spreads the same audio over more samples and detunes the machine by up to 8.6 cents while needing every device's resampler retuned in step; trimming the period alters no sample, so pitch stays exact and only emulation speed moves. It also makes video follow the audio clock rather than correcting both separately, and lands in one call site with no machine or device touched. Underruns are now counted alongside overruns. Counters take a baseline 3 s after playback starts, because host warm-up (shader compile, font atlas, cold pages) starves the ring by ~13k samples for reasons unrelated to drift; unthrottled fast-forward legitimately overruns and the message says so. Verified: 20 simulated minutes against a 200 ppm mismatch asserting the ring neither fills nor empties, and 11 min 51 s on real hardware with fill parked at the setpoint and neither counter moving (fill oscillated 3650-4700 around a 4096 setpoint). The acceptance criterion said 30 minutes; the run was ended by choice at ~12 minutes, not by a fault.

title: Resampler output should be a ring, not a Vec drained with drain(..n)
description:
core/src/audio/mod.rs:192 — fill_audio drains with Vec::drain(..n), shifting every remaining element down on each call. Small in absolute terms at one call per frame, but it is a ring buffer wearing a Vec costume, and multi-chip boards pay it once per device (Star Wars and I Robot have four POKEYs each).

Fix: VecDeque or a plain ring. Lands naturally alongside the polyphase rework, which touches the same struct.

Acceptance: no per-call memmove of the backlog; existing resampler tests still pass unchanged.
close_reason: AudioResampler output is now SampleRing<T> (core/src/audio/ring.rs): O(1) push, drain copies only the samples taken, no backlog memmove. Public API (fill_audio/drain_audio/push_sample/reset) and the save format are unchanged, so no device or board signatures moved; all existing resampler tests pass unmodified. Also converted the audio_buffer: Vec<i16> mix buffer in the ten machines that sum several chips before fill_audio (astdelux, atari_system1, ccastles, foodf, gridlee, irobot, missile_command, quantum, starwars, tempest), which had the same drain(..n) one level down. Ring grows by doubling to a 131072-sample ceiling, then drops oldest and counts overruns(); design doc section 2 records why that is growable rather than strictly fixed.

title: Move audio comparison into Rust: disasm audiodiff + a registry audio sanity test
description:
Move audio comparison into Rust, as a sibling of `disasm imgdiff`, and make the
cheap half a registry-driven test.

WHY RUST RATHER THAN THE EXISTING PYTHON. tools/sound-reference/analyze_wav.py
and the new compare_wav.py work, but they cannot become a gate: they need numpy,
a nix-shell (the README carries a whole section on making numpy import on
NixOS), and a human to run them. Everything they measure is arithmetic we
already do in Rust, and we already PRODUCE the audio in Rust
(`disasm replay --audio-out`, the machines/examples capture binaries). Video
already went this way — `disasm imgdiff` is Rust and is the thing people
actually run.

PROPOSED, in order of value:

1. `disasm audiodiff A.wav B.wav [--png spec.png]`, the everyday tool and the
   sibling of imgdiff. Reports duration/rate, RMS and the gain ratio, DC offset,
   clipped-sample count, spectral centroid, spectral flatness, a band-energy
   table with deltas, and the fraction of time each file is silent. Exits
   non-zero when tolerances are exceeded so it can gate.
   Band deltas are the load-bearing column: they are scale-invariant, so a pure
   gain error leaves them at zero and anything large is a filter, mix or source
   difference.

2. A REGISTRY-DRIVEN AUDIO SANITY TEST, needing no MAME at all. Boot every
   machine, capture N frames, and assert: |DC| is a small fraction of full
   scale, the output is not permanently saturated, and it is not permanently
   silent unless the machine declares it. This would have caught both bugs in
   the sibling issue today, with no reference capture and no human listening.
   The audio counterpart of golden_frame_test's guards.

3. PER-VOICE SOLO CAPTURE — the one that actually helps discrete modelling. A
   mixed sum cannot tell you WHICH voice is wrong. The discrete framework has
   nodes; add a way to render a single node or voice to its own WAV, so a
   comparison can be made voice by voice rather than against the sum. This is
   the difference between "our dkong sounds wrong" and "our dkong walk voice's
   RC decay is too fast".

4. IMPULSE / STEP RESPONSE of a filter chain. Feed a known impulse (or white
   noise) through a discrete filter section and compare the magnitude response
   against the same section in MAME. This separates a SOURCE error (LFSR taps,
   oscillator divider, envelope shape) from a FILTER error (RC corner, Q,
   order), which a spectral diff of the mixed output fundamentally cannot do.

MECHANICS: spectrograms need no plotting library — STFT, log magnitude,
colormap, then the existing gfxsheet::write_png. That also composes, since
`disasm imgdiff` can then diff two spectrograms. FFT can be a hand-rolled
radix-2 (~40 lines, in keeping with a codebase that hand-rolls a 101-tap FIR and
a Bresenham resampler) or rustfft in the disasm crate, which already carries
non-core dependencies.

WHAT PYTHON KEEPS: exploratory one-offs, where iterating is faster. It stops
being the documented path for anything repeatable.
notes:
SCOPE NOTE from the Donkey Kong audio comparison: which comparisons survive the
fact that two independent emulators never share state.

Measured on burgertime driven through `disasm movie mame`: at frame 200 the two
differed by 0.22% of pixels and the diff was ONLY the player sprite's animation
phase; by frame 2500 the sessions had diverged outright (score 2450 vs 2950).
Any timing difference compounds under player-controlled physics, so a long
gameplay replay is two different sessions by the end.

That splits audio comparison in two:

SURVIVES DIVERGENCE — whole-capture, session-independent properties. The dkong
DC offset was found this way and the finding stands despite the sessions
differing, because a constant -6699 mean is a property of the output path, not
of which barrel was where. Also: clipping, gross band balance, whether the
output ever returns to silence, overall gain. These are exactly what
`disasm audiodiff` should assert, and why the registry-driven sanity test needs
no MAME at all.

DOES NOT SURVIVE — per-effect fidelity. "Does the jump sound right" cannot be
answered by comparing two gameplay captures, because the jumps happen at
different moments in different game states.

For per-effect work the existing rig is already the right shape and sidesteps
the problem entirely: tools/sound-reference/drive_*_sound.lua plus the
machines/examples/*_capture.rs siblings feed BOTH emulators the same register
writes on the same timeline, so game state never enters into it. Extend that
(a dkong driver already exists) rather than trying to make gameplay replays
line up.

So: movie-driven MAME comparison is for video at a short, specific scenario, and
for gross audio properties. It is the wrong tool for per-effect sound character,
and no amount of alignment work will make it the right one.
close_reason: Absorbed into the discrete-sound-fidelity epic (phosphor-emulator-discrete-sound-fidelity-l5r3). Item 1 (disasm audiodiff + Rust analysis module) is .2; item 2 (registry audio sanity test) is .3; items 3 and 4 (per-voice solo render, impulse/step response) are .5. Its core argument — that Python can never gate and the arithmetic is already Rust over audio already produced in Rust — is Decision 4 of docs/designs/discrete-sound-fidelity.md.

title: audiodiff cannot write a single trimmed capture
description:
`--subtract-to` writes `a - b` and needs two inputs. There is no way to write out
ONE capture trimmed to a `--range`, which is wanted constantly: MAME's -wavwrite
starts at reset, so a reference is 23 s long with the effect at 17-21 s, while
`sndcmp capture` writes only the analysis window. The two describe the same
event at different origins, and listening to them back to back means trimming
one by hand.

FIX: a `--write-to PATH` that emits whatever the command produced — the ranged
capture for one input, the difference for two — and fold `--subtract-to` into it
so there is one mechanism rather than two nearly-identical flags.

title: Add Battlezone (Atari b/w vector, M6502 + DVG + Mathbox)
description: Atari Battlezone (1980) arcade machine. Hardware: M6502 + DVG b/w vector generator + Mathbox coprocessor + POKEY. All devices (M6502, DVG, Mathbox, POKEY) are already implemented and validated, so this is largely board wiring + ROM definitions. First shipping machine to exercise the Mathbox. See README Future > Games.

title: Make Cpu::reset generic over the bus type
description:
Cpu::reset takes '&mut Self::Bus' where BusMasterComponent::Bus is the associated type 'dyn Bus<Address = .., Data = ..>', implicitly 'static. A borrowed bus view (the concrete-dispatch shape) cannot be passed to it -- its lifetime cannot be named -- so every board whose CPU fetches a reset vector through the bus is blocked: M6502, M6809, M68000 (M6502 reads 0xFFFC/0xFFFD, M6809 reads 0xFFFE/0xFFFF).

Both prototypes sidestepped it because the Z80 ignores the bus at reset: Pac-Man resets against the board, Galaga uses Z80::hardware_reset.

Shape:
  fn reset<B: Bus<Address = Self::Address, Data = Self::Data> + ?Sized>(&mut self, bus: &mut B, master: BusMaster)
which needs Address/Data associated types on Cpu (or a similar bound). Makes Cpu non-object-safe -- no dyn Cpu exists in the workspace, so that costs nothing.

Touches every CPU impl and every reset call site. First task of the rollout; blocks steps 5-9 in docs/designs/concrete-bus-dispatch.md.
close_reason:
Done in 5bbae94.

Instead of keeping 'type Bus = dyn Bus<..>' and bounding reset by <Self::Bus as Bus>::Address, the associated type is now the bus *widths*: BusMasterComponent carries 'type Address' and 'type Data', and both tick_with_bus and Cpu::reset take 'B: Bus<Address = Self::Address, Data = Self::Data> + ?Sized'. That removes the trait object from the trait entirely rather than working around it, and makes tick_with_bus monomorphise too.

?Sized keeps '&mut dyn Bus' a legal argument, so every board still on bus_split! compiles untouched and the rollout can proceed one board at a time. Both traits lose object safety; nothing used dyn Cpu or dyn BusMasterComponent (verified by grep across the workspace).

Call-site churn was small: the seven CPU impls, the Cpu trait, and simple_system.rs's generic bounds (BusMasterComponent<Bus = dyn Bus<..>> -> BusMasterComponent<Address = u16, Data = u8>).

Payoff demonstrated immediately: Ms. Pac-Man dropped its workaround and now resets through its own borrowed bus view.

New regression test core/tests/cpu_bus_generic_test.rs: a 6502 and a 6809 reset through a borrowed view (reading their reset vectors), a cycle runs against one, and a &mut dyn Bus is still accepted. If the signatures ever go back to an associated dyn type, that file stops compiling.

Verification: phosphor-core, phosphor-machines, phosphor-macros, phosphor-frontend, phosphor-cpu-validation (including the slow single-step validators) and the ROM-gated harness suites all pass; golden frames unchanged for all 39 machines; clippy and fmt clean. The C++ cross-validator matches its documented baseline (M6809 99.28%, known indexed-mode cycle-table FIXME) -- unaffected, since this is a signature-only refactor and the committed vectors are unchanged. (The m6800/i8035 validator binaries in cross-validation/bin are stale builds for another platform and will not exec; that predates this change.)

Unblocks 8v1a (Williams), hv5p (Atari DVG/AVG), 3hnp (Atari System 1 + Gottlieb), 642d (standalone + delete bus_split!).

title: Burgertime (Data East btime) — dual-6502 DECO CPU-7 arcade
description:
Add Burgertime (MAME driver btime), the first game on Data East's btime.cpp hardware, structured as a reusable BtimeBoard (machines/src/btime.rs) + thin BurgertimeSystem wrapper (machines/src/burgertime.rs) so siblings (Bump'n'Jump, Lock'n'Chase, Zoar, Disco No.1) slot in later.

Pass 1 is VIDEO FIRST, AUDIO STUBBED: main DECO CPU-7 (encrypted 6502) + video + inputs, playable & silent. Audio (sound M6502 + 2x AY-3-8910) is a deferred child.

No phosphor-core changes: DECO CPU-7 opcode encryption lives in the machine bus via existing M6502::is_sync() (pattern: machines/src/missile_command.rs:762). M6502 and Ay8910 already exist (btime is the first AY-8910 machine).

Full plan: ~/.claude/plans/plan-for-burgertime-and-jolly-abelson.md
Hardware ref: ~/ws/mame/src/mame/dataeast/btime.cpp + decocpu7.cpp
Key reuse: missile_command.rs (is_sync hook, palette-RAM, DIP/VBLANK), donkey_kong.rs (dual-CPU dispatch, for audio), core/src/gfx/{decode,tilemap,sprite}.rs, core/src/device/ay8910.rs.
close_reason: All 8 children complete. Burgertime (Data East btime) fully emulated: DECO CPU-7 main M6502 with opcode encryption + X/Y-swap mirror, 3bpp char/sprite/background video with inverted BGR palette and ROT270 3:4 portrait display, inputs/DIPs/live VBLANK/coin IRQ, frame loop, and audio (second M6502 + 2x AY-3-8910). Reusable BtimeBoard + BurgertimeSystem wrapper. Boots, plays, and has sound; verified in the frontend. Full test coverage (unit + integration + save-state).

title: Scaffold BtimeBoard + BurgertimeSystem + registration + ROM regions
description: New machines/src/btime.rs (BtimeBoard struct + BtimeConfig) and machines/src/burgertime.rs (BurgertimeSystem wrapper). Add pub mod to machines/src/lib.rs. Define static RomRegions (MAIN 0xB000/0x5000, GFX1 0x6000, GFX2 0x1800, BG_MAP 0x800, SOUND 0x1000 defined-not-wired) with CRCs from btime.cpp:2546. inventory::submit! MachineEntry::new("burgertime", &["btime"], create). Board Wrapper Pattern per joust.rs/gridlee.rs; impl_default_frontend_capabilities! (no NVRAM).
close_reason: Scaffolded BtimeBoard (shared btime.cpp hardware) + BtimeConfig in machines/src/btime.rs and BurgertimeSystem wrapper in machines/src/burgertime.rs. Board-wrapper pattern (Bus/MachineCore/capabilities delegated), all 5 ROM regions defined with CRCs from btime.cpp, registered as 'burgertime' (btime set). title: Main memory map + DECO CPU-7 encryption + X/Y-swap mirror
description: impl Bus for BtimeBoard (main CPU): decode 0x0000-07FF RAM, 0x0C00 palette, 0x1000/0x1400 video/color RAM, 0x1800/0x1C00 X/Y-swapped mirrors (swap(off)=32*(off%32)+off/32), 0x4000-4004 I/O, 0xB000-FFFF ROM. DECO CPU-7: main_had_written set on any write; on is_sync() fetch with the flag, clear it and bitswap8(v,6,5,3,4,2,7,1,0) when (addr&0x0104)==0x0104. No core changes. Ref: decocpu7.cpp, missile_command.rs:762.
close_reason: Implemented in machines/src/btime.rs: X/Y-swap sprite-RAM mirror at 0x1800 (videoram) / 0x1C00 (colorram) via swap(off)=32*(off%32)+off/32 (btime.cpp:534), and DECO CPU-7 opcode decryption — main_had_written armed on any write, consumed on is_sync() opcode fetch, applying bitswap8(v,6,5,3,4,2,7,1,0) when (addr&0x0104)==0x0104 (decocpu7.cpp read_sync). No phosphor-core changes. 9 new tests (swap involution, both mirrors, decrypt vectors + address gating + flag lifecycle). clippy+fmt clean.

title: GFX decode (chars/sprites/bg) + BGR_233_inverted palette
description: decode_gfx (core/src/gfx/decode.rs): chars 8x8x3 (1024, planes 0/0x2000/0x4000), sprites 16x16x3 (256, tile16layout), bg_tiles 16x16x3 from gfx2 (64). Palette update_palette_entry: BGR_233_inverted = invert then r=pal3bit(v&7), g=pal3bit((v>>3)&7), b=pal2bit((v>>6)&3). NOT the weighted PROM btime_palette().

Three GfxLayouts (btime.cpp:2099-2135) with planes reversed for phosphor's LSB-first convention: chars 8x8x3/1024 (gfx_8x8x3_planar, planes 0/0x2000/0x4000), sprites 16x16x3/256 (tile16layout, x-offsets 128..135,0..7), bg_tiles 16x16x3/64 from gfx2 (planes 0/0x800/0x1000). decode_gfx into GfxCache fields; bg_map copied. title: Video render: chars + sprites + background + ROT270
description: Render native 256x256 then crop visible 8..248 and apply ROT270 (core/src/gfx/mod.rs rotate). Background if bnj_scroll0&0x10 (16x16 bg tiles from bg_map, scroll from (scroll0&3)<<8). Chars 32x32: code=videoram[off]+256*(colorram[off]&3), x=31-(off/32), y=off%32 (hand-rolled blit due to transpose). Sprites: 8, interleave 0x20 in videoram, x=240-b3, y=240-b2 (+1), flipX/Y, wrap +/-256, draw_sprite_row. display_size (240,240). Ref btime.cpp:659-766.
close_reason: Renderer implemented in btime.rs render_frame: chars (32x32 transposed grid, code=videoram+256*(colorram&3), transparent when background enabled else opaque), 8 sprites (attrs interleaved 0x20, x=240-b3/y=239-b2, flipX/Y, +/-256 wrap), and 4-column 16x16 background (bg_map tiles, scroll (scroll0&3)<<8, palette base 8) drawn into a native 256x256 index buffer; crops the visible [8,248) square and rotates ROT270 into the 240x240 RGB output. Verified end-to-end against the real btime ROM set (draws varied attract graphics once the VBLANK bit toggles; uniform without it, which the live VBLANK bit in .5 resolves). 3 render tests + smoke. clippy+fmt clean.

title: Inputs + DIPs + live VBLANK bit + coin IRQ
description: InputControl table (coin1/2, start1/2, tilt, P1/P2 4-way + button, cocktail) reusing input_defaults.rs. handle_input: P1/P2/start/tilt active-low, coins active-high; coin rising edge sets main_irq (HOLD_LINE approx). title: Follow-up: audio — sound M6502 + 2x AY-3-8910
description: Separate PR. Add sound_cpu M6502 @500kHz, sound_map (donkey_kong.rs dispatch on master), sound_ram, ay1/ay2 Ay8910::new(1_500_000) (btime is first AY-8910 machine), ClockDivider::new(1,3). AY writes 0x2000/4000/6000/8000; latch read 0xA000 acks sound_irq; NMI-enable write 0xC000 bit0 (AUDIO_ENABLE_DIRECT, NOT AY port A). sound_irq on main 0x4003 write; sound NMI = enable && ((scanline>>3)&1). title: Epic: CI and build foundation
description:
No CI exists in this repo: no .github/, no workflow file, no CI configuration of any kind. Build, cargo fmt, cargo clippy and all 83 test suites are manual steps enforced only by CLAUDE.md.

The codebase is already written for a CI that does not exist. machines/tests/input_contract_test.rs:11 explains that the suite avoids MachineEntry::create because 'CI does not have' ROMs — the design accommodation was made, the runner never was.

Deliberately small and first, so every later epic is checked automatically from here on.

Baseline measured at 89c1b92: 3,165 tests passing across 83 suites, plus one environment-only failure covered by child .2.
close_reason:
All three children closed; the project now has automated verification it did not have before.

.1 CI workflow (b90dcc1, refined in a8e3085) — .github/workflows/ci.yml with three jobs: 'check' (fmt, clippy -D warnings, workspace tests, pinned to the flake's rustc 1.95.0) gating every push and PR; 'future' (same lints on current stable, continue-on-error) as an early-warning signal; 'validate' (submodules, generated M6800/M6809 vectors, all 7.1M) weekly plus workflow_dispatch. Verified green on GitHub, and 'validate' verified to genuinely validate rather than skip — 2,577,000 I8088, 1,604,000 Z80 and 1,000,058 M68000 vectors passed in a 6-minute job, with the explicit presence check confirming all six vector sets present.

.2 Validator skip (dfca3be) — scope proved wider than filed: cpu-validation/test_data is gitignored in full, so ALL six validators panicked on a fresh checkout, not just i8088. Added require_test_data() and converted all six.

.3 Release profile (72ac233) — lto = 'fat', codegen-units = 1, kept on measured evidence: +15.0% joust, +9.4% pacman, +8.3% galaga, +4.7% marble against a ~1.7% noise floor.

Two things this epic surfaced that are tracked elsewhere rather than left implicit: the vector generators write relative to CWD so the documented command silently misfires (contained-fidelity-np9x.7, currently worked around in the validate job by working-directory plus a presence check), and the toolchain pin now lives in both flake.lock and the workflow with nothing enforcing agreement — noted in the workflow comment, to revisit if it drifts.

title: CI: run fmt, clippy and the workspace test suite on push and PR
description:
Add .github/workflows/ci.yml running, in order: cargo fmt --all --check; cargo clippy --all-features --all-targets -D warnings; cargo test --workspace.

Notes:
- flake.nix already pins the toolchain (cargo, rustc, clang, SDL2, pkg-config, libGL). Either use the Nix shell in CI or install SDL2 via apt — phosphor-frontend is the only crate needing system packages, so core/machines/macros/harness can build on a plain toolchain if a split job is preferred.
- Do NOT check out the cpu-validation submodules in the default job: the single-step suites are designed to skip without them (see sibling .2). A separate scheduled job can init submodules and run the full 7.1M-vector validation.
- ROM-gated tests (frameshot parity, future golden frames) already skip cleanly when PHOSPHOR_ROMS is unset.

Acceptance: a red CI on a deliberately introduced clippy warning and on a failing test; green on 89c1b92 as-is.
close_reason: Implemented in b90dcc1 as .github/workflows/ci.yml. Two jobs: 'check' (fmt --check, clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -D warnings, cargo test --workspace, all --locked) on push to main + PRs, with SDL2/GL installed via apt since --workspace builds phosphor-frontend; and 'validate' (submodules: true, generate M6800/M6809 vectors, run all 7.1M) on a weekly cron plus workflow_dispatch. The split keeps per-push CI fast while still validating the CPUs regularly. Two hazards handled explicitly: the generators write relative to CWD so they run under working-directory: cpu-validation (underlying bug filed as contained-fidelity-np9x.7), and 'validate' asserts every vector directory exists before running, because a skipped validator reports success and libtest captures its skip message. Baseline verified green before landing: fmt exit 0, clippy no warnings, 3165 tests passing. Not yet exercised on GitHub — first real run happens on push.

title: All six single-step validators should skip, not panic, without vector data
description:
In a checkout without submodules the M6502, M6800, M6809, Z80 and M68000 single-step tests each report '0 passed' and move on. The I8088 one panics:

  cpu-validation/tests/i8088_single_step_test.rs:189
  'No SingleStepTests data. Run: git submodule update --init cpu-validation/test_data/8088'

It is the one test that turns a fresh CI run red for an environment reason rather than a code one. Reproduced at HEAD in a clean worktree.

Fix: match the five siblings — eprintln! the hint and return, rather than panic.

Acceptance: cargo test --workspace passes in a submodule-free checkout.
close_reason: Fixed in dfca3be. Scope was wider than filed: cpu-validation/test_data is gitignored in full, so a fresh checkout has neither the four SingleStepTests submodules nor the generated M6800/M6809 sets — all six validators panicked, not just i8088. (The earlier 'five skip gracefully' reading was wrong: cargo stops after the first failing test binary, so the other three submodule-backed validators were never reached, and the '0 passed' lines were the lib and gen_* bin targets.) Added require_test_data() to the cpu-validation lib and converted all six to return early through it. Verified in a submodule-free worktree: six ok/1-passed results, zero panics, message visible under --nocapture. Noted in the doc comment that libtest captures the message for a passing test, so the real guard against a permanently-skipping validator is the scheduled full-validation job, not the eprintln.

title: Tune the release profile: fat LTO and codegen-units=1
description:
Cargo.toml:6-13 raises dev builds to opt-level 2 for real-time emulation and then never mentions [profile.release], so release ships stock: no LTO, 16 codegen units.

The workload is one hot loop calling across three crate boundaries per emulated cycle (machines -> core CPU -> core devices), which is exactly the case cross-crate inlining serves.

  [profile.release]
  lto = 'fat'
  codegen-units = 1

Acceptance: measured against the benchmark harness. Record before/after frames-per-second in a comment; keep the change only if it helps. Blocked on the benchmark issue only for the measurement, not for the edit.
close_reason:
Landed in 72ac233. [profile.release] lto = 'fat', codegen-units = 1.

Kept because it measurably helps, per the issue's own acceptance criterion. Measured with phosphor-bench (600 frames, 120 warmup, 5 reps, best of two full runs each side; tool noise floor ~1.7%):

  machine   emul ms/f before -> after   fps change
  joust           0.746 -> 0.648           +15.0%
  pacman          0.845 -> 0.772            +9.4%
  galaga          1.021 -> 0.935            +8.3%
  marble          2.473 -> 2.355            +4.7%
  tempest         1.146 -> 1.131            +1.3%  (within noise)

Four of five boards improve well clear of the noise floor. Tempest is flat, consistent with it spending proportionally more time inside phosphor-core's AVG and Mathbox devices, where calls were already intra-crate and inlinable — i.e. the win really is cross-crate inlining, which is the mechanism the issue predicted.

Cost is release build time only. CI's gating 'check' job runs the test suite under the dev profile and is unaffected; the scheduled 'validate' job builds release and trades a slower build for a faster 7.1M-vector run. Observed ~50s to rebuild the bench binary's dependency chain after the change.

Side note worth carrying forward: this is the first use of phosphor-bench in anger, and it did the job — the effect was large enough to be unambiguous against the noise floor, which is evidence the tool is sensitive enough for the concrete-bus-dispatch A/B it was built for.

title: M6809 reset sequence costs 0 emulated cycles
description: Cpu::reset for the M6809 (core/src/cpu/m6809/mod.rs:616) reads the FFFE/FFFF vector outside the tick loop, so the reset sequence consumes no emulated cycles. MAME's cycle-stepped core spends 4 (base6x09.lst INTERRUPT_VECTOR: dummy_vma, vector hi, vector lo, dummy_vma). Measured on esb: our first instruction begins at machine cycle 2, MAME's at 7 — 4 cycles of vector fetch plus 1 because ORCC #imm costs 3 on MAME and 2 on ours. Not the cause of j63p (verified inert: correcting it leaves the first divergence, the bank-change counts and the derail cycle all bit-identical), but it is a real fidelity gap and probably applies to every CPU whose reset() fetches vectors outside the clock. Also check ORCC/ANDCC #imm timing against the datasheet — 3 cycles is the documented figure.
close_reason: Fixed in b9942fa. RESET_SEQUENCE_CYCLES = 4, burned in execute_cycle before the first fetch; at_instruction_boundary is false while they run. The correct figure is 4, not the 5 the raw measurement suggested: MAME's INTERRUPT_VECTOR is 4 cycles (base6x09.lst:51) and the extra 1 was our trace's labelling convention (it tags an instruction with the cycle the previous one finished). +5 was tried first and overshot by one instruction. ORCC #imm was NOT wrong at 2 cycles as first suspected — it is 3, matching MAME; that reading came from misreading a held-CPU trace. Verified: first divergence from MAME moves 454,189 -> 463,991 and the run-wide cycle offset drops to the -1 of the labelling convention. Does not fix j63p on its own.

title: Epic: Unified clock tree
description:
Design: docs/designs/clock-tree.md (rev 3)

Give every board one declared crystal set and derive its sub-clocks from it,
replacing scattered ClockDivider fields and hand-rolled Bresenham accumulators.

THE PROBLEM. Every board documents its crystal in a comment and stores it in a
type in none of them. What TimingConfig stores is the leaf (cpu_clock_hz), so
sub-clocks are re-derived per board against it in three different idioms: 14
ClockDivider fields across 11 boards, 5 hand-rolled Bresenham accumulators, and
rounded integer constants standing in for a ratio between two crystals.

On docastle, mrdo and mario_bros the VIDEO clock is on a different crystal than
the CPU, so cycles_per_scanline is not a hardware constant at all — it is a
rounded conversion between two crystals, computed by hand, in a comment,
differently in each file (docastle 254 vs true 253.97; mrdo 261 vs 261.06). That
is the error-prone thing worth centralising. Nothing checks any of it.

The Votrax bug (phosphor-emulator-1fg) is the failure mode: a rate neither
derived from a declared crystal nor atomically paired with the device's own
set_clock.

REV 3 SCOPE. Rev 2's "deterministic frame scheduler" is DROPPED — its
master-rate frame loop was an 8-20x iteration-count regression on half the
registered boards (Crystal Castles 163,840 iterations/frame becoming 1,310,720),
plus a per-iteration u64 divide, plus the loss of the existing scanline hoist.
The tree does BOOKKEEPING, NOT SCHEDULING: a domain still steps once per CPU
cycle with the same single add-and-compare ClockDivider does today. Ratios to
the crystal are retained for hz(), validation and the debugger — not for
stepping.

Also dropped from rev 2: deleting `pub const TIMING` (threaded through two
macros across 34 files and 40 machines for no correctness gain). Boards declare
a tree ALONGSIDE TIMING and a registry-driven test asserts they agree.

STEPS 1-2 DELIVER MOST OF THE VALUE and are worth landing even if 3-9 never
happen.

SEQUENCING NOTE: steps 4+ change per-board save layout, which under the current
positional format means a SAVE_VERSION bump each time. If tlv-save-state Stage A
lands first that cost disappears. A reason to sequence it first, not a blocker.
close_reason:
All nine steps landed. Every board declares its crystals in a type, every sub-clock is derived from them, and a registry-driven test holds each board's TimingConfig to its declaration.

What the epic set out to remove is gone. 14 ClockDivider board fields, 5 hand-rolled Bresenham accumulators, and the rounded constants standing in for cross-crystal ratios are all tree domains now. The only ClockDivider left in machines/src is gridlee's audio_clock, which paces against the host audio rate and is not a board clock; it says so in its own doc comment, since it is now the only one and the next reader would otherwise try to finish the job.

The bug class is closed at both ends. A rate can no longer be written down twice and drift (the Gottlieb divider and its resampler disagreed by 127 ppm in opposite directions from the truth, which is the Votrax bug one level down), and a retune now moves the domain and the device in one call with no shadow field to fall out of step.

Behaviour changes, each landed alone so a bisect can find it:
- jv78.5, Gottlieb's sound CPU: 179/1000 to the crystal's 715909/4000000, 127 ppm. Measured on Q*Bert as 718.25 to 718.17 audio samples per frame against an ideal 718.03, moving toward it.
- jv78.6, Atari System 1's TMS5220: under half a ppm, from dividing by the exact 1789772.625 instead of a truncated 1789772.

Corrections to the design doc's own numbers, found by computing them exactly: the scanline rounding is -125 ppm on Do! Castle and +235 on Mr. Do!, not -122 and +230 (the doc rounded an intermediate to three decimals). Atari System 1's CPU is exactly 7159090.5 Hz, so its stored 7159090 is a rounding, which is why the consistency test compares against the exact rational rather than a rounded accessor. And jv78.5's proposed 447443/2500000 was itself a rounding.

Left open deliberately: phosphor-emulator-nndj, Scramble's sound crystal (14.318 rounded from 14.318181, 12.6 ppm). Same shape as jv78.5 and split out for the same reason. jv78.7 kept the old rate and pinned it, so that fix arrives against a failing test.

Cost: SAVE_VERSION 7 to 12, five bumps. Four were unavoidable one-per-commit; jv78.8's nine boards went in one commit at the user's direction, saving eight. tlv-save-state Stage A (phosphor-emulator-tlv-save-state-hc61.1) is what removes that cost for whatever comes next.

Two things worth carrying forward. A board section that runs on its own loop rate needs its tree renominated with set_step_domain (Atari System 1's speech runs per sound-CPU cycle, not per main-CPU cycle); nothing catches getting that wrong except a test, so there is one. And DebugRegister now carries two kinds of row, register contents in hex and magnitudes in decimal, distinguished by the width field.

title: ClockTree/ClockDomain core type with no callers
description:
core/src/core/clock_tree.rs with NO callers: ClockTree, ClockDomain, DomainId,
RootId, ClockDomainName, FrameParams.

ClockDomain stores BOTH ratios: root_num/root_den (the auditable hardware
statement, save-skipped) and step_num/step_den (precomputed ratio to the
stepping domain, SAVED so a retuned domain reloads at its retuned rate), plus
phase_accum.

    advance(&mut self) -> u32   // times this domain fired; >1 when it outruns
                                // the stepping domain (congo_bongo's 4 MHz
                                // sound Z80 vs its 3.041 MHz main CPU)
    tick(&mut self) -> bool     // fast path, identical cost to ClockDivider::tick
    hz(&self, root_hz) -> u64
    set_domain_hz(&mut self, id, hz)          // folds phase_accum %= step_den
    cycles_per_scanline(&self, video, htotal) -> (u64, i32)   // count + ppm error

MULTI-ROOT IN ONE TREE, not one tree per crystal. A board with a video crystal
and a CPU crystal must hold both in one type, because the relationship between
them is precisely the rounding this design exists to audit.

TWO CONSTRAINTS FROM THE SAVE FORMAT (rev 2 got these wrong):
- #[derive(Saveable)]'s array path (macros/src/lib.rs:1042-1094) delegates
  non-primitive elements to Saveable::load_state, and there is NO
  `impl Saveable for Option<T>` in core/src/core/save_state.rs. So
  `domains: [Option<ClockDomain>; 6]` would not compile. Use
  [ClockDomain; MAX_DOMAINS] with unused slots inert (step_num = 0) and a
  save-skipped len. MAX_DOMAINS = 8 is generous; the current max is two divider
  fields on any one board.
- ClockDivider (core/src/core/clock.rs:23) STAYS unchanged for the uses that are
  not board clocks (e.g. gridlee.rs:357 is a resampling divider). ClockDomain is
  its named, tree-owned sibling.

UNIT TESTS: 1/8 fires 1 in 8; congo_bongo's 4_000_000 over 3_041_250 fires 4
times per 3 steps and never twice in a row wrongly; set_domain_hz folds phase and
survives a save/load round trip; cycles_per_scanline(dot, 312) on a 4 MHz /
9.828 MHz pair returns (254, -122).

Acceptance: builds and tests green with zero production callers.
close_reason:
Landed in 0156409. core/src/core/clock_tree.rs: ClockTree, ClockDomain, DomainId, RootId, ClockDomainName, DomainInfo, FrameParams, plus Raster added in step 2. 18 unit tests and a doctest, zero production callers at the time of the commit.

The save split is as specified: root_num/root_den save-skipped, step_num/step_den saved, so a retuned domain reloads retuned. hz() reads the step ratio (special-casing the step domain itself) rather than the root ratio, which is what makes that split self-consistent after a load: a domain restored at a retuned rate reports the retuned rate.

advance() proved on congo_bongo's 4_000_000 over 3_041_250 before anything depended on it: reduces to 3200/2433, fires once or twice per main cycle, never zero, and the running total equals floor(n*3200/2433) at every step.

Deviation from the issue text: cycles_per_scanline(dot, 312) on 4 MHz / 9.828 MHz returns (254, -125), not (254, -122). 312*2000/2457 is 253.96825, and 254 against that is 125 ppm. The -122 in the design doc comes from a 253.969 intermediate. Mr. Do! is +235 rather than +230 for the same reason. Sign convention kept from the doc: the ppm is the error in the video rate the integer count implies, so negative means the count runs the video clock slow.

title: Declare a clock tree per board + registry-driven consistency test
description:
Add `pub fn clock_tree()` to each board beside its TIMING, transcribing the
crystal comment that is already there. Migrate NO dividers. Add the
registry-driven consistency test.

    // machines/src/docastle.rs — a genuine two-crystal board
    pub fn clock_tree() -> ClockTree {
        let mut t = ClockTree::new(4_000_000);              // CPU crystal
        let vid = t.add_root(9_828_000);                    // video crystal
        let cpu = t.add_domain(Cpu,   RootId::MAIN, 1, 1);  // 4 MHz
        let dot = t.add_domain(Pixel, vid,          1, 2);  // 4.914 MHz
        let sn  = t.add_domain(Psg,   RootId::MAIN, 1, 16); // SN76489 / 16
        t.set_step_domain(cpu);
        t
    }
    // tree.cycles_per_scanline(dot, 312) == (254, -122 ppm)

THE TEST, over registry::all() with the usual the_registry_is_not_empty guard:
tree.hz(cpu) == TIMING.cpu_clock_hz for every machine, and where a video domain
is declared, tree.cycles_per_scanline(video, htotal) matches
TIMING.cycles_per_scanline within a per-board declared tolerance. The board
states the ppm it accepts and the test asserts the actual error is within it, so
a tightened divider shows up as a failing bound rather than a silent
improvement. Mr. Do! would declare ~250 ppm; docastle ~122.

THIS STEP DELIVERS MOST OF THE EPIC'S VALUE. No behaviour changes, no save-state
churn, no hot-path change. The three hand-rounded cross-crystal scanline counts
become asserted-with-known-error instead of a rounding buried in a comment.

The multi-crystal boards are docastle, mrdo, mario_bros, congo_bongo, scramble,
tkg04 and gottlieb — NOT Atari System 1, which rev 2 wrongly listed (its POKEY
and 6502 both hang off the single 14.31818 MHz crystal;
atari_system1_sound.rs:35-38,45).

Vector boards (atari_dvg, atari_avg, starwars, quantum) declare a tree for this
test and keep their loops; atari_dvg's 60 Hz is a chosen budget, not a crystal
derivation (atari_dvg.rs:33-42).

GATING: Gottlieb's crystal row depends on the crystal-verification task in this
epic. Declare the other boards first if it has not landed.
close_reason:
Landed in f2df73f. All 40 registered machines declare a tree; 23 board modules gained clock_tree(). No dividers migrated, no behaviour change, no save churn.

Plumbing: MachineCore::clock_declaration() returns the tree and the TimingConfig together, emitted by machine_core_metadata! from the same $timing expression, so the pair cannot drift. The macro's two-argument arm was removed, which made the compiler enumerate all 28 call sites; the 8 machines with hand-written MachineCore impls use machine_clock_declaration! directly.

The tolerance lives on the tree as ClockTree::set_raster(video, htotal, ppm) rather than in the test, so the board states what it accepts. docastle declares 130 against an actual -125; mrdo 240 against +235; every single-crystal board declares 0.

Non-vacuity, checked by breaking things on purpose before keeping the test: a 1 Hz crystal error, HTOTAL 312 to 313, a 5000 ppm tolerance, a removed set_raster, a stale NO_RASTER_DERIVATION entry, and a Cpu domain renamed to Cpu2 each failed the check that should catch them. Two checks exist only to close vacuity holes: declared_tolerance_is_tight (a loose bound now fails, so tightening a divider fails a stale bound rather than passing silently) and every_raster_board_derives_its_scanline (a board drawing scanlines must derive them or be named with a reason).

The three AVG_CYCLES_PER_CPU_CYCLE constants added this session (quantum 2, atari_avg 8, starwars 8) are fixed rather than filed: each board declares a Vector domain, and a per-board test derives the integer from the 12.096 MHz crystal and holds the constant to it.

Findings:
- atari_system1's CPU is exactly 7159090.5 Hz, so TIMING's 7_159_090 is a rounding, not a division. The test compares against the exact rational (within half a hertz) instead of a rounded hz(), so no board's agreement with its crystals depends on which way an accessor rounds.
- scramble's SOUND_CLOCK_HZ rounds the sound crystal to 14.318 MHz against the real 14.318181, putting that CPU 7 ppm slow. Noted in the board comment; correcting it is a behaviour change for jv78.7.
- williams is the only raster board deriving its scanline count from nothing: 64 cycles from an approximate 15.6 kHz horizontal rate, no dot clock documented. It and its two siblings are in NO_RASTER_DERIVATION.
- Domains left undeclared where the crystal is genuinely undocumented in-tree, rather than guessed: mcr2's 2 MHz SSIO, btime's 500 kHz sound 6502, williams' sound CPU, quantum's 600 kHz POKEY (not a whole division of 12.096 MHz), and gottlieb's Votrax VCO (not a crystal division at all).

title: Verify Gottlieb's two crystals against the schematic
description:
Research, not code. Resolve the epic's one open question before Gottlieb's tree
is declared as authoritative.

gottlieb.rs:8 says the I8088 is 15 MHz / 3. gottlieb.rs:51 says the pixel clock
is 20 MHz / 4. Both give 5 MHz, which is why the discrepancy has gone unnoticed.
15 MHz / 3 is the textbook 8284A arrangement for a 5 MHz 8088, so both are
plausibly real and this is genuinely a two-crystal board — but that has not been
checked.

The CPU domain's Hz is unaffected either way. What is affected is the declared
CRYSTAL, which is the thing this whole design claims to be authoritative about,
so getting it wrong would bake a fiction into the type that replaces the
comments.

Verify against the board schematic or a reference driver's clock definitions.
Per project convention, cite the hardware in the commit message, not in a source
comment.

Acceptance: gottlieb.rs's two clock comments agree with each other and with
whatever the tree declares, or the discrepancy is explained in the file.
close_reason:
Answered from the Q*Bert instruction manual parts list (arcade-museum PDF, pages 14-19): the main board carries two crystals, 15 MHz and 20 MHz, and the sound board carries a third at 3.579545 MHz.

So gottlieb.rs:8 (I8088 at 15 MHz / 3) and gottlieb.rs:51 (pixel clock at 20 MHz / 4) are both correct and neither is stale. Gottlieb System 80 is a three-crystal board whose two main-board crystals happen to divide to the same 5 MHz, which is why the discrepancy went unnoticed.

Declared in f2df73f as gottlieb::clock_tree(): roots 15 MHz, 20 MHz, 3.579545 MHz, with Cpu 1/3, Pixel 1/4 of the video crystal, SoundCpu 1/4 of the sound crystal. The raster derivation is exact (318 pixel clocks = 318 CPU cycles, 0 ppm) because both main-board crystals land on 5 MHz.

The Votrax SC-01 is deliberately not a domain: it is an RC VCO steered by a DAC write, not a crystal division, so it belongs with the retune work in jv78.4/.6.

title: Pilot: migrate Gottlieb sound/Votrax clocks onto the tree
description:
Pilot the migration on Gottlieb System 80. Replace sound_clock + votrax_clock +
the votrax_clock_applied shadow field with tree domains and a single
set_domain_hz at the DAC write.

    fn write_speech_dac(&mut self, data: u8) {
        let hz = convert_speech_clock(data);          // gottlieb.rs:107
        self.tree.set_domain_hz(self.votrax, hz as u32);
        self.sound.set_votrax_clock(hz);
    }

One call site. No _applied shadow field, no per-cycle comparison in end_cycle,
and no re-derive-after-load hack — because ClockDomain SAVES its step ratio
rather than save-skipping it. The shadow field exists today only because
ClockDivider save-skips its ratio so a state load has to re-derive it; the
comment at gottlieb.rs:684 says exactly that.

KEEP 179/1000 as an explicit ratio in this commit. Correcting it is a behaviour
change and gets its own issue, so a bisect can separate the refactor from the
retune.

Layout changes, so this needs a SAVE_VERSION bump unless tlv-save-state Stage A
has landed. Say so in the commit message.

Acceptance: Q*bert golden frame unchanged, convert_speech_clock tests unchanged,
cargo test -p phosphor-machines and the golden frame suite green.
close_reason:
Landed in 521ac15. GottliebBoard's sound_clock, votrax_clock and votrax_clock_applied become one ClockTree built from the same clock_tree() the registry test validates.

Where the tree lives: on GottliebSoundBoard, not GottliebBoard. The speech-clock DAC write arrives in the sound board's Bus impl (the sound 6502 runs against it), so the outer board cannot see that write. Holding the tree where the retune lands is what makes the issue's one-call-site shape possible; keeping it on GottliebBoard would have forced either the shadow field back or an hz() comparison per CPU cycle, and hz() is a u128 divide. The Cpu and Pixel domains ride along unstepped as the reference the others are expressed against.

The load path is the payoff. ClockDomain saves its live ratio, so the speech domain reloads retuned with no re-derive. Only the SC-01 needs re-feeding, because VotraxSc01 save-skips main_clock_hz and the sclock/cclock/resampler rate under it; load_state now hands it back from the tree in one call where it used to zero a shadow and wait for the next tick. Added VotraxSc01::clock_hz() so a test can check that re-application rather than assume it.

Rate-preserving, and checked rather than asserted:
- The sound domain is retuned at construction to LEGACY_SOUND_CLOCK_HZ (179/1000 of the I8088 = 895000 Hz exactly), with a test pinning step_ratio() at (179, 1000).
- The Votrax's 19/100 is the reduced form of the old 950000/5000000. A reduced Bresenham ratio fires identically to an unreduced one from phase zero, so the nominal case is bit-identical.
- Q*Bert's golden frame is unchanged (run explicitly with --ignored, since every_pinned_machine_still_draws_its_frame is disabled for the vector rework).
- A probe over 3600 frames gave an identical audio sample count before and after: min 718, max 719, mean 718.25 per frame, never saturating the frontend's 2048-sample scratch buffer.

Behaviour note: at a retune the old code carried its accumulator into a fixed 5 MHz denominator; the tree folds phase into the reduced period. Fire rate identical, but the sub-cycle phase at a DAC write can shift by at most one Votrax tick.

SAVE_VERSION 7 to 8 (the issue's text predates two intervening bumps). The sound board's own tag goes 3 to 4. tlv-save-state Stage A has not landed, so a positional layout change still costs a global bump.

title: Gottlieb exact sound ratio: 179/1000 -> 447443/2500000
description:
Separate commit BECAUSE IT IS A BEHAVIOUR CHANGE. Gottlieb's sound-CPU divider
179/1000 is a hand-rounding of 894886/5000000 (3.579545 MHz / 4 over the 5 MHz
CPU). Replace it with the exact ratio 447443/2500000 — a 0.013% faster sound
6502.

Golden frames should be unaffected (the sound CPU does not drive video). The
AUDIO differs. Land it alone so a bisect can find it.

This is the concrete instance of the epic's thesis: 179/1000 is separately
plausible and separately unverifiable, and only becomes checkable once the
crystal it derives from is stored rather than commented.
