Acceptance: golden frames byte-identical; the new ratio is expressed as a
derivation from the declared crystal, not another magic pair.
notes:
CORRECTION from the jv78.4 pilot, before this is implemented.

The target ratio in the title is wrong. 447443/2500000 is 894886/5000000 reduced, but 894886 is itself the TRUNCATION of the real rate: 3.579545 MHz / 4 is 894886.25 Hz. Against the 5 MHz I8088 that is 715909/4000000, which is what gottlieb::clock_tree() already derives from the declared crystal. Use it, and do not re-round through an integer hertz on the way.

  179/1000        = 0.179          (today: 895000 Hz, 114 Hz fast, 127 ppm)
  447443/2500000  = 0.1789772      (proposed: from the truncated 894886 Hz)
  715909/4000000  = 0.17897725     (correct: straight from the crystal)

The fix is now a deletion rather than an edit. gottlieb.rs constructs the tree from clock_tree() and then calls set_domain_hz(sound_dom, LEGACY_SOUND_CLOCK_HZ) to hold the old rate; removing that one line and the constant leaves the crystal-derived ratio in place. The test sound_cpu_still_runs_the_legacy_ratio pins (179, 1000) and will fail, which is the point: it is there so this is a deliberate act.

SECOND HALF, easy to miss: SOUND_CLOCK_HZ (894_886) is what AudioResampler is told the sound board emits at, while the divider actually ticks 895000 times a second. Those disagree by the same 127 ppm today, in opposite directions from the truth. Correcting the divider without correcting the resampler's input rate leaves the inconsistency in place, just relocated. Feed the resampler from the tree so both come from one derivation, which is the Votrax bug's lesson (phosphor-emulator-1fg).

Audio changes, video does not. Q*Bert's golden frame should be unaffected; a probe over 3600 frames measured 718.25 audio samples per frame, and a 127 ppm rate change moves that by about 0.09 samples per frame.
close_reason:
Landed in 10fdee4, alone, as a behaviour change.

Used 715909/4000000, not the 447443/2500000 in the title. That figure is 894886/5000000 reduced, but 894886 is the truncation of 894886.25, so it would have swapped one rounding for a smaller one. clock_tree() already derives the exact ratio from the declared 3.579545 MHz crystal, so the fix turned out to be a deletion: LEGACY_SOUND_CLOCK_HZ and the set_domain_hz call that held the old rate are gone, and the crystal ratio stands. Nothing in gottlieb.rs rounds a clock on the way to being used any more.

Both halves moved together. SOUND_CLOCK_HZ (894886) was the resampler's input rate while the divider ticked 895000/sec: two hand-written constants, 127 ppm apart in opposite directions from the truth. Both now read the same domain. Added AudioResampler::input_rate() so the_resampler_input_rate_is_the_domain_rate can assert the two agree rather than leaving it to inspection.

Scope confirmed before changing anything: the main board only writes to the sound board (write_sound_command, 0x2000). There is no read path back, so sound timing cannot reach the main CPU or video. Audio-only, as predicted.

Measured on Q*Bert over 3600 frames, before and after:
  mean audio samples/frame  718.25 -> 718.17   (ideal 718.03)
  sample checksum           fc5f38fee06f7424 -> 24d7a713c88c69d0
The 0.08 shift is the predicted 127 ppm (0.09), and it moves toward the ideal rather than away. Golden frame unchanged. Buffer occupancy unchanged: max 719 against the frontend's 2048-sample scratch, never saturating.

Loose thread for whoever wants it, not chased here: the measured 718.17 still sits ~200 ppm above the ideal 718.03. fill_audio returns count.max(speech.len()), so the Votrax path can set the sample count when it runs marginally ahead of the DAC resampler. Worth a look if per-frame sample count ever matters.

title: Retune sites onto set_domain_hz: TMS5220 clock select, starwars
description:
Move the two remaining runtime-retune sites onto ClockTree::set_domain_hz,
deleting their private accumulators. Each is currently a different hand-rolled
protocol for the same thing.

- TMS5220 CLOCK SELECT, atari_system1_sound.rs:128-133. Port B bit 4 picks a
  divisor, retuning tms_clock_hz and the device against a separate clock_acc
  accumulator (atari_system1_sound.rs:68). Rev 2 of the design did not know this
  site existed.
- STARWARS, starwars.rs:701 tms_clock_acc — a third variant of the same idiom.

For a retuned device that feeds audio, pair set_domain_hz with
AudioResampler::set_input_rate (core/src/audio/mod.rs:300), which preserves
buffered output and the FIR delay line. Never a phase reset.

Acceptance: both accumulators deleted; golden frames unchanged; a save/load round
trip across a retune restores the retuned rate.
close_reason:
Landed in 6b86d66. Both accumulators deleted.

STAR WARS was not actually a retune site: TMS_CLOCK_HZ is a constant, so tms_clock_acc was the same idiom without the retuning. 672000/1512000 reduces to 4/9, and the tree's speech domain against the CPU domain is 4/9 exactly (master/18 over master/8), so this half is rate-preserving with nothing to round. Confirmed rather than assumed: the golden vector list hash is unchanged at b86f6889 over 3158 vectors, and the frame hash is unchanged too. Star Wars and ESB still fail the golden comparison for the pre-existing vector-renderer reason that has the test disabled; what matters here is that both hashes are identical before and after.

ATARI SYSTEM 1 was the real retune site. tms_clock_hz + clock_acc + a hand-kept device set_clock become one select_clock() that moves the domain and the device together, with the selection carried by the domain's saved ratio. load_state hands the restored rate back to the TMS (which save-skips its own clock) instead of reading it from a separate field. Declared the speech domain in atari_system1::clock_tree() at its nominal master/22, so it sits with the crystals the registry test checks.

Design point worth keeping in view for jv78.8: Speech renominates the sound 6502 as its tree's stepping domain, because Speech::tick runs once per sound-CPU cycle, not per main-CPU cycle. Same declaration and same crystals, different reference. set_step_domain recomputes every ratio, so this is a supported use rather than a second tree, but nothing would have caught getting it wrong (the ratio would simply have been 4x too slow), so there is a test pinning it.

Not bit-identical in one place, stated plainly: the old accumulator divided by a truncated 1789772 while the domain divides by the exact 1789772.625. Under half a ppm, toward the crystal. Marble and Road Runner golden frames unchanged.

SAVE_VERSION 8 to 9.

Acceptance met: accumulators deleted, golden frames unchanged, and a_retuned_tms_clock_reloads_retuned covers the save/load round trip across a retune.

title: Ad-hoc accumulators onto the tree: congo_bongo, scramble
description:
Replace the remaining hand-rolled Bresenham accumulators with tree domains. One
commit each.

- CONGO_BONGO, congo_bongo.rs:394-397,494 — the motivating case for
  advance() -> u32. Its sound Z80 at 4 MHz against a 3.041 MHz main loop
  genuinely fires more than once per main cycle, which ClockDivider::tick() ->
  bool cannot express. This is the ONLY such case among board clocks: checked,
  and mario_bros' I8039 is not a second one (SOUND_TICK_NUM/DEN = 11/60 at
  mario_bros.rs:103-104 is the I8039's MACHINE-CYCLE rate, 11 MHz / 15 =
  733,333 Hz, and 733333/4000000 reduces to exactly 11/60 — at most once per
  main cycle).
- SCRAMBLE, scramble.rs:179.

device/discrete/mod.rs:810 is not a board clock; leave it.

Acceptance: golden frames unchanged per board; congo_bongo's sound timing
identical to today (verify the fire pattern, not just the rate).
close_reason:
Landed as two commits, one per board.

CONGO BONGO (0322cf8) is advance() -> u32's first production caller. 4000000/3041250 reduces to 3200/2433 with a common factor of 1250, and a reduced Bresenham tracks its unreduced form step for step when both start from zero phase, so this is exactly pattern-preserving.

The acceptance asked to verify the fire pattern rather than the rate, so the test does exactly that: the_sound_domain_fires_on_the_same_cycles_as_the_old_accumulator reproduces the old arithmetic verbatim and compares the fire count on every one of 7299 main cycles (three whole periods of the ratio). It also asserts the double-step really occurs, about 2300 times, so the comparison cannot pass by matching two streams of ones. That guard matters because the failure it covers is invisible: a fire landing one main cycle early or late would shift the sound CPU against the latch writes it reads, at an unchanged average rate, and nothing else would notice.

SCRAMBLE (12d7975) is a plain tick, shared by Scramble, Scobra and Frogger. All three golden frames unchanged.

Kept Scramble's current rate rather than taking the tree's. SOUND_CLOCK_HZ divides a rounded 14.318 MHz while clock_tree() declares the real 14.318181 MHz colourburst part, so the constructor retunes the domain back to the old rate and the correction is filed separately as phosphor-emulator-scramble-sound-crystal-p3xq. Same discipline as jv78.4 and .5: move the mechanism, then move the rate. the_sound_domain_still_runs_the_rounded_crystal pins it so the correction arrives against a failing test.

Corrected a figure I got wrong when declaring Scramble's tree in jv78.2: the rounding costs 22.6 Hz and 12.6 ppm, not 13 Hz and 7 ppm. 181 Hz at the crystal, over eight.

SAVE_VERSION 9 to 10 to 11, one per commit. device/discrete/mod.rs:810 left alone as instructed; it is not a board clock.

title: Migrate the remaining ClockDivider board fields
description:
Migrate the remaining ClockDivider fields to tree domains. Mechanical once the
pilot and the accumulator cases have set the pattern; one commit per board.

Boards: atari_system1, tkg04, mcr2, mario_bros, docastle, mrdo, btime,
congo_bongo, namco_galaga.

The payoff is that chip_hz becomes tree.hz(sound) instead of a per-board
`const SOUND_CLOCK_HZ`, so AudioResampler's input rate and the divider's ratio
are provably the same derivation rather than two independently plausible
constants.

NOT a board clock, leave alone: gridlee.rs:357 (a resampling divider).

Each board's layout changes, so each needs a SAVE_VERSION bump unless
tlv-save-state Stage A has landed first. Note it per commit.

Acceptance: golden frames byte-identical per board; `sak fs grep ClockDivider
machines/src` returns only the deliberate non-board-clock uses.
close_reason:
Landed in 6e9af11 as one commit, not nine, at the user's direction. Nine boards, eleven fields.

Acceptance met on both counts. 'sak fs grep ClockDivider machines/src' now returns only gridlee's audio_clock, which is the deliberate non-board-clock use; it gained a doc comment saying so, since it is now the only one left and the next person would otherwise reasonably try to finish the job. Golden frames verified per board: marble, roadrunner, burgertime, congobongo, docastle, mariobros, shollow, mrdo, galaga, digdug, xevious, dkong, pacman. dkongjr has no ROM set in this collection, and dkong covers the same tkg04 board.

Every ratio preserved exactly, and checked rather than asserted. the_migrated_dividers_kept_their_ratios is a table of all eleven: the tree-derived ratio against the literal the ClockDivider was constructed with. Each is the reduction of the same fraction, and a reduced Bresenham fires identically to its unreduced form from zero phase, so equality of reduced ratios is equality of fire patterns. Confirmed the test can fail by mutating btime's declared divider.

Two boards had a clock jv78.2 had declined to declare rather than guess, and both could now be stated honestly:
- btime's sound 6502 is 12 MHz / 24. Its 1/3 was a ratio against a leaf; 500 kHz is a whole division of the crystal whatever counter chain reaches it.
- mcr2's SSIO is a second clock SOURCE, not a division: 19.968 over 2 MHz is 9.984, so no divider produces it. Declaring the sound board's own 2 MHz oscillator as a root makes 125/156 a consequence of two stated clocks rather than a hand-reduced fraction.

Atari System 1 now holds two trees built from the same declaration: the main board's stepped in main-CPU cycles, the speech section's stepped in sound-CPU cycles. That is what set_step_domain is for, and it is the pattern jv78.6 established.

One deviation from the issue's stated payoff. It suggested chip_hz should become tree.hz(sound) so the resampler input rate and the divider ratio share a derivation. That already happened where the two genuinely disagreed (Gottlieb, jv78.5). On these nine boards the chip constructors take the chip's own clock (an SN76489's 4 MHz, an AY's 1.5 MHz), which is not the same quantity as the tone-generator domain the divider steps, so rewriting them would have been churn without the guarantee. The table test gives the guarantee that mattered instead.

SAVE_VERSION 11 to 12.

title: Expose live clock domains in debug_registers/overlay_stats
description:
Make the live clock tree introspectable. ClockTree::domains() yields
(name, hz, num, den) per domain; surface it through debug_registers() and
overlay_stats().

WHY. ClockDivider has good unit tests (clock.rs:91) but the set of live clocks on
a running board is invisible to the debugger and the profiler. Answering "is the
sound chip running at the right rate?" today means reading the constructor. After
a runtime retune (Votrax VCO, TMS5220 clock select) the constructor is not even
the right answer.

Small, and only useful once boards actually carry trees — hence last.

Acceptance: a Gottlieb debug session shows the votrax domain's live Hz changing
when the speech DAC is written.
notes: Correction to the close reason above: the hex example was mangled by shell expansion. It should read "nobody checks $000DA6E6 against a datasheet".
close_reason:
Landed in 262ade0.

ClockTree implements Debuggable and Device, so a board marks its clocks field #[debug_device("Clocks")] and the panel lists every domain at its live rate. Device turned out to be a real fit rather than a convenience: its contract says configuration survives a reset and only runtime state clears, which is exactly what ClockTree::reset does to the phase accumulators. read/write/tick keep their no-op defaults, since a clock tree has no register file.

Eleven boards by attribute. Gottlieb's sound board and the three Namco wrappers hand-write their debug surface, so they list it by hand. Q*Bert also gained overlay_stats, the first machine to use that macro flag; its speech clock is the VCO the game steers, so its rates are the ones worth watching move.

Acceptance met directly: the_debugger_shows_the_live_votrax_rate writes 0x3000 and watches SPEECH_HZ follow convert_speech_clock. the_overlay_names_every_domain_and_its_rate pins the overlay line and checks it tracks a retune.

FOLLOW-UP FROM USE. The user ran it and the rates rendered in hex, which is useless for a clock: nobody checks /run/current-system/sw/bin/zshDA6E6 against a datasheet. Added DebugRegister::DECIMAL, a width of zero, and a branch in draw_register_grid that formats those with thousands separators (894,886). Zero is the honest spelling because such a row has no width in bits and no real register has one either. Chose that over a fourth field on DebugRegister, which would have meant threading a value through some 250 struct literals across every device and CPU file for a display nit; this keeps it to one constant, one branch, and one formatter with its own tests.

That formatting split is worth knowing about for anything added later: DebugRegister now covers two kinds of row, register contents in hex and magnitudes in decimal, and the width field is what distinguishes them.

title: Epic: Concrete bus dispatch (remove the per-access vtable)
description:
README.md:264 describes the Bus trait as 'compile-time polymorphism with no vtable overhead'. That is the design intent and not what ships.

core/src/core/bus.rs:96 — bus_split! coerces the machine to &mut dyn Bus, and all 91 execute_cycle call sites across machines/src pass a trait object (264 bus_split! sites in total). So every memory read, opcode fetch and device write in every running machine goes through a vtable — millions per second per CPU — and, more costly than the indirect call itself, the optimiser cannot inline bus dispatch into the CPU inner loop or keep board state in registers across it.

Largest single structural performance item in the codebase.

Root cause: the trait object exists only to work around the borrow split, because CPU and bus state live in one struct. Separating them (struct X { cpu: Z80, bus: XBus }) makes self.cpu.execute_cycle(&mut self.bus, ..) borrow-check natively at a concrete type, monomorphising the whole loop and deleting the unsafe as a side effect.

Sweeping — roughly 40 machine files — so this epic is deliberately prototype-first. The design doc is written from prototype results, not before them.

Blocked by the benchmark harness (nothing here is arguable without it) and by golden frames (this is exactly the change most likely to move pixels).
close_reason: Done. Every machine in the registry dispatches at a concrete bus: CPU state in one field, bus state in another, so cpu.execute_cycle(&mut bus, ..) borrow-checks natively and the cycle monomorphises. bus_split! is deleted and there is no unsafe left on any CPU<->bus path (the only unsafe in core/machines is one get_unchecked in the address-space page lookup). Measured 0 to -19% emulation time per frame, tracking how much of a frame is CPU bus cycles: quantum -19.0, pacman -18.3, mariobros -17.8, dkong -16.8, roadrunner -15.1, galaga -14.5 at the top; docastle -4.1 and qbert -2.3 at the bottom, where per-cycle device work dominates. Two findings worth keeping: splitting the bus view inside the cycle loop is SLOWER than the trait object (split once per frame), and inverting the frame loop to scanline-outer/cycle-inner is worth as much again on fast boards. See docs/designs/concrete-bus-dispatch.md for the shape, the numbers and the regressions only the ROM-gated suites caught. Follow-up headroom is tracked in icym.

title: Correct the README's vtable claim
description:
README.md:264 states the Bus trait gives 'compile-time polymorphism with no vtable overhead'. Every shipped machine dispatches through &mut dyn Bus, so the claim is false today regardless of what the rest of this epic concludes.

Fix now, independently of the refactor: describe what actually happens and why (the borrow split), and reference this epic as the intended direction. If the refactor lands later, update again.

Trivial, unblocked, and worth doing immediately so the document stops misleading.
close_reason: README.md:311 now describes the actual dispatch (bus_split! -> &mut dyn Bus, virtual call per access, unsafe reborrow because CPU and bus state share a struct) and points at this epic. Commit 66a4f84.

title: Prototype: convert Pac-Man to concrete-typed bus dispatch and measure
description:
First prototype — chosen for the cleanest signal: single Z80, one AddressSpace16, one board struct.

Split NamcoPacBoard so CPU state and bus state are separate fields of the wrapper, then call self.cpu.execute_cycle(&mut self.bus, BusMaster::Cpu(0)) directly with a concrete bus type. Remove the bus_split! use and its unsafe on this path only.

Report:
- frames/sec before and after, from the benchmark harness
- whether the generated inner loop actually inlines bus dispatch (cargo asm or perf)
- how much of the board had to move, and what fought back

Do not generalise yet. The point is a number and a shape, not coverage.

Blocked by the benchmark harness.
close_reason:
Converted in 498374b. Shape: the board keeps everything the Z80 talks to, the CPU moves up into the game wrapper, and the two are disjoint fields, so cpu.execute_cycle(&mut board, ..) borrow-checks natively. Base decoding (A15 mirror, IM2 vector latch) became 'impl Bus for NamcoPacBoard'; Ms. Pac-Man's daughter card became MsPacmanBus, a view struct built from disjoint field borrows (split()), since its state is not board state. bus_split! and its unsafe are gone from this hardware.

Codegen: the Pac-Man Z80 cycle instantiation has 0 indirect calls vs 48 in the dyn one -- the vtable really is gone. But bus dispatch became a *direct call* to bus_read_common/bus_write_common (29+17 sites), not an inlined access: those functions are too big to inline (page lookup, watchpoint check, trace check).

Numbers (phosphor-bench, release, 400f x 5 reps, best of 12 alternating runs of both binaries, host under load ~12): pacman emul 0.756 -> 0.737 ms/f, -2.5%. Core-pinned rounds with +/-0.5-1.7% spread: 1.733 -> 1.704, -1.7%. mspacman similar. So the vtable is worth ~2%, not the 'largest structural item' the epic assumed.

What fought back:
1. The BusDebug derive. With the CPU out of the board, the board loses cpus() and its debug read/write arms. Fixed generally in 057a13d: #[debug_bus] merges a nested BusDebug, and map-driven read/write arms no longer require a local #[debug_cpu].
2. Cpu::reset takes '&mut dyn Bus + 'static', which a borrowed view struct cannot satisfy. Worked around for Z80 (reset ignores the bus) by resetting against the board. CPUs that fetch a reset vector -- 6502, 6809, 68000 -- will need Cpu::reset generic over the bus before their boards can convert.
3. MachineDebug::debug_tick assumed bus_split! + board.tick(bus); added a split_cpu arm calling the machine's inherent step_cycle().

Golden frames unchanged for all 39 machines.

title: Prototype: convert Galaga (3x Z80) and measure
description:
Second prototype — confirms whether the win scales to a multi-CPU board, where vtable dispatch should cost most: three Z80s sharing NamcoGalagaBoard, plus the 06XX/51XX devices ticking per cycle.

This is also where the borrow split is genuinely harder: three CPUs and the board all want to move independently, and namco_galaga.rs:461 mutates board state (namco51 LLE, interrupt latches) around each CPU tick.

Report the same three things as the Pac-Man prototype, plus: whether a shared-bus-with-multiple-CPUs shape needs a different pattern than the single-CPU case.

Blocked by the Pac-Man prototype.
close_reason:
Converted in 3d8886b (galaga + digdug + xevious together -- they share NamcoGalagaBoard).

Numbers (phosphor-bench, release, 400f x 5 reps, best of 8 alternating runs, idle host):
  galaga  0.887 -> 0.759 ms/f  -14.5%
  xevious 1.164 -> 1.037       -10.9%
  digdug  2.091 -> 1.956        -6.5%
  pacman  0.748 -> 0.706        -5.6%  (unchanged binary, re-measured idle: the -2.5% in .2 was taken under load average 12)

So the win is real and scales with CPU count on a shared bus, as the epic expected -- galaga (3 Z80s) gains 2.5x what pacman does.

Shape for multi-CPU: the CPUs group into one GalagaCpus field beside the bus; the board's tick splits into begin_cycle/latch_pc/end_cycle and the per-cycle sequence becomes a free generic fn over a NamcoGalagaBus trait. Each game's bus is a view struct of disjoint field borrows (board + that game's bus-visible state). No new pattern was needed for multiple CPUs -- the same split works, because the three CPUs are stepped by one generic tick that holds the bus.

The load-bearing finding: WHERE the split happens decides whether the change wins at all. Splitting per cycle (the obvious translation of the old per-cycle tick) made galaga 6% SLOWER than the trait object (0.883 -> 0.938) -- a multi-pointer view rebuilt 50,688 times a frame costs more than the indirect call it removes. Hoisting the split to once per frame-boundary run turned that into -14.5%. Pac-Man, whose bus needs no view at all (the board *is* the bus), never had this problem.

Also: SAVE_VERSION 4 -> 5, since the CPU block now precedes the RAM block in these machines' state. Golden frames unchanged for all 39 machines.

title: Decision and design doc from the prototype results
description:
With two measured data points, decide: roll out across roughly 40 machine files, apply selectively to the hot boards, or abandon.

If proceeding, write docs/designs/concrete-bus-dispatch.md covering the target struct shape, what happens to bus_split! and its three arms (u16, u32, u32-word), how multi-bus-master boards (blitter, DMA, DmaVram) fit, the migration order, and the mechanical ast-grep pattern for the bulk of the work.

Then decompose the rollout into per-board-family child issues under this epic.

Blocked by both prototypes.
close_reason:
Decision: PROCEED with the full rollout. Design doc written at docs/designs/concrete-bus-dispatch.md (commit 23f89d7) from the two prototypes' measured results.

Numbers that decided it (idle host, best of 8 alternating A/B runs): galaga -14.5%, xevious -10.9%, digdug -6.5%, pacman -5.6% emulation ms/frame. Codegen confirms the mechanism: 0 indirect calls in the converted Z80 cycle instantiation vs 48 in the dyn one. The win scales with how much of a frame is CPU cycles, so multi-CPU boards gain most.

The doc covers: the two target shapes (board-is-the-bus, preferred; bus view of disjoint field borrows where the game interposes state), the per-family generic tick, frame-boundary renders, what the BusDebug derive needed (#[debug_bus]), the SAVE_VERSION bump rule, and the load-bearing constraint -- split once per run, never per cycle, since a per-cycle split measured 6% SLOWER than the trait object.

Open problems recorded: Cpu::reset takes '&mut dyn Bus + 'static' and blocks every reset-vector CPU (6502/6809/68000); Williams' blitter as a second bus master; the two wide-bus bus_split! arms (which are not width-specific work -- they vanish with the trait object).

Rollout decomposed into child issues, ordered by payoff per unit of risk:
  bek7 (P1) Cpu::reset generic over the bus  <- blocks the four below
  129w      TKG-04 (Donkey Kong, DK Jr, Mario Bros)
  hwd9      Galaxian + MCR II
  ra3r      Do Castle family
  8v1a      Williams (blocked by bek7)
  hv5p      Atari DVG/AVG family (blocked by bek7)
  3hnp      Atari System 1 + Gottlieb System 80 (blocked by bek7)
  642d (P3) standalone machines, then delete bus_split! (blocked by bek7)
Plus icym (related): an inlinable fast path for backed-memory reads -- the next lever, available only because dispatch is now concrete.

CLAUDE.md (machines + core) and the README were updated to describe the mixed state rather than the old advice.

title: Invert run_frame to scanline-outer / cycle-inner
description:
Every board's tick() opens with clock % cycles_per_frame, a scanline-boundary divisibility test, and a ladder of frame-position comparisons — VBLANK, sound NMI scanlines, watchpoint context latching — all evaluated on every one of the roughly 50,000 cycles in a frame to be true on a few hundred of them. Galaga runs this ladder three times per cycle, once per Z80.

  machines/src/namco_pac.rs:451-492
  machines/src/williams.rs:465
  machines/src/namco_galaga.rs:461

The divisions themselves are likely folded to multiplies since the timing constants are const, so this is about branch volume and instruction cache rather than division cost — but the structure is doing per-frame work at per-cycle frequency.

Fix: run_frame iterates scanlines outer, cycles inner. Boundary work then happens 264 times per frame instead of 50,688, and the inner loop shrinks to CPU-plus-device ticks.

Independent of the dispatch change but touches the same loops, so sequence them together. Blocked by the benchmark harness and by golden frames — this reorders when board state is observed relative to CPU execution, which can legitimately move pixels.
close_reason:
Done for the Namco boards in 2b1667f (namco_pac + namco_galaga). Williams was deliberately left out: it still dispatches through bus_split!, so its inversion is folded into its conversion issue (8v1a), whose notes now carry the pointer.

Shape: the board's per-cycle work splits into begin_scanline (render, VBLANK, 51XX TC pin, sound-NMI scanline timer -- all of which fire on scanline boundaries) and begin_cycle_inner (no frame-position test at all). run_scanlines iterates scanlines outer / cycles inner; run_frame and run_cycles route whole scanlines through it and any partial scanline through the per-cycle tick, so a clock the debugger left off-phase still runs the identical cycle sequence. tick remains the debugger's single-cycle path. Both paths call the same pieces of work, so they can only differ in how often the frame position is tested.

Measured (phosphor-bench, release, 400f x 5 reps, idle host) -- this change, and cumulative against the dyn baseline the epic started from:
  galaga  0.759 -> 0.646  -14.9%  (-27.2% cumulative)
  xevious 1.037 -> 0.850  -18.0%  (-27.0%)
  pacman  0.706 -> 0.611  -13.5%  (-18.3%)
  digdug  1.956 -> 1.826   -6.6%  (-12.7%)
Dig Dug gains least because much of its frame is the background tilemap renderer, which neither change touches.

Golden frames unchanged for all 39 machines.

title: Epic: Conformance ROMs as the video timing oracle
description:
Conformance ROMs as the video timing oracle, across boards rather than one.

THE AMBITION. Replace what golden frames are being asked to do and cannot: tell
"we draw the picture differently" apart from "the machine is in a different
state". A conformance ROM is our own code, its expected output is derived from
the schematic and the datasheet rather than borrowed from another emulator, its
verdict is a byte in RAM, and it needs no arcade ROMs, so it runs in CI. Williams
is the proof of concept and is filed as its own epic; this one is the programme
it belongs to.

WHY IT IS NOT SIMPLY "DELETE GOLDEN FRAMES", AND THIS HAS TO BE SAID PLAINLY. A
conformance ROM draws its own patterns. It can prove when a machine samples video
state, that the beam and the CPU are phase locked, that a palette write splits
the picture where the beam is, that an interrupt arrives on the right line. It
cannot prove that Joust's artwork is right: tile and sprite decode, palette
derivation from the PROMs, orientation and the ROM loading itself are all outside
what a synthetic program exercises, and those are exactly what a golden frame
pins. Anyone who reads this epic as "conformance ROMs retire golden frames"
will delete a real check and replace it with a different one.

The honest claim is narrower and still worth the work: golden frames currently
carry two jobs at once, and they only do one of them well. They pin artwork,
which nothing else does. They also stand in as the only guard against timing
regressions, which they do badly, because a timing change and an attract-loop
phase change look identical in a hash. Conformance ROMs take the second job.
What that leaves golden frames doing, and whether it is worth the recapture
cost, is phosphor-emulator-gr27, which asks exactly this question and predates
this epic.

THE CENTRAL TECHNICAL RISK: SELF-SYNCHRONISATION DOES NOT GENERALISE FOR FREE.
The Williams ROM never uses a delay loop. It polls the video counter at $CB00,
which reads scanline & $FC, so a constant cycle offset between two
implementations cancels and the program stays locked to the beam. That is
precisely why Williams was chosen first, and it is not a property the other
candidate boards obviously share. A quick look at the tree: btime derives an
in-vblank bit from its scanline and exposes that to the CPU, which is one edge
per frame rather than a counter, and most of the other candidates expose no beam
position at all. A board that can only see vblank can synchronise per frame but
must count cycles to place anything inside a frame, which reintroduces the
sensitivity the Williams design specifically avoided. How coarse a primitive is
still good enough, and which boards have what, is the first question and it is
research, not code.

THE TOOLCHAIN DECISION ALREADY GENERALISES. The Williams epic ports its source
to asl rather than packaging lwtools, and asl assembles far more than 6809. A
second board on a Z80, a 6502 or a 68000 needs no new assembler in the dev shell.
That was not the reason for the choice but it is a real dividend of it.

SEQUENCING. Williams lands first and completely, including the blitter bug it
already found and the golden-frame recapture that fix will force. Nothing else in
this epic starts before there is one working instrument in the tree, because
every generalisation decision below is better made against a working example
than against a design document.

RELATED WORK. docs/designs/raster-sampling-fidelity.md and
phosphor-emulator-raster-sampling-6kae ask when each board's video circuit reads
each piece of state; a conformance ROM is how an answer to that gets pinned once
it is known. W3 in particular is research whose result needs an instrument.
docs/designs/frame-regression.md is the ancestor of this idea.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
The survey (hl4t.1) is done: docs/designs/conformance-rom-board-survey.md, with
the result and its reasoning on that issue's comment thread.

THE HEADLINE ANSWER TO THIS EPIC'S FIRST QUESTION. Self-synchronisation does
generalise, but not through the primitive Williams used. No other board in the
candidate set has a video counter register. Two have something better in a
different shape:

  atari_system1 (roadrunner only): a motion-object list entry flagged 0xFFFF
  fires IRQ3 at a scanline the program picks, one line wide, with the state
  readable at 0x2E0000 bit 7. A programmable scanline interrupt with a poll path.

  mcr2: the Z80 CTC. Prescale 256 is exactly one scanline on the MCR clock tree,
  so a timer channel is a programmable scanline interrupt and its readable down
  counter is a vertical line counter, started from the board's own line-0
  trigger.

Three more boards (gridlee, namco_galaga, foodf) can place an event at
hard-wired lines and nowhere else, which the epic's three-way scale had no room
for and which is the class that decides where effort goes. Two boards
(gottlieb, mrdo) and one game (marble) have frame-level anchors only. btime the
same, with a DECO CPU-7 opcode-encryption tax on top. Nothing scored NONE.

The second thing the survey settled, which the epic did not ask and should
know: all seven W3 boards render once per frame. gridlee, which is not on that
list, is the only other board in the tree rendering per scanline. So a picture
assertion on any W3 board lands red and stays red until the raster work
finishes. That does not make it worthless, since W1/W2/W3 have no acceptance
test today other than "golden frames unchanged", but it is a different kind of
artifact from the Williams suite and worth deciding about deliberately.

THE DECISION THIS EPIC NOW OWNS. Which board is second. The survey deliberately
did not pick, because the three candidates are each the best answer to a
different question and the choice is a programme call:

  roadrunner  widest structural jump from Williams, the only candidate that
              exercises AddressSpace32, so the strongest test of what hl4t.2's
              shared contract really is. Serves W3. Lands red. Carries xvz6.
  shollow     serves W1, which is the furthest-along raster issue. Z80, IM2,
              dirty-tile cache, palette inside video RAM. Lands red. 1kk2
              (its frame rate) should be settled first.
  gridlee     cheapest and the only one green on landing, but a sibling of
              Williams in CPU, video model and lineage, which is the thing
              hl4t.2 was written to avoid.

hl4t.2 stays blocked either way; it should be written against whichever of these
lands, not before.

FOUR DEFECTS FELL OUT OF THE READING, all filed, none fixed:
phosphor-emulator-1kk2 (mcr2 frame rate, P2), phosphor-emulator-d4d5 (mcr2 CTC
cascade), phosphor-emulator-xvz6 (atari_system1 IRQ3 on Marble),
phosphor-emulator-1ydi (foodf IRQ1 scanlines). Three of the four are in code no
test in this tree exercises for timing.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
DECIDED: Road Runner is the second board. Filed as phosphor-emulator-roadrunner-video-conformance-wfop with three children.

The survey offered three candidates and this is the one that answers hl4t.2's question rather than dodging it. Road Runner is FULL at one-line resolution through the motion-object timer interrupt, and it is as far from Williams as the tree gets: M68000 against M6809, AddressSpace32 against 16, tilemap plus motion objects against a bitmap, autovectored levels against a PIA. A shared contract derived from Williams plus gridlee would have been a contract for one kind of board wearing a plural; derived from Williams plus Road Runner it is a fact.

What it costs, and both were known going in. The picture assertions land RED, because Road Runner is one of the nine render-once machines, so a mid-frame write affects the whole picture until W3 (raster-sampling-6kae.3) converts the board. That is the point rather than the price: W1/W2/W3 have no acceptance test today beyond 'golden frames unchanged', and these assertions are it, written in advance. And the watchdog on this board actually bites at 8 frames, unlike Williams's, so the skeleton has to strobe 880001 from the first line of code.

hl4t.2 is now blocked on wfop rather than on itvk, so it unblocks when the second board lands rather than looking actionable while no second board exists.

title: Survey: what can each board's CPU see of the beam?
description:
Survey: what can each board's CPU see of the beam? Research, not code.

THE QUESTION THIS ANSWERS. The Williams ROM is immune to a constant cycle offset
between implementations because it never waits by counting cycles. It polls the
video counter at $CB00, which reads scanline & $FC, so every wait is keyed to
where the beam actually is. Reproducing that on a second board requires the
second board to expose something equivalent. Nothing says it does.

WHAT TO DETERMINE PER BOARD, FROM THE SCHEMATIC AND A REFERENCE DRIVER, NOT BY
PROBING OUR OWN EMULATOR. Inferring structure from behaviour has failed every
time it has been tried in this repository.

1. Is there a CPU-readable vertical counter, and at what resolution? Williams
   has four scanlines. Some Atari boards latch a vertical count or expose
   individual 2V/4V/8V/16V lines, which is the same thing at coarser grain.
2. If not a counter, is there a CPU-readable level that changes inside the
   frame: a vblank bit, an hblank bit, a 32V-style divider output? btime derives
   an in-vblank bit from its scanline and hands it to the CPU
   (machines/src/btime.rs:559), which is one edge per frame. That is enough to
   synchronise TO a frame and not enough to place anything inside one.
3. If neither, is there an interrupt that fires at a known scanline? An IRQ at a
   fixed line is a beam-locked event even when nothing is readable, and a
   handler can timestamp itself against whatever else the board offers.
4. What does the board give a program for storage that is not displayed? The
   Williams ROM hides its variables, stack and result block in undisplayed video
   RAM columns. A board with a small tilemap and a separate work RAM is easier;
   a board with no spare RAM is a problem to solve before writing any code.
5. What CPU, what link address, and does asl target it?

BOARDS. The seven raster-sampling-fidelity names first, since that is where an
instrument is already wanted: namco_galaga (galaga, digdug, xevious), btime,
mrdo, foodf, gottlieb, mcr2, atari_system1. Add gridlee, which is the other
board in the tree already rendering per scanline.

THE OUTPUT is a table: board, CPU, synchronisation primitive and its resolution,
scratch storage, and a verdict of one of three. FULL means a Williams-style
self-synchronising ROM is possible. FRAME means only frame-level synchronisation
is available, so a ROM can test what happens across a frame boundary but cannot
place an event at a scanline without counting cycles, and any such test carries
the cycle-offset caveat explicitly. NONE means a conformance ROM buys nothing
over the existing tests and the board keeps its golden frame.

A FRAME or NONE verdict is a real result, not a failure. The value of this
survey is deciding where NOT to spend the effort.
close_reason: Survey complete: docs/designs/conformance-rom-board-survey.md, eight boards, table plus per-board derivations. No board scored NONE. Two are FULL (roadrunner via the motion-object timer interrupt, mcr2 via the Z80 CTC as a line counter), three place events at hard-wired lines only, three are frame-level. The three-way verdict scale needed a fourth value and the doc says why. Four defects filed: 1kk2, d4d5, xvz6, 1ydi. Choice of second board deliberately left to the epic.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
Survey done, 2026-08-27, against dac620d. Full write-up with every citation is
docs/designs/conformance-rom-board-survey.md; this is the result and the parts a
reader needs before opening it.

WHAT WAS READ. Per board, MAME's driver header comment and machine
configuration, then the driver source for anything the header left open, then
our board file. Nothing was determined by probing our emulator. Eight boards: the
seven from raster-sampling-fidelity W3 plus gridlee.

THE LOADING MECHANISM GENERALISES AND WAS NEVER THE HARD PART.
AddressSpace32::debug_poke ignores AccessKind exactly as the 16-bit space does
(address_space32.rs:466), so "poke an image into the program-ROM window of a
bare machine and reset" works on all eight. Reset vectors land inside the window
everywhere, including Gottlieb, where the 8088's 0xFFFF0 aliases to 0xFFF0
because A16-A19 are undecoded (MAME's map.global_mask(0xffff)). asl assembles
every CPU in the set: 6809, Z80, 6502, 68000, 68010, 8086 all accepted (there is
no "8088" type name; 8086 is the same encoding). Checked by assembling a cpu
directive for each, not assumed.

THE THREE-WAY VERDICT SCALE DID NOT FIT AND I ADDED A FOURTH. FULL, FRAME and
NONE leave no room for the three boards whose beam is visible only through
interrupts hard-wired to particular scanlines. Those boards can place an event at
those lines and nowhere else, without counting cycles, which is much stronger
than FRAME and clearly weaker than FULL. I called it FIXED. Collapse it back if
you disagree, but the distinction is what decides where to spend the effort.

  FULL   atari_system1 (roadrunner only), mcr2
  FIXED  gridlee, namco_galaga, foodf
  FRAME  atari_system1 (marble), btime, gottlieb, mrdo
  NONE   nothing

TWO BOARDS CAN NAME AN ARBITRARY SCANLINE, AND NEITHER DOES IT WITH A COUNTER
REGISTER.

atari_system1 has the finest primitive surveyed. An entry in the motion-object
list flagged 0xFFFF in its second word is a timer: IRQ3 fires at the top of that
entry's band, one scanline wide, and the state is readable at 0x2E0000 bit 7. The
program picks the line. One-line resolution with both an interrupt path and a
poll path, plus a live vblank level at 0xF60000 bit 4. Road Runner has that
hardware and is in our registry against the roadrunn set; Marble does not. MAME
splits the driver in two over exactly this (atarisy1.cpp:2686: "hardware to
generate interrupt 3 only exists on LSI Cart 2, 3, 4 & cockpit boards"), and
atarisy1_state::update_timers is an empty function. Our board file implements the
timer unconditionally, which is right for Road Runner and wrong for Marble; filed
as phosphor-emulator-xvz6.

mcr2 was the surprise. Satan's Hollow has no video counter and no vblank bit, and
I nearly graded it FRAME on that. The Z80 CTC at ports 0xF0-0xF3 is fully
program-controlled, the board triggers channel 2 at scanlines 0 and 240, and the
MCR clock tree makes 256 CPU cycles exactly one scanline (19.968 MHz, Z80 at /8,
dot clock at /4, 512 dots per line). So a timer channel at prescale 256 is a
programmable scanline interrupt, and the Zilog CTC's readable down counter is a
vertical line counter. That is a hardware timer counting the board clock, not a
software delay loop, so it does not reintroduce sensitivity to CPU instruction
timing.

THE SECOND FACT THAT SHAPES THE PROGRAMME. All seven W3 boards render once per
frame. Only gridlee, which is not on that list, renders per scanline today. So on
every W3 board a T6/T7-style picture assertion fails by construction until the
raster work lands. That is not a reason to skip them, since a failing conformance
assertion is a specification and W1/W2/W3 have no acceptance test other than
"golden frames unchanged", but a ROM there lands red and stays red, which is a
different artifact from the Williams suite.

WHAT MAKES FIXED USABLE, WHICH THE WILLIAMS DESIGN DID NOT NEED TO NOTICE. Seven
of the ten Williams assertions are CPU-observable and put their verdict in RAM.
The two picture assertions are not: the harness reads the framebuffer. That
second readout is a measurement of beam position in its own right. A write issued
promptly on a beam-locked interrupt changes the picture from a row that says
which scanline the interrupt fired on, and the harness reads that row without the
program knowing anything. Interrupt latency is a small constant, well under one
scanline on every board here. So a FIXED board carries T6 and T7 keyed to its
wired lines. What FIXED cannot carry is the T1/T2/T3 family, which measures where
a signal's edges are and needs a readable position.

WHAT I DID NOT DO. No code, no schematic check, no board run. Every resolution
figure is what the primitive can express, not a measurement of what our
implementation does with it. The FIRQ at gridlee scanline 92 is recorded as
unusable rather than surveyed further: MAME's header says "FIRQ generated by ???
(but should be around scanline 92)", so an expectation built on it would pin the
guess.

FOUR DEFECTS FOUND WHILE READING, ALL FILED, NONE FIXED.
  phosphor-emulator-1kk2  mcr2 declares 36.93 Hz; the reference says 30 Hz, and
                          our constants give neither 30 nor 60. P2.
  phosphor-emulator-d4d5  mcr2 does not cascade CTC channel 0's zero-count into
                          channel 1's trigger, which MAME wires.
  phosphor-emulator-xvz6  atari_system1 enables IRQ3 for both its games and only
                          Road Runner's cartridge has it (above).
  phosphor-emulator-1ydi  foodf fires IRQ1 on 0/64/128/192; the hardware is 32V,
                          i.e. 32/96/160/224, and MAME says in its own source
                          that its positions are wrong and it does not know why.

Three of the four are in code that no test in this tree exercises for timing,
which is the argument for the programme restated as evidence.

THE FORK I DID NOT SETTLE, AND WHY. Choosing the second board is a programme
decision, not a survey result. Three candidates, each the best answer to a
different question, laid out as a table in the doc:

  roadrunner  the widest structural jump from Williams and the only candidate
              that exercises AddressSpace32, so the strongest test of what the
              shared contract in hl4t.2 actually is. Serves W3. Picture tests
              land red. Slapstic window to steer around, and xvz6 underneath.
  shollow     the primitive that surprised the survey, and the board whose open
              raster issue (W1, per-scanline palette) is furthest along. Z80,
              IM2, tilemap with a dirty-tile cache, palette inside video RAM.
              Picture tests land red. 1kk2 should be settled first.
  gridlee     cheapest by a wide margin and the only one green on landing:
              already per-scanline, M6809 so the source idioms and the asl build
              port unchanged, palette bank latched per scanline so a T6-style
              split needs no palette RAM. But it is a sibling of Williams, and
              hl4t.2 exists to avoid deriving a contract from one kind of board
              wearing a plural.

Recorded on the epic for a decision.

title: Shared conformance-ROM harness contract, after the second board
description:
Generalise the Williams harness into a shared conformance-ROM contract, once
there is a second board to generalise against.

DO NOT DO THIS FIRST. The Williams harness is about 480 lines and most of it is
assertions about Williams. What is genuinely shared is smaller than it looks:

- Load an image into a bare machine through BusDebug::write at a per-board link
  address, then reset. This works because AddressSpace16::debug_write ignores
  AccessKind and backed ReadOnly regions take the write, and because the CPU
  fetches its reset vector through the bus. Both are core properties, not
  Williams ones, so this part generalises directly.
- A result block at a board-specific address, read back through the debug bus
  after each frame, with a magic byte that must be present or the run is a wedge
  rather than a pass. The vacuous-pass guard is the part worth standardising
  most, because it is the part every future board will be tempted to skip.
- A phase counter the harness watches to decide which frames to capture.
- Re-assembly drift guard, one per ROM, sharing the assembler-present check.

What does not generalise is every expectation, the ROM's storage layout, and the
synchronisation primitive. Resist folding those into a trait.

WRITE IT WHEN THE SECOND BOARD ARRIVES, NOT BEFORE. A shared shape derived from
one example is a guess. Derived from two it is a fact. The second board comes out
of the survey issue, which may also report that no second board can host one, in
which case this issue closes unstarted and that is the correct outcome.

WHERE IT LIVES. The Williams suite sits in machines/tests because it is
registry-driven and needs no ROMs, which is what puts it in CI. Shared helpers
belong beside it rather than in phosphor-harness, whose tests are all ROM-gated
by design.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
The second board is decided: Road Runner, phosphor-emulator-roadrunner-video-conformance-wfop. This issue's blocks edge now points at that epic instead of the closed Williams one, so it stops appearing in br ready while there is still only one example to generalise from.

Why this pairing makes the question answerable. This issue exists because a shared shape derived from one example is a guess. Road Runner differs from Williams in every axis the harness touches: the CPU (M68000 against M6809), the address space (AddressSpace32 against AddressSpace16, which the loader half of the contract rests on), the video model (tilemap plus motion objects against a bitmap), the interrupt structure (autovectored levels against a PIA), the scratch storage (work RAM against undisplayed video RAM columns), and the synchronisation primitive (a programmable one-line interrupt against a four-line counter register).

That last one matters most for the contract. The Williams harness has 'poll a counter' baked into its shape; if the second board also had a counter, the contract would enshrine it, and the third board would break it. Deriving from a counter and an interrupt at once is what forces the primitive to be the thing that does not generalise, which this issue already predicted in its description.

One prediction to check when writing it. The description lists four shared parts: the loader, the result block with its magic-byte wedge guard, the phase counter, and the drift guard. The Road Runner epic's first child (phosphor-emulator-uzbt) builds exactly those four and nothing else, so it is a direct test of that list. If a fifth thing turns out to be shared, or one of the four turns out not to be, that is the finding.

title: Epic: Contained fidelity and coverage fixes
description:
Six independent, well-scoped items from the codebase review. No shared design, no ordering between them — take them as appetite allows. Grouped only so they do not get lost between the large structural epics.

Three are hardware-fidelity gaps (68000 byte strobes, 6522 timers, x86 disassembler); three are coverage gaps (MB88xx/I8035 validators, untested devices, frontend logic).

title: 68000 byte writes should be a single half-word transaction, not a word RMW
description:
core/src/cpu/m68000/README.md, 'Word bus' section: a byte write is implemented as read-word / patch-byte / write-word. Correct for RAM and it passes state-only validation, but it is wrong against any side-effecting memory-mapped register — the read half triggers a phantom access the hardware never performs, and the write half puts a stale value back into the neighbouring byte.

The README already flags this as 'not faithful for side-effecting memory-mapped registers'. Four shipped boards drive 68000-class hardware through it (foodf, quantum, marble, roadrunner), so this is a latent bug class: the symptom would be an intermittent, hard-to-localise device misbehaviour.

Fix: carry UDS/LDS strobe width in the bus contract so a byte write is one half-word transaction. Then audit the four boards for registers currently absorbing a phantom read.

Note the interaction with the cycle-accurate M68000 epic — that work will touch the same bus interface, so sequence them deliberately rather than in parallel.

Acceptance: a write-only device register on a 68000 board sees exactly one access for a byte write, and no read.

title: MOS 6522 VIA: implement T1/T2 timers and the IFR/IER interrupt path
description:
core/src/device/via6522.rs:1 describes itself as a 'register-file stub'; :92 notes it 'emulates no interrupt sources (no timers/SR/CxN)'. It stores port and direction registers and nothing else.

It sits on Road Runner's speech board, where a real 6522 times the TMS5220 handshake. Speech works today because the surrounding code does not depend on the timer; the next board that needs one will find nothing there.

Fix: implement T1 (one-shot and free-run), T2 (one-shot and pulse counting), the interrupt flag/enable registers, and CA1/CA2/CB1/CB2 edge handling. Well-specified chip, contained job.

Acceptance: unit tests for both timer modes and the IRQ assert/clear path; Road Runner speech unchanged or improved.

title: Real I8088 disassembler to replace the DB $xx stub
description:
core/src/cpu/i8088/mod.rs:452 — 'Stub disassembler: show raw opcode byte. Full x86 disassembly TBD.' It returns the opcode as a define-byte pseudo-op.

Every other core has a real disassembler with its own test file (m6809, m6800, m6502, z80, m68000, i8035). This one blanks the debugger disassembly pane and the standalone disasm tool for the whole Gottlieb System 80 family — precisely where you would most want to read the code, with Reactor and Mad Planets on the roadmap.

Fix: the ModR/M decoder already exists in core/src/cpu/i8088/addressing.rs; reuse it rather than reimplementing the operand grammar. Intel syntax, matching the register naming already in registers.rs.

Acceptance: an i8088_disasm_test.rs in the shape of the other five; disasm --machine qbert --region main produces readable output.

title: MB88xx and I8035 single-step validators in cargo test
description:
MB88xx is the only CPU with no tests of any kind: no test file in core/tests/, no inline #[test] in core/src/cpu/mb88xx/, and no validator in cpu-validation/tests/. It drives core/src/device/namco51_lle.rs — the low-level Namco 51XX handling input for Galaga and Xevious.

Both MB88xx and I8035 have vector generators (cpu-validation/src/bin/gen_mb88xx_tests.rs, gen_i8035_tests.rs) but no matching tests/ validator, so cross-validation runs through the manual C++ make path outside cargo test entirely. I8035 at least has five unit-test files behind it; MB88xx has nothing.

Fix: add mb88xx_single_step_test.rs and i8035_single_step_test.rs alongside the other six, so cross-validation is a suite gate rather than a remembered ritual. Follow the skip-without-data convention (see the i8088 skip fix in the CI epic).

Acceptance: cargo test -p phosphor-cpu-validation covers all eight CPUs when data is present, skips cleanly when not.

title: Tests for the six untested devices, Namco WSG first
description:
Device coverage is better than it first appears — 26 of 41 device files carry inline tests, Votrax alone has 60. The untested set is: namco_wsg, namco06, namco53, namco51_lle, output_latch, dac.

Namco WSG is the odd one out and should come first: it is the sound chip for Pac-Man, Ms. Pac-Man, Galaga, Dig Dug and Xevious, it is 261 lines, and it has no test at all.

Directly assertable without a running machine: waveform-ROM decode, frequency accumulator stepping, per-voice volume, and the sound-enable gate.

Acceptance: each of the six has at least the register-contract and reset-behaviour tests the other devices carry.

title: Testable seam for frontend logic, starting with state.toml migration
description:
frontend/tests/ exists and is empty. There is genuinely testable SDL-free logic in the crate: binding resolution (input.rs), host-key conflict detection (host_keys.rs), and state.toml migration of the legacy top-level input_bindings/dip_switches maps into the per-machine [machines.<name>] section (state.rs).

The migration path matters most: it silently rewrites user config, and a bug there loses someone's rebinds.

frontend/src/emulator.rs:1366 shows the inline-test pattern already works for the pure helpers (presentation, fit_aspect).

Acceptance: migration is covered by round-trip tests over legacy and current state.toml shapes, including the both-present and neither-present cases.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
phosphor-emulator-mame-function-keys-kp4n will change the state.toml shape this
issue is about testing.

kp4n replaces HostBindings.overrides (HashMap<String, i32>, host_keys.rs:143)
with a shift-aware chord, so every persisted hotkey override changes from a bare
integer to a struct. Deserialization has to accept the old bare integer as
shift:false or it silently drops somebody rebinds, which is exactly the hazard
this issue names.

Whoever lands second inherits the other set of tests. Do not build two migration
frameworks. frontend/tests/ is still empty, so the first one there sets the
pattern for the legacy input_bindings/dip_switches migration as well.

The one thing worth insisting on across both: the fixture must be a literal
old-format string, not something built by the current serializer. A round-trip
test that constructs its input from the code under test cannot fail.

title: Vector generators write relative to CWD, so the documented command silently misfires
description:
cpu-validation/src/bin/gen_m6800_tests.rs:425 (and the i8035/m6809/mb88xx siblings) do:

  let out_dir = Path::new("test_data/m6800");

That is relative to the current directory. The validators read the same relative path with CWD = the crate root, because that is where cargo runs integration tests.

So the command the validators themselves print on a missing-data skip —

  cargo run -p phosphor-cpu-validation --bin gen_m6800_tests -- all

writes to <repo>/test_data/m6800 when run from the repo root, while the test looks in <repo>/cpu-validation/test_data/m6800. It only works if you happen to cd into cpu-validation first, which the message does not say.

The failure is silent in the worst way: the generator reports success, the validator then finds no data and skips, and libtest captures the skip message for a passing test — so the suite goes green having validated nothing.

Found while writing the CI validate job, which works around it with working-directory: cpu-validation plus an explicit directory check (.github/workflows/ci.yml). The workaround is correct but the underlying footgun should go.

Fix: resolve the output directory against env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR") in all four generators so the documented command works from anywhere, and update the hint text in require_test_data call sites if the command changes.

Acceptance: running the printed command from the repo root produces vectors the validator then finds.
close_reason: Generators and validators both resolve their vector directory against CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR, so the printed command works from the repo root; verified by removing the m6800 set, generating from the repo root, and watching the validator find it. The silent-pass the footgun created is closed too: PHOSPHOR_REQUIRE_VECTORS turns a missing directory from a skip into a failure, CI sets it, and the bespoke directory-existence loop and working-directory workaround are both gone.
