not at any top level, so the claim could not be met without touching those
files. williams.rs, starwars.rs and atari_system1_sound.rs now frame their
components and declare the per-variant ones optional. Williams gained three
optional chunks (SRAM, CVSD, blitter window-enable) rather than the one this
issue named; all three were append-and-guard.

A RULE THE OPTIONAL PATH IMPOSES, which rev 2 did not anticipate. Absence is
detected by peeking at the next tag, so an optional chunk must be followed by
another chunk or by the end of its enclosing reader. Inline scalars after an
optional chunk would be read as a tag, and if they matched, a component would be
parsed out of scalar bytes. There is no way to check this inside read_optional;
it is a rule for the calling body. Documented on read_optional and obeyed by all
three boards. Found by a test failing, not by reasoning.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO, stated because it would otherwise be assumed. Ordinal
tags renumber when components are reordered, so a reorder is caught only where
the two bodies differ; two components that encode alike swap silently and
nothing says so. Insertion and removal change the chunk count and are always
caught. Reordering is a wire change and needs the parent's save_version bumped.
Pinned by swapping_two_identically_shaped_components_is_not_detected in
core/tests/save_state_framing_test.rs, which should start failing when Stage B's
explicit ids land.

TESTS THAT CAN FAIL. core/tests/save_state_framing_test.rs models a component
rewrite in three states and checks where the failure lands. Verified by
disabling framing in the derive and re-running: 6 of 10 fail, including
a_component_that_grew_fails_against_its_own_name, which without framing LOADS
SUCCESSFULLY with a corrupted sibling. That silent corruption is the failure
mode the format existed to permit. Plus 29 unit tests in save_state.rs (CRC
check vector 0xCBF43926, flipped bit at three positions, version floor, child
under-read and over-read bounding, tag mismatch, unread-body, optional present/
absent/skipped/missing, reserved tags) and three new Williams board tests.

MEASURED COST. 6 bytes per chunk. Pac-Man 24 bytes on 3701 (0.65%), Tempest 66
on 7716 (0.86%, the worst measured), Empire Strikes Back 102 on 23961 (0.43%),
Joust 60 on 51114 (0.12%), Marble Madness 42 on 1081334 (0.004%).

VERIFIED. Full workspace clippy and tests clean. All four ROM-gated suites pass
(golden_frame, boot_check, save_state_rom, audio_sanity). Note golden_frame's
main registry sweep is disabled by phosphor-emulator-ukgy, so it did not
contribute; this change does not touch rendering.

LEFT: Stage B (hc61.3), unchanged in scope. Stage C (hc61.4) still deferred.
The 'region blobs' open question in the design doc is still open: regions stay
inline under write_bytes, so read_bytes_into's length check has NOT been relaxed
to take(len). That becomes redundant under Stage B, not Stage A.

title: Stage D: disasm dump-save tooling
description:
Stage D — `disasm dump-save <file>`, iterating tag/len and printing
`tag | len | hex preview`. Does not exist today in any form.

Cheap once Stage A's framing exists, and it makes every later stage easier to
debug: without it, diagnosing a chunk-boundary bug means reading hex by hand.
Sequenced right after Stage A for that reason, ahead of Stage B in the design's
own A/B/C/D lettering.

Should also report which top-level tags were required vs optional and which the
machine actually declares, so a "missing required chunk" error can be
investigated from the file rather than from the source.

Acceptance: dumping a save from a machine with an optional component present and
one with it absent shows the difference.
close_reason: disasm dump-save is implemented. It walks the file by loading it with a tracing reader rather than iterating tag/len, because a body interleaves inline scalars with framed components and a speculative walk would be guesswork. Acceptance met on both the Joust/Sinistar and Star Wars/Empire pairs.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
IMPLEMENTED on branch tlv-save-state, but NOT the way this issue describes.

WHY 'ITERATE TAG/LEN AND PRINT A HEX PREVIEW' CANNOT WORK. A component body
interleaves inline scalars with framed components: only nested Saveable fields
carry a tag and length, scalars and Vec<u8> blobs do not. So nothing about the
bytes says where a chunk starts. A walker that reads six bytes, treats them as
tag+len, and checks the length fits would produce a tree that reads plausibly
and is wrong wherever scalar data happened to look like a header. That is
diagnosing from the output.

WHAT SHIPPED INSTEAD. disasm dump-save walks the file by LOADING it. StateReader
gained an optional trace sink (Option<&'a RefCell<ChunkTrace>>, propagated by
sub(), no lifetime churn) that records depth, tag, name, absolute offset, length
and skipped-ness for every chunk entered. SaveState gained load_state_traced,
generated by machine_save_state!. The names printed are therefore the reader's
own (WilliamsBoard.cvsd, not 'tag 9'), and they are exact rather than inferred.

Four hand-written impl SaveState blocks (ccastles, gridlee, irobot,
missile_command) were byte-identical to machine_save_state! and now use it, so
they get the traced method rather than needing it written out. The trait's
default load_state_traced ERRORS rather than loading untraced: a default that
silently ignored the trace would print an empty tree and read as 'this machine
has no chunks'.

A BUG THE TESTS FOUND. load_machine_traced originally verified the CRC first,
which meant a corrupt or truncated file was refused before any walking, leaving
the tool useful only on files that were already fine. That is the opposite of
what it is for. It now splits the trailer without enforcing it and the caller
reports the checksum. Caught by
a_truncated_file_prints_the_chunks_it_reached_then_the_failure, not by review.

ACCEPTANCE MET, both ways.
- Joust vs Sinistar, same WilliamsBoard: Joust shows 10 chunks, Sinistar 13,
  the extra three being sram (4100 bytes), cvsd (18) and blitter_window (1),
  each with its own tag, length and offset.
- Star Wars vs Empire Strikes Back: the Slapstic is optional in the MIDDLE of
  the stream, tag 3 present for esb and absent for starwars, with tag 4 (the
  pokey array) following directly in both. That is the case the flat format
  could not express at all.

'WHICH TAGS ARE REQUIRED VS OPTIONAL' is answered differently from how this
issue framed it. There is no declared required/optional table to print; a chunk
is optional if the body reads it with read_optional. What the tool gives instead
is --machine <name> with no file, which saves a freshly built machine and dumps
the layout THIS BUILD expects. Diff that against a file that will not load and
the disagreeing chunk is visible directly. That seemed more useful than a static
table, and it needs no new declaration to maintain.

Also prints envelope version against the readable range, machine id, and
checksum (reported, not enforced). A load that fails prints the chunks reached
and then where it stopped.

TESTS: 8 end-to-end tests in tools/disasm/tests/dump_save_cli_test.rs driving
the real binary, covering the acceptance pair, the layout query, corrupt,
truncated, non-save, unknown machine and a v12 envelope. Plus 3 header unit
tests. ROM-free: create_bare gives real hardware with zero-filled ROM, and state
layout does not depend on ROM contents.

NOT DONE: no hex preview of chunk payloads. The names made it unnecessary for
every case tried; add it if a payload-level question actually comes up.

title: Stage B: opt-in field TLV for the types that need it
description:
Stage B — opt-in FIELD TLV, for the structs that actually need it.

    field_tlv := field_tag:u16 | field_len:u32 | field_payload

Under TLV, field_payload drops the redundant inner length: [u8;N] and Vec<u8>
write raw bytes, since field_len already is the length.

Add #[save(id=N)] to the derive and a #[save_tlv] struct opt-in. Structs WITHOUT
it keep emitting positional bodies inside their Stage A chunk — the two
interoperate, which is what makes this opt-in rather than a sweep.

MIGRATE ONLY WHERE THE PAYOFF IS CONCRETE:
- Boards with conditional fields that today append-and-guard: williams,
  starwars, atari_system1_sound.
- Any struct whose version has bumped more than once: tms5220, gottlieb.
- Any struct being reworked anyway — TLV-ify it as part of that commit.

That is where order-immunity and additive compatibility actually arrive, for the
~10 types that have ever needed them.

TAGS: per-struct, u16, stable across releases, assigned explicitly. 0 and 0xFFFF
reserved. A retired tag is never reused and readers skip it — add
#[save_retired(3, 7)] at the struct level so the derive can ASSERT no live field
collides with a retired id, rather than leaving "never reuse" to reviewer
discipline. Name-hashed tags are rejected: renames would silently break the wire.

Components need BOTH a version byte and TLV — TLV handles additive change, the
version byte handles semantic change (x: u16 -> u32, or a re-interpretation of an
existing field). Keep both.
close_reason: Field TLV is implemented and the six derive sites whose version had ever moved are migrated. The wire needed a field count this issue did not have, because 49 hand-written impls frame nothing and a TLV child in one of them reads past its own end; see the comment thread.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
IMPLEMENTED on branch tlv-save-state.

WHAT SHIPPED, AND THE ONE STRUCTURAL THING THIS ISSUE DID NOT HAVE.

#[save_tlv] opts a struct into field TLV; #[save(id = N)] per field;
#[save_retired(3, 7)] asserts at compile time that no live field reuses a
retired id. Positional and TLV structs nest in either direction, so the opt-in
is real. The writer emits in ascending id order rather than declaration order,
so the bytes are a function of the ids alone and a source reorder is a no-op on
the wire in both directions, not just for the reader.

THE FIELD COUNT. A TLV body is version:u8 | count:u16 | field_tlv{count}. The
count is not in this issue's wire format and is not optional. A TLV reader
dispatches in a loop, and a loop bounded only by its reader's end is correct
only when the reader IS the struct's own bytes. Stage A made all 68 derive sites
frame their children, but 49 Saveable impls are HAND-WRITTEN AND FRAME NOTHING:
they call a child's save_state straight into their own stream. GridleeSystem
does exactly that with its M6809, so the moment the M6809 became TLV its loop
read on into Gridlee's RAM blob.

Found by save_state_rom_test failing, not by review. Four such sites existed
(GridleeSystem, IrobotSystem, GottliebBoard, AtariSystem1Sound's speech
section). Hand-fixing them was rejected and the question was put to the user:
the requirement is invisible at the call site, no compile-time check is possible
because framing is the parent's choice, and the failure is NOT reliably loud.
Gridlee errored only because the stray bytes happened not to parse as TLV
headers; had they parsed, it would have loaded silently wrong. Two bytes per
struct buys the ability to opt a struct in without auditing everyone who embeds
it. This does not contradict 'children never frame themselves': a child cannot
know its own TAG, but it always knows how many fields it has.

ABSENT FIELD CONTRACT, which this issue left open. Required by default;
#[save(id = N, default)] opts into absence, keeping the constructed value.
Asked rather than picked. Making absence the default is what the design doc
literally describes, but it softens one level down exactly what Stage A
established: rev 2 rejected 'a missing chunk means keep current state' as a
correctness hazard, and a missing FIELD leaving a device at power-on while the
rest of the machine is at frame N is the same hazard. Additive compatibility now
costs one word, at the moment the field is added.

MIGRATED: the six derive sites whose version had ever moved, which is this
issue's own criterion. m6809 (2), tms5220 (3), votrax_sc01 (2),
williams_blitter (2), gottlieb (4), tempest (2). All derive sites, so migration
is attributes only.

NOT MIGRATED, and why: williams, starwars and atari_system1_sound, which this
issue also lists. Their append-and-guard problem was already solved at the CHUNK
level in Stage A, so field TLV would buy order-immunity for their scalars only,
in exchange for hand-rolling dispatch loops over about sixty fields in
hand-written impls. Offered as an option and not chosen.

THE ENVELOPE STAYED AT 13. Ten of thirty-three machines lose their saves (joust,
robotron, sinistar, starwars, esb, gridlee, irobot, qbert, roadrunner, tempest);
the other twenty-three keep BYTE-IDENTICAL ones, verified with disasm dump-save.
Under the pre-Stage-A format this would have invalidated all thirty-three. That
is the first time Stage A's containment has actually been exercised.

TESTS. 14 in core/tests/save_state_tlv_test.rs, each modelling a change that
used to be a wire break or a failure that must stay loud: reorder, add with
default, older-reader-skips-newer-field, retired id skipped, required field
absent, repeated id, version byte still catching a semantic change, a widened
field failing against its own name, a pinned byte sequence, interop in both
directions, and the unframed-parent case in miniature so the Gridlee bug has a
guard that needs no ROMs. Verified by sabotaging the reader to ignore the count:
8 of 14 fail, including that guard.

A GAP, STATED PLAINLY. The eight compile-time checks (missing id, reserved id,
duplicate id, retired collision, save_tlv without save_version, save and
save_retired without save_tlv, save_elements under TLV) were each verified by
writing the bad struct and watching it fail, and each reports its own reason.
But there is NO PERMANENT REGRESSION TEST for them. That needs trybuild, whose
expected-output files are brittle across toolchain bumps, and this repo pins its
toolchain precisely so local and CI clippy agree. Re-verify by hand if the
derive is reworked.

COST, measured with disasm dump-save rather than assumed: 6 bytes a field plus 2
a struct, less the 4-byte inner length each byte array stops carrying. Tempest
+2, Joust +190 (0.37%), Empire Strikes Back +346 (1.4%), Q*bert +442 (1.9%, the
worst, because the Votrax's 71 fields are mostly one byte each). Pac-Man,
Mr. Do! and Marble Madness are byte-identical.

dump-save gained --max-depth, because a TLV struct's fields are chunks and now
appear in the tree by name: Q*bert went from 20 lines to 94.

LEFT: Stage C (hc61.4). Its deferral condition was 'do this only if Stage B
proves the ergonomics are good'. The answer is split, and is recorded in the
design doc: for a derive site the ergonomics are good and the sweep is
automatable except for assigning the ids, which cannot be automated safely
because the ids are the wire contract (VotraxSc01 took 71 hand-numbered
attributes). For a hand-written impl nothing changed. The count byte does remove
the argument that a mixed codebase is risky, since a TLV struct is now safe
anywhere, so the case is purely cost against benefit.

title: Stage C: full TLV sweep of the remaining types
description:
Stage C — migrate the remaining ~107 Saveable types to field TLV.

DEFERRED, AND THE DESIGN EXPLICITLY DOES NOT RECOMMEND IT BY DEFAULT. Recorded so
the decision is visible rather than rediscovered.

THE CASE AGAINST: the 68 derive sites are mechanical, but the 49 hand-written
impls each need tag assignment and skip arms BY HAND, and 28 of 34 versioned
components have never changed once. A Pia6820 that has been at version 1 since
the project began does not need order-immunity. The cost is concentrated exactly
where the benefit is absent.

A MIXED CODEBASE IS A LEGITIMATE END STATE — TLV where it earns its keep,
positional where it does not — precisely because Stage A's chunk framing makes
the two interoperate.

DO THIS ONLY IF Stage B proves the ergonomics are good AND the sweep can be
largely automated. Revisit after Stage B has landed on its ~10 types; close this
if the answer is still no.

If it does happen, #[save_elements] becomes a no-op alias under TLV (bulk bytes
are the default and field_len is the length) and is retired at the end of this
stage.
close_reason:
Done, and re-shaped from what the description proposed. All 49 hand-written Saveable impls are gone: the address spaces got their own impl (which alone unblocked 22 boards that hand-enumerated memory a region at a time), five derive features were added because impls were blocked on them, and TLV came last and cost least because by then it is attributes.

Three impls remain in the tree and none is a leftover. AddressSpace16/32 ARE the mechanism. Namco51Wrapper must not build the variant the bytes name, because its LLE variant cannot be constructed from a file at all.

#[save_elements] is retired, as this issue planned.

NOT DONE, DELIBERATELY: about 66 of 125 derive sites are still positional. The description called for migrating those too; the decision is not to. TLV a struct when you are changing it anyway, leave it positional otherwise -- 28 of 34 versioned components have never changed once, and Stage A's framing plus Stage B's field count make the mixture safe rather than merely tolerable. The design doc now states this as the rule from here rather than as an open question.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
Stage B has landed, so this issue's deferral condition ('do this only if Stage B proves the ergonomics are good AND the sweep can be largely automated') can now be answered. The answer is split, and does not change the recommendation.

FOR A DERIVE SITE the ergonomics are good: #[save_tlv] plus one #[save(id = N)]
per field, no impl touched. But the sweep is NOT automatable in the part that
matters. Assigning ids is the wire contract, so a tool that numbers them is a
tool that can silently renumber them; VotraxSc01 took 71 hand-numbered
attributes and each one has to be right. The mechanical part (adding the
attribute) is not where the risk is.

FOR A HAND-WRITTEN IMPL nothing changed. It still needs a dispatch loop written
by hand, and that is where 49 of the remaining types are.

ONE ARGUMENT AGAINST THIS ISSUE DID GO AWAY. Stage B's TLV bodies carry a field
count, so a TLV struct is self-delimiting and correct inside any parent, framed
or not. A mixed codebase is therefore no longer risky, only mixed. The case is
now purely cost against benefit, and the benefit is still absent for the 28 of
34 versioned components that have never changed once.

So: still deferred, and the reason is now measured rather than predicted. Close
this if the answer is meant to stay no.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
SCOPING PASS: how many of the 49 hand-written impls could actually become derives.

This issue and the design doc both assume the 49 are hand-written because they
are irreducibly bespoke, and price Stage C accordingly. That is wrong for about
two thirds of them. All 49 were read and classified by what a derive would be
unable to produce.

THE HEADLINE. 22 of the 49 exist substantially because ADDRESSSPACE16/32 DO NOT
IMPLEMENT SAVEABLE. They hand-enumerate their board's memory, two lines per
region: w.write_bytes(map.region_data(Region::Ram)) and the matching
read_bytes_into. That is not bespoke logic, it is a missing impl in core.

AddressSpace16::regions() already returns &[RegionDescriptor] and each carries
its AccessKind, so an impl that saves exactly the writable regions is
well-founded rather than a heuristic: ROM is ReadOnly and drops out by
construction. It also removes a live bug class, since a board that forgets a
region in its hand-written list is silently wrong today and there is nothing to
catch it.

BREAKDOWN.

A. DERIVABLE NOW, no new derive features, 15 impls:
   core: galaxian_sound, namco51_lle, starwars_math, avg
   machines: asteroids_sound, btime, congo_sound, dkong_sound,
             docastle (DocastleSystem), galaxian_video, llander_sound,
             namco_galaga (GalagaCpus), pisces, roadrunner, z80dma
   Most are already a plain field sequence. Two need a note: starwars_math casts
   i16 to u16 and i32 to u32 purely for wire compatibility, which a migration
   changes anyway; avg calls self.display_list.clear() on load, which
   #[save_skip(default)] does exactly.

B. UNLOCKED BY THE ADDRESSSPACE IMPL ALONE, about 15 more:
   atari_system1, congo_bongo, docastle (board), galaxian, gottlieb, gridlee,
   mario_bros, mcr2, mrdo, namco_pac, scramble, tkg04 have NO other blocker.
   atari_avg, atari_dvg and missile_command add only a post-load clear, which
   #[save_skip(default)] covers.

So roughly 30 of 49, about 61%, are reachable with ONE core addition and
otherwise mechanical work.

C. NEEDS ENUM SUPPORT IN THE DERIVE, 3: m6502 InterruptType, m68000
   M68kVariant, slapstic (self.state.to_u8()). All three are fieldless enums
   with an explicit discriminant mapping. The derive only accepts structs with
   named fields. This is a small, general feature.

D. NEEDS THE INNER STRUCT TO DERIVE TOO, 3: konami_sound, atari_system1_sound,
   ssio flatten self.bus.* to keep the CPU first in the stream. Give the bus its
   own derive and the outer struct is cpu + bus. Same shape as the board case,
   without a memory map.

E. TYPE-SUPPORT GAPS, 5: irobot_mathbox ([Vec<u16>; 2] and [usize; 16], neither
   supported), i8035 and mb88xx (a length-tolerant RAM read: they save
   ram[..ram_mask+1] and reload with len.min()), ym2151 (index loops over
   per-channel arrays), namco50 (usize fields plus load-side masking that clamps
   a corrupt value into range, which a derive would silently drop).

F. GENUINELY BESPOKE, about 6: ccastles, foodf, quantum, irobot, williams,
   starwars. These combine accessor-backed state (stick position, novram, the
   blitter window-enable), conditional components, post-load remapping and
   variable-length reads. Leave them hand-written.

WHAT THIS CHANGES ABOUT STAGE C. The issue frames it as a TLV sweep across ~107
types and prices it by the 49 hand-written ones. But the expensive part is not
TLV, it is that the 49 are hand-written, and most of them are hand-written for
ONE removable reason. Splitting them is the better shape:

  C1  impl Saveable for AddressSpace16/32 over the writable regions. Enables ~15
      and removes the forgotten-region bug class. Worth doing on its own merits
      whether or not the rest of C ever happens.
  C2  Convert the ~30 mechanical impls to derive. Deletes roughly a thousand
      lines of paired read/write that today stay in sync by eye, and each one
      converted is one fewer place that can frame nothing, which is the class
      that broke Gridlee in Stage B.
  C3  Derive features for enums (3 impls) and, if wanted, accessor fields.
  C4  TLV opt-in for whatever comes out, which is then just attributes.

TLV is the LAST step and the cheapest, not the framing of the work.

CAVEAT, stated because it decides the real cost. 'Derivable' here means the
save/load bodies are a field sequence a derive could emit. It does NOT verify
that each struct's declaration order matches its current wire order, or that
every non-saved field already carries #[save_skip]. Both are per-struct work at
implementation time, and declaration order can be changed freely under TLV but
not under a positional derive. Expect real work per impl even in category A.

Every conversion is a wire change for that component, so it costs that
component's saves. Stage A means it costs only the machines containing it, which
is what makes doing this incrementally viable at all.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
C1 IMPLEMENTED on branch tlv-save-state: AddressSpace16 and AddressSpace32 now
implement Saveable.

THE RULE. A region is saved when the CPU can change it and it has backing:
AccessKind::is_cpu_writable() covers ReadWrite and WriteOnly, so ROM drops out
because it is ReadOnly and I/O because it has no bytes. Derived from the map
rather than listed by each board, which is the point: 'forgot to save a region'
stops being a silent bug with nothing to catch it.

    body   := version:u8 | count:u16 | region{count}
    region := id:u16 | len:u32 | bytes

Keyed on the BACKING region id, not on descriptors. A banked window or a mirror
is a second descriptor over bytes already accounted for; on the 32-bit side that
is explicit, since RegionTarget::Backing names a region that may differ from the
range's own. A 32-bit region counts as saveable if ANY range exposing it is
writable, so a pool reachable read-only through one window and writable through
another is still saved.

The count makes the body self-delimiting, for the same reason Stage B's TLV
bodies carry one: 49 hand-written impls frame nothing, so a map inside one would
otherwise be handed a reader running to the end of its parent's bytes. That is
the Gridlee failure again, and the fix is the same shape.

WHAT IS NOT SAVED: the page table. Where a region is currently mapped is rebuilt
by the board from its own bank register on load, which is what already happens
(see starwars.rs remapping after it reads self.bank). Saving it here as well
would give two sources of truth for one thing. Region CONTENTS only.

A FINDING FOR C2, from running the rule over every registered machine: NOT EVERY
BOARD KEEPS ITS MEMORY IN THE ADDRESS SPACE. Burgertime holds ram, videoram,
colorram, palette_ram and sound_ram as plain board fields and registers only ROM
in its map, so its main map has no CPU-writable region at all. It gets nothing
from C1. This was found by a test asserting every machine had one, which was my
wrong assumption rather than a defect; the test now asserts the property that
actually holds. Consistent with the scoping pass, which had already put
burgertime in the derivable-now group precisely because it makes no region_data
calls.

TESTS. 9 in core/tests/address_space_save_test.rs covering the rule at its
edges: writable round trip, ROM not saved (checked by loading into a DIFFERENT
ROM, since a round trip cannot see it), I/O not saved, a region the map has and
the file lacks erroring by name, a region the file has and the map lacks being
skipped, a resized region failing against its own name, a remapped window not
double-counting, self-delimiting inside an unframed parent, and the 32-bit
sibling. Plus 4 registry-driven ones in
machines/tests/address_space_regions_test.rs checking the derived set is exactly
the writable-and-backed set across every real machine map, which is where the
banked/mirrored/ROM-pool shapes a synthetic test would miss actually live.

NOT DONE, and worth being plain about: NOTHING USES THIS YET. No board has been
converted, so the rule is proven against real maps but not yet against a real
board's expectations. The first conversion is the test that matters, because it
answers the question these tests cannot: does the derived set match what a board
currently hand-saves? Two ways it could differ, both to check per board:
  - the blanket rule saves MORE, e.g. williams saves only palette[..16] of a
    larger palette region, and any writable region a board deliberately omits;
  - the blanket rule saves LESS, if a board persists something reachable only
    through a region marked ReadOnly or Io. None seen, but not ruled out.
Size is not a concern either way.

Gridlee is the natural first conversion: map-only blocker per the scoping pass,
and it is the board Stage B broke.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
FIRST C2 CONVERSION: gridlee, the board Stage B broke.

WHY IT ANSWERS SOMETHING C1's TESTS COULD NOT. C1 proves the rule is
self-consistent; only a conversion proves it matches what a board expected.
Gridlee's map is Ram(RW), VideoRam(RW), Io(Io), Nvram(RW), Rom(RO), so the
derived set is exactly {Ram, VideoRam, Nvram} and exactly what the hand-written
impl listed. First evidence that the two agree.

WHAT CHANGED. GridleeSystem's 60-line hand-written impl is gone. GridleeBoard
and GridleeSystem both derive Saveable with #[save_tlv]; the map is a single
#[save(id = 1)] and persists its own regions. Converted straight to TLV rather
than to a positional derive, because under TLV declaration order never has to be
reconciled with wire order, which is the one real cost the scoping pass flagged
for category A.

Net: -60 lines of paired read/write that stayed in sync by eye, and one fewer
impl that frames nothing.

VERIFIED. save_state_rom_test passes on real ROMs, which is the test that
matters: it snapshots a running game and checks the frames after a load match
the frames after running straight through. All four ROM-gated suites pass, plus
clippy and the full workspace.

disasm dump-save --machine gridlee now shows the map naming its own regions:

      1    33045      GridleeBoard.map
      1     2048          RAM
      2    30720          Video RAM
      4      256          NVRAM

ROM and I/O are absent, by the rule rather than by anyone remembering.

ONE JUDGEMENT CALL WORTH KNOWING. dip_switches was not saved by the old impl and
is now #[save_skip] rather than a saved field, so behaviour is unchanged: the
operator's switches survive a load the way the switches on a cabinet do. Every
other unsaved field (gfx_rom, sprite_cache, palette_rgb, rand17, audio_buffer,
scanline_buffer) is ROM, derived from ROM, or a transient buffer.

Size 33507 -> 33652, +145 bytes, which is per-field TLV framing.

REMAINING for C2, per the scoping pass: 11 more in category A (derivable now)
and ~14 more in category B (map-only blocker, now unblocked). burgertime is in A
but gains nothing from C1, since it keeps its memory in plain board fields.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
C2 PROGRESS: 15 of 49 hand-written impls converted, and a CORRECTION to the
scoping pass.

CONVERTED (all to #[derive(Saveable)] + #[save_tlv], since the wire changes
anyway and TLV means declaration order never has to be reconciled again):
  gridlee (the first, onto C1's address-space impl)
  namco51_lle, congo_sound, galaxian_sound, asteroids_sound, dkong_sound,
  llander_sound
  z80dma, galaxian_video, pisces, roadrunner, namco_galaga (GalagaCpus),
  docastle (DocastleSystem)
  starwars_math, avg

THE CORRECTION. My census classified impls by looking for cross-boundary field
access, accessor calls, conditionals and casts, and for post-load side effects
it looked only for .clear() and .reset(). That missed REBUILD CALLS. btime was
in the derivable-now group and is not: its load_state ends with
rebuild_palette() and render().

A re-scan for any bare self.method(...) statement inside load_state finds NINE
impls that need a post-load hook:

  btime            rebuild_palette(), render()
  ccastles         update_palette_entry(i) per entry, update_rom_bank()
  foodf            update_palette_entry(i) per entry, refresh_dip_pots()
  gottlieb         rebuild_palette(), sound.reapply_speech_clock()
  irobot           board.apply_banking()
  mcr2             rebuild_palette()
  quantum          board.refresh_dip_pots()
  starwars         novram.load_nvram(...)
  williams         blitter.set_window_enable(...)

Plus four whose side effect is a field reset that #[save_skip(default)] already
covers: ym2151 (native.clear()), atari_avg, atari_dvg, missile_command.

WHAT THIS CHANGES. A POST-LOAD HOOK IS NOW THE SINGLE MOST VALUABLE REMAINING
DERIVE FEATURE, ahead of enum support (3 impls). It is what the derived-cache
pattern needs: a board holds a palette expanded from palette RAM, or a page
table implied by a bank register, and after a load the derived thing has to be
rebuilt from the restored source. That is not incidental to these boards, it is
how they are all built, and it is why mcr2 was wrongly in the map-only group.

It also narrows C1's payoff: of the map-only boards, mcr2 and gottlieb and
irobot also need the hook, so the address-space impl alone does not finish them.

REMAINING: 34 impls. Roughly:
  ~11 blocked only on the address space (C1 done, so ready): atari_system1,
      congo_bongo, docastle (board), galaxian, mario_bros, mrdo, namco_pac,
      scramble, tkg04, atari_avg, atari_dvg
   ~9 need a post-load hook (list above)
   ~3 need enum support: m6502 InterruptType, m68000 M68kVariant, slapstic
   ~3 need the inner bus to derive: konami_sound, atari_system1_sound, ssio
   ~5 type-support gaps: irobot_mathbox, i8035, mb88xx, ym2151, namco50
   ~3 genuinely bespoke

All four ROM-gated suites pass at each step, plus clippy and the full
workspace.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
C1 FOLLOW-UP: AddressSpace16 now saves its page table. This corrects a decision
in C1 that was inconsistent with C1's own argument.

WHY IT WAS WRONG. C1 saved a map's regions on the grounds that 'forgot to save a
region' was a silent bug with nothing to catch it, and in the same commit
deliberately left the page table out, reasoning that boards rebuild banking from
their own saved bank register and that persisting it here too would give one
fact two sources of truth.

But that rebuild IS the hook. It is a call each board has to remember to make
from its load_state, it runs NOWHERE ELSE on the normal path (ccastles'
update_rom_bank runs on a bus write and on reset; irobot's apply_banking only on
reset), and a board that forgets it comes back with the CPU reading through
pages aimed where they were aimed before the load. Identical bug class, one
level up, and I argued against it for regions while accepting it for pages.

Prompted by the question 'do we actually need the post-load methods, or can they
just be state we save'. For banking the answer is that they are needed only
because we chose to derive rather than save.

    body       := version:u8 | count:u16 | entry{count}
    page table := tag = 0x100, payload = 256 x (region_id:u8 | base_offset:u32)

Tag 0x100 cannot collide with a region id, which is a u8. 1280 bytes a map.
ADDRESS_SPACE_SAVE_VERSION goes to 2.

WATCHPOINT FLAGS ARE NOT RESTORED. They belong to whoever is debugging, not to
the machine, so a load leaves them where they were set. Pinned by a test.

A NARROWING, stated because it is a real behaviour change. An unknown region's
BYTES are still skipped by length, but if that region is mapped, the page table
names it, and a page naming a region this map lacks is now REFUSED rather than
partially applied. Mapping it would send every read through it somewhere
arbitrary. So two maps that disagree about what is mapped where no longer load
into each other at all. That is the right way round (they are not the same
machine, and board variants that legitimately differ already differ by
machine_id, which the envelope checks first), but it is stricter than C1's
region-skipping alone implied.

ADDRESSSPACE32 IS NOT DONE, and is now loud about it rather than silent. Its
mapping lives in per-range RegionTargets, not a page table, so it needs a
different wire format. NO BOARD CALLS remap_range TODAY: all four banking boards
(ccastles, irobot, starwars, williams) are 16-bit. Rather than invent an
untested format, remap_range sets a flag and save_state debug_asserts on it, so
the first 68000 board to bank trips it in any test run instead of shipping saves
that come back pointing at the wrong bank.

VERIFIED by disabling the page restore and re-running: banking_survives_a_round_trip
fails, which is the check that matters. All four ROM-gated suites pass, plus
clippy and the full workspace.

WHAT THIS REMOVES FROM THE POST-LOAD-HOOK LIST: irobot apply_banking and
ccastles update_rom_bank, once those boards convert. Down from nine to seven,
and of the seven, five are palette_rgb rebuilds that saving the palette would
also remove.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
C2 PROGRESS: 17 of 49. mcr2 and ccastles converted, and the derive gained
tuple arrays.

TUPLE ARRAYS. Five boards held an expanded palette as [(u8, u8, u8); N], which
the derive did not support, so each kept it #[save_skip] and bolted a rebuild
onto load_state. gen_primitive_io now generates read/write for one primitive at
a named place, which lets an array element and a tuple field inside one share
the same code; an array of primitive tuples writes flat, since the array length
and the tuple arity are both fixed by the type.

Rebuilding at render time was the other option and is NOT available:
Renderable::render_frame takes &self, so a board cannot rebuild a cache there.

MCR2. Map plus palette were its only blockers, both now solved. Its map's
writable set is exactly the {Nvram, SpriteRam, VideoRam} the hand-written impl
listed. The load_state tail turned out to be attributes throughout: the two
dirty bitsets take #[save_skip(default = DirtyBitset::new_all_dirty())] so a
load redraws rather than trusting the pre-load frame, and the CTC acknowledge
flags take #[save_skip(default)].

CCASTLES, and the first board where the page table earns its keep. It banks ROM
through output latch 0 bit 7 and used to replay update_rom_bank() on load. That
call is gone: the bank is page-table state and the map carries it.

Its writable set is exactly the {VideoRam, Sram, SpriteRam, Nvram} the hand list
had. THIRD independent agreement between the derived rule and a hand-written
list, which is the evidence C1's tests could not give.

VERIFIED, not assumed. Added ccastles::tests::the_rom_bank_survives_a_save_and_load:
fill bank 0 with 0x11 and bank 1 with 0x22, select bank 1, save, load into a
fresh board that starts on bank 0, and read through 0xA000. Disabling the page
restore makes it fail with 0x11 where 0x22 is expected, which is the stale-bank
bug exactly. Worth having because the ROM-gated suites could pass vacuously
here: nothing guarantees ccastles switches banks inside the window
save_state_rom_test snapshots.

RUNNING TALLY of what the answer to 'do we need the post-load methods' has
removed: nine hooks down to four. irobot's apply_banking and ccastles'
update_rom_bank went with the page table; mcr2's and ccastles' palette rebuilds
went with tuple arrays. Left: btime (rebuild_palette + render), gottlieb
(rebuild_palette + reapply_speech_clock), foodf (update_palette_entry +
refresh_dip_pots), quantum (refresh_dip_pots). Three of the four are palette
rebuilds removable the same way; the genuinely different ones are
reapply_speech_clock and refresh_dip_pots, which re-establish a config-to-device
link that saving cannot fix because the config deliberately is not in the save.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
C2/C3/C4 PROGRESS: 44 of 49 converted, 5 hand-written impls left. The design doc
now has a 'What Stage C shipped' section; this is the running record.

CONVERTED SINCE THE LAST NOTE (19 more): congo_bongo, docastle (board),
atari_system1, ssio, konami_sound, m6502 InterruptType, m68000 M68kVariant,
slapstic, quantum, foodf, missile_command, marble, btime, i8035, mb88xx,
namco50, gottlieb, atari_system1_sound, namco_galaga (board).

FIVE DERIVE FEATURES, each added because impls were blocked on it rather than
for its own sake. Two were already recorded (tuple arrays; the address space's
own impl); three are new.

  NESTED ARRAYS, [[u8; 3]; 2]. gen_array_element_io recurses on an array
  element and names each loop binding by depth. An array of arrays is inline
  rather than a nested component, the same answer already given for an array of
  primitive tuples: every dimension's length is fixed by the type. Unlocked the
  SSIO board's per-chip per-channel duty cycles, which was the one type in
  either sound board the derive could not emit.

  FIELDLESS ENUMS. One byte carrying the variant's Rust discriminant, so
  #[repr(u8)] with an explicit = N and a bare enum counting from zero both
  encode the way the source reads. This is the whole of three impls: m6502's
  InterruptType, m68000's M68kVariant, the Slapstic's State.

  AND A BEHAVIOUR CHANGE WORTH STATING: an unrecognised discriminant is now an
  error naming the type. All three hand-written impls ended in a `_ =>` arm
  that turned an unknown byte into variant zero, so a corrupt save resumed as a
  plausible one.

  OPTION<T> FIELDS. Written exactly when Some; the id is simply absent
  otherwise. That is a per-variant component expressed as a field, and it
  replaces the chunk-level read_optional Stage A had to add by hand to the
  three conditional-field boards. Both directions of the mismatch fail naming
  the field, which is what makes 'optional' mean 'per variant' rather than
  'sometimes skipped'. An Option in a positional struct is rejected: a
  positional body writes every field and has nowhere to say a component is
  absent. The field count stops being a compile-time constant when a struct has
  one.

  #[save_after_load(a, b)]. Inherent methods called in order after the body and
  after every #[save_skip(default)]. Documented as a LAST RESORT, not the
  normal way to restore a derived value.

BOX IS TRANSPARENT, as a smaller fifth. gen_field_io generates against a place
expression rather than a field ident, so a 4 KB RAM behind a Box encodes
exactly as it would inline.

THE ANSWER TO 'DO WE NEED THE POST-LOAD METHODS' IS MOSTLY NO, and that
question did more work than any single feature. The tally, finished:
  - banking (irobot, ccastles): gone with the page table.
  - palette rebuilds (mcr2, ccastles, foodf, btime, gottlieb): gone with tuple
    arrays. Five boards, all of which held the expanded palette #[save_skip]
    and bolted a rebuild onto load_state.
  - refresh_dip_pots (quantum, foodf): gone because the POKEY saves its own pot
    inputs and the board saves its DIP byte, so the link the call re-established
    now comes out of the file. Same argument the page table settled one level up.
  - dc_blocker.reset (quantum, foodf): gone because DcBlocker documents its
    two-sample history as live state a save has to carry, and both boards saved
    it and threw it away in the same load.
WHAT IS LEFT is the state a save deliberately does not carry: a device
re-reading a clock from configuration (gottlieb reapply_speech_clock,
atari_system1_sound resync_tms_clock), a framebuffer that cannot be rebuilt
lazily because Renderable::render_frame takes &self (btime render), and a value
that must be brought back into range before something indexes with it (slapstic
banks, foodf adc_channel, namco50 player/read_index, mb88xx RAM length).

THE DERIVED WRITABLE SET HAS NOW AGREED WITH A HAND LIST ON TWELVE BOARDS
independently. namco_galaga is the strongest of them: its saved_region_ids
helper filtered regions() on AccessKind::ReadWrite and wrote each in turn,
which is C1's rule already spelled out by hand.

TWO usize FIELDS BECAME u8 (foodf adc_channel, namco50 player). usize is not a
wire type, both old impls already wrote them as bytes, and both hold a few bits
the address decode gives them.

WHAT IS LEFT, and why each is genuinely bespoke rather than merely unconverted:
  irobot_mathbox  [Vec<u16>; 2] and [usize; 16], neither a wire type
  ym2151          index loops over per-channel arrays
  irobot          accessor-backed state plus post-load remapping
  starwars        novram.load_nvram on the way in, variable-length reads
  williams        blitter window-enable through an accessor, palette[..16] of a
                  larger region
Plus one NEW hand-written impl I added deliberately: Namco51Wrapper, a
two-variant enum whose live variant is decided by whether a 51XX firmware ROM
was found and whose LLE variant cannot be constructed from a file at all. A
derive that built the variant the bytes name would be wrong. Twenty lines,
against the hundred-line board impl it let me delete.

VERIFIED at every commit: all four ROM-gated suites (39 booted machines round
trip), clippy with CI's exact flags, the full workspace. The two MCUs also went
through cross-validation: mb88xx is 256000/256000, and i8035's 34 failures on
0x57 are byte-identical on the unmodified tree, so they predate this work.
dump-save confirms the optional components on real ROMs: speech present on
roadrunner and absent on marble, namco50 present on xevious and absent on
galaga.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
STAGE C IS DONE: all 49 hand-written Saveable impls are gone. #[save_elements]
is retired. Three impls remain in the tree and none is a leftover; see below.

THE LAST FIVE WERE NOT BESPOKE. irobot_mathbox, ym2151, irobot, starwars and
williams had been classified as irreducibly bespoke by the original scoping
pass, and I repeated that classification once without re-checking it. Re-reading
them against the features that had landed since, four were blocked on nothing of
the sort:

  accessor round-trips     AnalogAxis and X2212 already derive, so starwars'
                           stick[i].position() and novram.nvram() round-trips
                           and irobot's stick loop were all just older patterns
  optional components      starwars' Slapstic and williams' CVSD are Option
                           fields
  post-load banking        irobot's apply_banking and starwars' slapstic remap
                           both call remap_pages, so the page table carries them
  per-channel index loops  ym2151's feedback is [[i32; 2]; 8], which nested
                           arrays already covered

What was actually left in each was a field whose TYPE the derive could not
encode. The lesson worth keeping: a census taken before the tools existed goes
stale, and the classification is the thing to re-check, not the conclusion.

TWO PLANNED DERIVE FEATURES WERE NOT BUILT. The plan was Vec<T> for primitive T
and tuples in field position. Checking for callers first found that neither
would have one once the types were fixed: the only non-u8 Vec fields in the tree
are the mathbox's two, both allocated once at a constant size and never resized,
and the only tuple field is in a debug-view struct that is not Saveable. Adding
wire surface with no caller is worse than not adding it, so the types moved:

  irobot_mathbox  ram -> Box<[u16; N]>, comram -> Box<[[u16; N]; 2]>, and the
                  microcode stack -> [u16; 16]. usize is not a wire type and
                  the entries are op indices the impl already masked on load,
                  which is now #[save_after_load(clamp_stack)].
  irobot          polybitmap -> Box<[[u8; N]; 2]>
  starwars        audio_dc: (f32, f32) -> two named f32 fields

A TYPE THE DERIVE CANNOT ENCODE IS SOMETIMES THE TYPE BEING WRONG rather than
the derive being short. Three of the four here were Vecs that never resize.

THE BLITTER WINDOW-ENABLE IS THE BEST SINGLE ILLUSTRATION OF WHAT TLV BOUGHT.
It was #[save_skip] in the blitter and restored by the board through
set_window_enable, for one reason stated in its own comment: so that other
games' blitter saves stayed byte-identical. That is exactly the cost field TLV
removes. It is a plain field under its own id now; every Williams board carries
it, and the board's conditional chunk and accessor round-trip are both gone.

STAR WARS KEEPS ITS OWN DC FILTER. I had recommended folding audio_dc into
DcBlocker, which is what every other board uses. On reading the code they run
the identical one-pole difference equation but with different poles: DcBlocker
derives its from a corner frequency (0.995013 at 44.1 kHz), starwars hard-codes
0.995. Swapping it in would move this board's audio, which is an emulation
change and does not belong in a save-state refactor. Splitting the tuple into
two named fields is the zero-behaviour-change option. The consolidation is a
reasonable separate change if anyone wants it.

WHAT REMAINS HAND-WRITTEN, AND WHY EACH IS CORRECT RATHER THAN DEFERRED:

  AddressSpace16/32   These ARE the mechanism. A map that derived its own body
                      would have nothing to say about which regions the CPU can
                      write, which is the entire point of the impl.
  Namco51Wrapper      A two-variant enum whose live variant is decided by
                      whether a 51XX firmware ROM was found, and whose LLE
                      variant cannot be constructed from a file at all. A derive
                      must build the variant the bytes name; here that is
                      precisely what must not happen. Twenty lines that check
                      the variant instead, against the hundred-line board impl
                      they let me delete.

THREE TESTS CHANGED, each because the shape it pinned is now better:
  - williams' variant tests asserted the LENIENT direction, where a board
    without a CVSD silently skipped one present in the file. Both directions
    are refusals now, each naming what differed. Strict is the right way round
    (a board with a CVSD and one without are not the same machine) and the
    envelope's machine_id check is why the lenient case only ever arose in a
    test that constructed it on purpose.
  - the size-difference test drops the window-enable term and counts the SRAM
    as a map region rather than a board chunk.
  - the dump-save CLI test names the per-variant parts where they now live.

VERIFIED: cargo test --workspace, clippy with CI's exact flags, and all four
ROM-gated suites (39 booted machines round-tripping).

STILL OPEN AT EPIC LEVEL: roughly 66 of 125 derive sites are still positional.
That was C4's original scope and the doc argues against sweeping it: 28 of 34
versioned components have never changed once, and Stage A's framing makes mixed
interoperate. The policy actually applied here is the doc's own — TLV for
anything reworked.

title: TMS5220/5220C LPC speech synthesizer (shared core device) + Road Runner speech
description: Replace the status-only TMS5220 stub (t9r.3) with a faithful, host-agnostic LPC core device (16-byte FIFO, frame parse, 8-step interpolation, 10-pole lattice, chirp/LFSR excitation, real coefficient tables; TMS5220 + TMS5220C variants; speak-external only, no VSM). Wire it into the Atari System 1 sound board (VIA6522 bridge kept) so Road Runner speaks. Built reusable so a future Star Wars machine adds only its own MOS6532 RIOT bridge + with_variant(Tms5220, 672_000). Plan: ~/.claude/plans/plan-the-implementation-of-noble-lynx.md. Rolls up to t9r.6 for RR sound verification.
close_reason: TMS5220/5220C LPC speech synthesizer delivered as a reusable host-agnostic core device and wired into the Atari System 1 sound board; Road Runner speech user-confirmed working. Children: .1 coeff tables, .2 device core (variant/FIFO/command/handshake), .3 LPC synthesis (parse/interp/lattice/excitation/audio), .4 board wiring (PB4 clock-select + tick + audio mix, Marble byte-identical), .5 verify+docs. Also fixed a latent AudioResampler upsampling bug (slow/choppy speech). Star Wars can reuse the device via with_variant(Tms5220, 672_000) + its own RIOT bridge. Branch tms5220; suites/clippy/fmt green.

title: TMS5220 coefficient tables submodule
description: New private core/src/device/tms5220_tables.rs: transcribe the TMS5220 coefficient set from MAME tms5110r.hxx as const arrays: ENERGY[16], PITCH[64], K[10][32] (K1-K4 use 16 entries, K5-K10 use 32; size each to its bit width), CHIRP[52]: [i8], INTERP_SHIFT[8], K_BITS[10] = {5,5,4,4,4,4,4,3,3,3}. Per repo 'no MAME in code comments' rule, describe as TMS5220 tables; cite MAME only in the commit. Unit-test sizes + spot values.
close_reason: Added core/src/device/tms5220_tables.rs: TMS5220/5220C LPC coefficient ROM tables (ENERGY 16, PITCH 64, K1..K10 sized 32/32/16../8 per K_BITS, CHIRP 52 i8, INTERP_SHIFT 8) + metadata, transcribed from MAME tms5110r.hxx tms5220_coeff. #![allow(dead_code)] until the device core consumes them (child .2/.3). 2 unit tests (lengths match index widths, spot values) pass; clippy + fmt clean. Single commit on branch tms5220.

title: TMS5220 device core: variant + FIFO + command decode + host-agnostic handshake
description: Rewrite core/src/device/tms5220.rs preserving the existing public API. Add Tms52xxVariant {Tms5220, Tms5220C}; constructors new() (=5220C @650.8kHz nominal) and with_variant(v, clock_hz). data_w command decode by bits 6-4: SPEAK EXTERNAL (0x60) clears FIFO + arms speak-external; RESET (0x70) stops + clears; SET RATE stored only when 5220C; VSM commands (LA/SPK/RDBY/RB) decoded and no-op'd; else push a data byte. 16-byte FIFO + head/tail/count/bits_taken + read_bits(n). status_r (TS/BL/BE), ready()/int_asserted() from FIFO fullness/stop. set_clock(hz) (retunes resampler input=clk/80). Saveable (#[save_skip] tables/clock/resampler) + Device + Debuggable. Host-agnostic: no 6522/RIOT knowledge, no Atari PB4 math in the device. Silent handshake only; synthesis is the next child. Tests: FIFO fullness->ready/BL/BE, command decode, SET RATE variant-gated, save/load.
close_reason: Rewrote the TMS5220 stub into a host-agnostic device core: Tms52xxVariant {Tms5220, Tms5220C} + new()/with_variant(v, clock_hz); data_w command decode (SPEAK EXTERNAL/RESET/SET-RATE gated to 5220C/VSM inert), 16-byte FIFO with BL-edge SPEN start, BL/BE status + /INT edges, status_r (clears /INT), ready()/int_asserted(), set_clock(hz) retuning the resampler (clock/80). #[derive(Saveable)] runtime state (variant/clock/resampler skipped) + Device + Debuggable. Silent until synthesis (child .3): drain_audio empty, tick no-op. Handshake ported from MAME tms5220.cpp. 11 device tests + tables pass; clippy/fmt clean; machines builds. One commit on branch tms5220.

title: TMS5220 LPC synthesis (parse/interp/lattice/excitation/audio)
description: Port MAME tms5220.cpp synthesis into the device: parse_frame (4-bit energy, repeat bit, 6-bit pitch, K1-K10 by bit width; stop on energy 0/15; unvoiced when pitch 0), interpolation via INTERP_SHIFT[IP] unless inhibited, excitation (chirp table when voiced / 20x-per-sample 16-bit LFSR when unvoiced), unrolled 10-pole lattice_filter with clamped matrix_multiply, clip. tick() = one master clock with a /80 prescaler stepping one synthesis sample into AudioResampler<f32> (->44100); consume FIFO bits as frames parse; assert/clear talk. Real drain_audio(). Tests: known LPC frame -> non-empty non-DC audio; silence/stop frame stays quiet.
close_reason: LPC synthesis complete (2 commits on branch tms5220). (A) FIFO bit-reader (read_bits, LSB/MSB order) + parse_frame (energy/rep/pitch/K1-K4/K5-K10 with silence/stop/repeat/unvoiced early-outs) + full synthesizer state (save_version 2) + idle-frame/zpar/OLDE/OLDP setup on speak-external and SPEN start; TALK separated from TALKD. (B) process_one_sample state machine (frame parse at cycle boundary, interpolation-inhibit, INTERP_SHIFT B-cycle interpolation of energy/pitch/K, chirp/20x-LFSR excitation, unrolled 10-pole lattice_filter + matrix_multiply + clip_analog), advance_counters (RESETF3/RESETL4 TALKD+OLDE/OLDP latching, pitch counter), tick() ÷80 -> resampler, real drain_audio; Device::tick wired. Ported from MAME tms5220.cpp. Tests: bit order, voiced/unvoiced/stop parse round-trips, idle-silent, voiced-audible-varying; full core suite 833 pass; clippy/fmt clean.

title: Wire TMS5220 into Atari System 1 sound board (Road Runner speech)
description: machines/src/atari_system1_sound.rs (VIA6522 bridge kept). PB4 clock select computed board-side: on Port B write extract D4 and tms.set_clock(7_159_090/(16-(5|(bit4<<1)))) -> 650.8kHz (D4=0) or 795.5kHz (D4=1). Add a u64 fractional accumulator and, in tick(), step speech.tms.tick() for the (variable) TMS master clock vs SOUND_CLOCK_HZ (Bresenham). In drain_audio() drain speech and add to POKEY+YM mix (bipolar, gain ~1.0, tune vs MAME), guarded on speech.is_some(). Construct as 5220C via new(). Marble (speech off) byte-identical. Verify the via6522.rs stub suffices for a pure parallel-port bridge (confirm RR sound ROM doesn't need VIA timers/CA-CB); note any upgrade. Tests: streaming keeps /READY toggling without stalling, PB4 retunes, Marble parity.
close_reason: Wired the TMS5220 into AtariSystem1Sound (VIA6522 bridge kept). Port B bit4 clock-select retunes the TMS master clock (tms_clock_for_pb4: 650.8kHz nominal / 795.5kHz) via set_clock; Speech::tick steps the TMS at its variable clock vs the 6502 via a Bresenham accumulator; drain_audio mixes TMS output (SPEECH_MIX, tunable) with POKEY+YM. Marble (speech=None) byte-identical (no tick; +0.0 mix). Save state round-trips selected clock + accumulator and re-syncs the TMS resampler on load. 3 new tests (clock math, PB4 retune, ticks-drain-FIFO); 13 atari sound tests pass; full machines suite green; clippy --all-targets + fmt clean. 2 commits on branch tms5220 (+ isolated chore fixing a pre-existing galaxian_boot_check clippy identity_op). VIA6522 stub confirmed sufficient as a parallel-port bridge. End-to-end Road Runner audio verification is child .6/.5.

title: Road Runner speech end-to-end verification + docs
description: Run the frontend on roadrunn and listen for intelligible speech in attract/gameplay. Optional MAME diff: Lua-tap tms5220_device::data_w and diff the byte/command stream vs ours before chasing audio-quality differences (per the 'diff against MAME bus traffic' memory). Update README/roadmap. cargo test -p phosphor-core + -p phosphor-machines, clippy --all-features --all-targets, fmt clean. Relates to t9r.6.
close_reason: End-to-end verified: user confirms Road Runner speech now plays correctly. Root cause of the initially slow/choppy speech was NOT the TMS device but AudioResampler only supporting downsampling — the TMS at clock/80 (~8.1kHz) upsamples to 44.1kHz and the resampler degenerated to pass-through (~8135 samples/sec), airing ~1/5 of each frame then silence. Fixed AudioResampler::tick to emit one output per consumed input period (loop; sample-and-hold on upsampling), which also fixes Votrax's inaudible 1.1x error. README updated (Road Runner: TMS5220 LPC speech, not stub). Full core (835) + machines suites, clippy --all-targets, fmt clean. Optional MAME data_w Lua diff skipped — user-confirmed by ear. Commits on branch tms5220.

title: Epic: Accurate vector rendering and tunable beam effects
description:
Vector machines currently render as 1-pixel hard-edged lines at a flat colour, in both paths: the CPU rasterizer (atari_dvg::rasterize_vectors, Bresenham) and the GL path (vector_gl.rs, GL_LINES with additive blend). Neither models the beam. The goal is a renderer whose inputs are the tube and the beam, with the artistic knobs sitting on top as named deviations rather than as the model itself.

WHAT THE HARDWARE GIVES US

Spot size. Both Atari colour XY monitors (Wells-Gardner 19V2000 for Tempest, 19K6100 for Quantum and Star Wars) use the same 19 inch shadow-mask tube family as contemporary raster monitors. Two things bound the spot: the mask pitch, about 0.6 mm on a 19 inch tube, below which nothing is resolvable, and the focused spot itself at roughly 0.6 to 0.8 mm. A 19 inch 4:3 viewable area is about 360 x 270 mm. Tempest maps 570 units onto the 270 mm axis, so one unit is 0.47 mm and the beam is about 1.5 units. Quantum maps 900 units onto the 360 mm axis, one unit is 0.40 mm, and the beam is 1.5 to 2 units. So the core beam is 1.5 to 2 display units, not the 1 hard pixel we draw.

Dwell time. Brightness per unit length is set by how long the beam sits there, not by a code. The intensity code sets beam current; the deflection rate sets dwell. A short vector at a given intensity is brighter per pixel than a long one, and the beam lingers at a vertex where it changes direction, which is why real vector displays show bright dots at corners. We now have this quantity: strobe3 charges each vector its travel time in master-clock cycles (see phosphor-emulator-uqad, which made that a real elapsed time rather than a number computed and thrown away). It is not carried into VectorLine yet.

Bloom. Beyond the core spot there is a wide, low-amplitude halo from phosphor scatter and glass, and it grows with beam energy. This is most of what makes a vector display look like one.

STAGES

0. Carry dwell into the display list. Add the per-vector beam time to VectorLine so renderers have the physical input. DVG machines have their own timing and would supply 0, meaning "unknown, fall back to the flat intensity code". Changes the pinned vectors hash for every vector machine.

1. Beam geometry: width and anti-aliasing. Replace GL_LINES with expanded quads carrying distance-from-centreline, and a Gaussian falloff across the line in the fragment shader. Width from the spot size above. Round caps, or an explicit endpoint dot, so vertices join without notches. This is the single biggest visual win and it also fixes a real defect: Bresenham puts the same number of lit pixels per unit of x on a 45 degree line as on a horizontal one, so diagonals are currently about 1/sqrt(2) as bright per unit length as they should be.

2. Dwell-driven brightness. Luminance per unit length from stage 0 rather than from the intensity code alone, normalised so a typical vector keeps roughly its present brightness. The intensity code stays as the beam-current multiplier. Do not fit a curve: the relation is energy deposited equals beam current times dwell, and the normalisation constant is the only free parameter.

3. Phosphor persistence. An accumulation buffer decaying on elapsed time rather than a per-frame clear. Note that these are P22 colour triads, not a long-persistence P39, so the real decay is short and most of the apparent trail comes from the pass rate rather than the phosphor. Default should be modest. Blocked on the determinism decision below.

4. Bloom. HDR target, separable blur, additive composite, amplitude driven by the same energy figure as stage 2.

5. Tunables and presets. A VectorSettings block in config.toml with per-machine overrides in state.toml, matching how scale and fullscreen already resolve, and live sliders in settings_ui.rs. Presets: "measured" (everything derived from the tube figures above), "flat" (todays look, kept so a regression can be compared against it), and one punchier preset for people who want it.

DECISIONS NEEDED BEFORE STAGE 1

Which renderer gets the effects. Golden frames are captured through render_frame, which is the CPU rasterizer, but what ships to the eye is the GL path. Effects in GL only means the golden frames stop resembling the product and the two paths drift further apart, which phosphor-emulator-iitc already tracks as a live problem. The options are to keep the CPU path as a deliberate geometry-only pin and say so in the test, to implement the effects twice, or to move golden capture onto a headless GL path so the pin is of what ships.

Persistence versus determinism. A decaying buffer makes a rendered frame depend on every frame before it. That is still deterministic, but the golden frame stops pinning one frame and starts pinning a history. Either persistence is excluded from the capture path or captures happen after a fixed warm-up.

HOW WE WILL KNOW IT IS RIGHT

Photographs of real cabinets are the ground truth but are not a test. The falsifiable properties are: integrated luminance along a segment is proportional to its dwell time; brightness per unit length does not depend on the angle of the line, which is the diagonal defect above and is testable today; the rendered core width in units matches the figure derived from the tube; and total emitted energy is conserved when a long vector is split into two short collinear ones.
close_reason: All five filed stages closed. Beam geometry, dwell brightness, vertex dots, halation and the settings panel, with every figure derived from the tube except the halation fraction, which is labelled and on a slider. Persistence split out as phosphor-emulator-cwd9.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
All five filed stages are closed. What shipped, and what it cost.

The renderers model a beam rather than drawing lines, and almost every figure is derived rather than tuned. Spot size from a 19 inch shadow-mask tube (0.6 mm mask pitch, 0.7 mm focused spot, 360 mm long axis). Brightness per unit length from dwell, anchored at the beam top speed of 0x1FF * 255 >> 4, which is 8.05 cycles per unit along an axis and 5.69 on a diagonal; measured across all three AVG machines the observed floor is 5.7 and the 5th percentile is 8.0, so the derivation and the measurement agree without being fitted to each other. Bright vertices from the beam standing still while the sequencer fetches, about 64 cycles on one spot against 8 for a unit of moving line. Halation width from the faceplate critical angle, 2*t*tan(asin(1/n)), about 19 mm on 11 mm of glass.

Exactly one figure has no derivation behind it: what fraction of a spot light halates, which depends on phosphor isotropy and glass coatings we have no numbers for. It is labelled as such in the source and it is on the slider. That was the goal.

Three things fell out that were not planned. Display list coordinates now keep the 16 bits below the unit, because a unit has no size of its own and rounding charged Star Wars twice the precision penalty of Tempest on the same tube. display_size was doing two jobs, so rendered detail was capped at whatever numeric range a game data happened to use; Renderable::vector_field_size separates them and Star Wars went from 320x330 to 705x727. And Tempest was being rotated twice, which phosphor-emulator-iitc had been open on since August.

Costs, stated plainly. The CPU rasterizer went from 0.043 to about 1.4 ms per frame on Tempest, and Asteroids sits at 2.7 ms against 0.4 ms to emulate the machine. That path serves screenshots and the debug panel, not play. Halation is off there because a full-frame blur measured four to five times the beam sweep; the GPU does it for nothing.

Two errors worth remembering. A test asserted both that a full-intensity vector peaks at full white and that halation conserves total light; those cannot both hold while the fraction varies, because the gain correction raises the brightness to hold the peak. And the issue predicted the bright vertices would fall out of per-unit-length dwell, which they do not: that model gives each vector a uniform rate and nothing at the joins, and the dots needed the stationary time instead.

Left open: phosphor-emulator-cwd9 for phosphor persistence, which this epic described but never filed, and phosphor-emulator-gr27 for what the golden frame test is now for. The frame comparison is still ignored.

title: Stage 0: carry per-vector beam time into VectorLine
description:
Brightness per unit length on a vector display is set by dwell time, and strobe3 already computes each vector travel time in master-clock cycles. It is used to charge the sequencer and then discarded. Carry it on VectorLine so the renderers have the physical input rather than only the 4-bit intensity code.

DVG machines have a separate timing model and would supply 0, read as "unknown, use the flat intensity code". Decide whether the field is the raw cycle count or cycles per unit length; the renderers want the latter, but the raw count is the measured quantity and the length is already implied by the endpoints, so raw is probably the honest thing to store.

Changes the pinned vectors hash for every vector machine, so recapture with the frames reviewed.
close_reason: VectorLine carries beam_cycles from the AVG's own timing; DVG reports 0 since it models none. Raw cycles, in hash_vectors, three tests deriving their expectations from the timer.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
Done. VectorLine carries beam_cycles: the master-clock time the beam spent travelling that segment, which strobe3 already worked out to charge the sequencer and then discarded.

Stored raw rather than per unit length, as the issue proposed. It is the measured quantity, and the length is already implied by the endpoints, so dividing here would only throw away the ability to check the two against each other.

DVG supplies 0. It has no timing model at all: it decodes at the word level and never tracks beam travel, so there is nothing to report rather than something being withheld. The field documents 0 as "not known, fall back to the intensity code".

Added to hash_vectors, since it is machine output and that hash is what pins what a machine emitted rather than what a renderer made of it.

Three tests, with the expected values derived from the timer rather than read off the implementation:
- a Quantum delta needing no normalization costs the full 0x4000
- a delta of 1 is normalized up and costs 0x4000 >> 10
- the beam time on the list is consistent with what the sequencer was charged

Two arithmetic errors of mine that those tests caught, both worth recording because they are easy to repeat. Normalization stops when the sign bit differs from the one below it, so a delta of 1 shifts until its set bit reaches position 10, which is ten shifts and not eleven; I had the terminating condition one bit off. And the first vector in a list contributes no beam time, because add_point has no previous position to draw from and only parks the beam, so its segment and its travel time are both dropped. A real list opens with a CNTR, which is what does the parking there, so this is a property of a list that starts with a bare VCTR rather than a defect.

Nothing reads the field yet. That is ukgy.3.

title: Stage 1: beam geometry, real width and anti-aliasing
description:
Replace GL_LINES in vector_gl.rs with expanded quads carrying distance-from-centreline, and a Gaussian falloff across the line in the fragment shader. Round caps or an explicit endpoint dot so vertices join without a notch.

Width comes from the tube: the mask pitch is about 0.6 mm on the 19 inch tube and the focused spot is 0.6 to 0.8 mm, which is about 1.5 display units on Tempest (570 units over roughly 270 mm) and 1.5 to 2 on Quantum (900 units over roughly 360 mm). Not a tuned number; the tunable is a multiplier on it.

This also fixes a defect that exists today independent of any effect work: Bresenham lights the same number of pixels per unit of x whatever the angle, so a 45 degree line is about 1/sqrt(2) as bright per unit length as a horizontal one. That is testable without looking at anything: draw the same length segment at several angles and integrate the luminance.

Blocked on the epic decision about which renderer gets the effects.
close_reason: Both renderers draw the beam as a spot swept along the segment, sized from the tube. CPU path in 4062fe7 with four physics tests; GL path in cc87490, confirmed by eye. Shared figures live in phosphor_core::device::dvg so the two cannot drift.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
CPU rasterizer done in commit 4062fe7; GL path in the commit that follows this comment. Both now draw the beam as a spot swept along the segment.

Two errors worth recording, both caught by the tests rather than by looking at the picture.

Half-pixel convention. I evaluated the profile at pixel centres (px + 0.5) while the display list coordinates are pixel indices, so every line straddled two rows instead of landing on one, and a full-intensity vector peaked at 116 instead of 255. That is what made the first render look washed out, and I had already talked myself into a plausible physical story for why it "should" look dim before the test gave me the number. Measured peaks after the fix, full intensity, three angles across all three coordinate spaces: 254 to 255 everywhere.

Aliasing floor. At sigma 0.4 a Gaussian sampled on a unit grid ripples about 8% depending on where its centre falls between samples, and that ripple is brightness varying with the angle of the line, which is the exact defect this stage exists to remove. The ripple is 2*exp(-2*pi^2*sigma^2), so the floor has to be about 0.6 to get it under a quarter of a percent. Tempest is the machine it bites: its physical spot is just under the floor, so at display-list resolution it draws slightly wide. The GL path draws at window resolution, where a unit is several pixels, so it carries the true figure and only falls back to the floor if the window is very small.

The shared figures now live in phosphor_core::device::dvg (BEAM_SPOT_FRACTION, FWHM_TO_SIGMA, BEAM_CUTOFF_SIGMAS, MIN_SIGMA_PIXELS, beam_sigma_units) so the two renderers cannot drift apart on the numbers, and both use the same peak convention: a full-intensity vector reaches full white along its centre and no further. That convention is the monitor brightness control, and it has to be stated somewhere, because conserving energy per unit length while widening the spot lowers the peak in proportion, which would otherwise make a machine look dimmer purely because its coordinate space is coarser.

Render cost on tempest went from 0.043 to 1.362 ms/frame. The first cut was 4.9: it stamped a 2-D kernel every 0.3 units, about 83 exponentials per unit of length. Windowing each row to the stadium around the segment and evaluating one profile sample per pixel got most of that back, a profile lookup table and an accumulator kept across frames got a little more. What is left is spread evenly across the sweep, the buffer clear and the float-to-byte conversion, so there is no single remaining thing to fix. The GL path is unaffected by any of this; it is the CPU path that frameshot, screenshots and the debug UI fallback use.

Not verified: the GL path has not been looked at. It cannot be rendered headlessly, so it needs eyes on a running frontend. It is written to mirror the tested CPU model exactly, which is an argument and not evidence.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text: Verified by eye on a running frontend: pjl confirms the GL path looks right. That closes the one thing this stage could not check for itself, since the GL path cannot be rendered headlessly.

title: Stage 2: brightness from dwell time, not the intensity code alone
description:
Drive luminance per unit length from the beam time carried by stage 0. Energy deposited is beam current times dwell, so the intensity code stays as the current multiplier and dwell supplies the rest. Normalise so a typical vector keeps roughly its present brightness; that normalisation is the only free constant and it should be the only one.

The visible consequence is the characteristic vector look: bright dots where the beam turns a corner or starts and stops, dim long strokes, and short segments brighter than long ones at the same intensity code.

Falsifiable: integrated luminance along a segment tracks its dwell time, and splitting a long vector into two collinear halves conserves total emitted energy.
close_reason: Brightness from dwell with the anchor derived from the beam's top speed and confirmed against all three machines. Vertex dots added, which needed the stationary time rather than per-unit-length dwell. Sub-pixel coordinates and the field/raster split fell out of it.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
Done across commits f2ed085 (dwell brightness, sub-pixel coordinates, field/raster split) and 1796edb (vertex dots).

The anchor is derived, not fitted. Light per unit length is beam current times dwell, and the reference is the beam top speed: 0x1FF * 255 >> 4, which is 8.05 cycles per unit along an axis and 1/sqrt(2) of that on a diagonal. Measured across all three AVG machines the observed floor is 5.7 and the 5th percentile is 8.0, which are exactly those two figures, because it is the same deflection hardware in each. A full-intensity vector at that speed reads full white and anything slower blooms.

The issue predicted bright dots at vertices would fall out of this. They do not, and that is worth recording. Per-unit-length dwell gives each vector a uniform rate along its length and nothing at all at the joins, and the measured spread of dwell per unit length is only about 2x, because the AVG normalization exists precisely to hold deflection speed roughly constant and so works against the variation being rendered. The dots come from a different quantity: the beam stands still at a vertex while the sequencer fetches the next instruction, the DACs holding their last value, which is about 64 cycles on one point against about 8 for a unit of moving line. That is now carried as VectorLine::dwell_cycles and is what actually produces the characteristic look.

Two errors caught by tests rather than by looking. Travel and dwell are different quantities and I first scaled the vertex dot by the segment per-unit-length figure, which is meaningless. And the first brightness test compared a full-intensity vector against twice its dwell, which only measured the clamp, since the brightness control is set so full intensity at top speed already reads full white; it needed a dim vector to have any headroom.

Two things fell out of the work that were not in the issue. Display list coordinates now keep the generator 16 bits below the unit, because a unit has no size of its own and rounding charged Star Wars twice the precision penalty of Tempest on the same tube. And display_size was doing two jobs, the coordinate extent and the pixel count, so rendered detail was capped at whatever numeric range a game data happened to use; Renderable::vector_field_size separates them and Star Wars went from 320x330 to 705x727.

Confirmed by eye on Tempest and Star Wars.

title: Stage 4: bloom and halo
description:
HDR render target, separable blur, additive composite, with amplitude driven by the same energy figure stage 2 computes rather than by a flat constant. The halo comes from phosphor scatter and glass and grows with beam energy, so a bright short vector should bloom visibly wider than a dim long one.

Depends on stages 1 and 2 being in place, since it reads their output.
close_reason: Halo width derived from the faceplate's critical angle; fraction is the one undetermined figure, set to 0.07 by eye. GL has it, CPU rasterizer does not because a full-frame blur costs 4-5x the sweep.

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
Half done in commit 578f818: the model exists and is tested, but it is off in the CPU rasterizer and not yet in the GL path, which is where it will actually be seen.

What the physics gave us. The halo width is derivable and did not need fitting. The phosphor emits into the faceplate in every direction; light steeper than the critical angle cannot leave the front surface, so it reflects back, crosses the glass again and re-emerges at a radius of 2*t*tan(asin(1/n)). An 11 mm faceplate at n = 1.54 gives about 19 mm, or 5% of the tube long axis. Treated as a Gaussian skirt of that scale rather than as a ring, which is what the sum over all emission angles and depths looks like from the front.

The one figure that is NOT derived is the fraction of light that halates. It is an optical efficiency depending on phosphor isotropy, the aluminium backing, glass tint and coatings, and we have no numbers for any of them. It is labelled as such in the source and defaulted to 0.15, which is in the range measured CRT spot profiles show. This is the natural thing for stage 5 to expose as a knob.

One thing worth keeping: halation is light taken FROM the core, not added to it, so compositing is (1-f)*core + f*halo. That drops the peak, so the brightness gain is raised to compensate: for an isolated line both profiles have unit area, so the centre lands at (1-f) + f*sigma/halo_sigma of the core-alone value and the reciprocal restores it. Without that correction the existing peak-at-full-white test fails, which is how the omission was caught.

Why it is off in the boards, measured with phosphor-bench under release:

  asteroid  2.68 -> 13.52 ms/frame    emulating the machine costs 0.39
  llander   3.03 -> 13.37
  tempest   1.30 ->  5.06

Compositing a full-frame blur is O(pixels), not O(vectors), so the 1024x1024
machines were hit three times as hard as tempest at 580x570. Benching tempest alone hid it entirely; pjl spotted that and said to try Asteroids, which is the whole finding.
