title: Xevious: sound CPU runs away and clears misc latch, stalling attract
description:
Xevious boots through the power-on RAM test and PASSES the 50XX start-up protection into its main game loop (~frame 635, main PC 0x0437). It then stalls: the sound CPU (Cpu 2) writes the LS259 misc latch Q0=0 and Q3=0 (observed via bus-master trace), which disables the main VBLANK IRQ and re-holds the sub/sound CPUs in reset. The main loop at 0x0437 then spins forever waiting for the IRQ handler to set the frame counter at mem[0x8000]=1.

The sound ROM (xvi_7) never writes 0x6820/0x6823 in its reset/init/NMI paths (only Q2 at 0x6822), so the sound CPU has run away and is executing garbage that decodes as those latch writes — likely stack/RAM corruption or wrong NMI timing in the 3-Z80 interleave.

Next step (per repo guidance): trace+diff actual bus/latch traffic against MAME Lua taps rather than reverse-engineering ROM control flow. Reproduce with: cargo run -p phosphor-machines --example xevious_boot_check -- <extracted-xevious-dir> 800. Blocks M1 boot sign-off.
close_reason: FIXED in 0715d05. Root cause (via MAME bus-diff): the board latched the sound CPU's scanline NMI while it was held in reset (LS259 Q3), then delivered it the instant the CPU was released — before it ran its reset vector to load SP. The push went to the reset SP=0xFFFF, which on Xevious maps to the 0xF000-0xFFFF background-ROM window (not RAM), wrecking the stack -> sound CPU runaway that stomped the misc latch. Fix: clear pending sub/sound IRQ/NMI on reset release and don't latch the sound NMI while the CPUs are in reset. Verified: sound CPU now boots cleanly and idles in its command loop; matches MAME (sub2 only ever writes Q2).

title: Xevious: 50XX LLE returns wrong value for periodic protection check -> main reboots
description:
PROGRESS. The reboot is a periodic 50XX score/protection query: main handler 0x3B9E writes commands to the 50XX (06XX ctrl 0x64) and reads a 4-byte response into 0x8060-0x8063 (ctrl 0x74), then at 0x3BBC does LD A,(0x8063)/CP 5/JP NZ,0x0000 -- reboot unless byte3==5. It is a BCD score query: MAME returns {0x80,0x00,0x00,0x05} (byte0=flags, bytes1-3=BCD score 000005).

FIXED so far (3599cb6): the 50XX MB8842 was clocked 6x too fast (namco50_divider was /2 = 1.536 MHz; the MB88xx machine cycle is external/6, and the 50XX external clock is MASTER_CLOCK/6/2 = 1.536 MHz, so the machine cycle is 256 kHz = board/12). At /2 the MCU sat in its output loop (0x0013-0x0023); at /12 it now runs the same command/dispatch loop as MAME (0x04C-0x05A + 0x080-0x081). Only Xevious fits a 50XX so Galaga/Dig Dug are unaffected; all machines tests pass. (Note: the 51XX LLE divider is also /2 and likely wants /12 for the same reason, but it only carries inputs (level signals) so it tolerates the wrong rate; left as-is to avoid Dig Dug regression risk.)

REMAINING: the 50XX response is still {0x00,0x00,0x00,0xFF} (byte3 0xFF = the 4th read finds chip 2 deselected; O=0 on the first three). Command DELIVERY is fine -- MAME sends 0x10 (reset), 0x80 (+5), 0xE5; my MCU receives K=1 (0x10) and K=8 (0x80). But the MCUs internal score RAM stays 0, so the received commands are not applied. So the remaining bug is the fine command-latch handshake timing: WHEN the MCU samples K/R0 relative to the Z80 command write, governed by the 06XX chip-select pulse and the namco06 chip_select_delay (base_divisor cycles), which was tuned for the 51XX at /2 and likely needs adjustment for the 50XX at /12.

Next steps: (1) cycle-level compare of the 50XX MB8842 execution (RAM/registers/O) against MAME during a single command, to see where the score update diverges; (2) tune/verify the 06XX chip_select_delay and the write->chip_select ordering for the 50XX; (3) verify the read handshake outputs all 4 bytes without deselecting on the 4th (the 0xFF). Repro: cargo run -p phosphor-machines --example xevious_boot_check -- <dir> 1600 shows Q3/main cycling. Blocks M1 boot sign-off.
close_reason: FIXED in ed91e91. The 50XX periodic protection check now passes. Root cause chain: (1) 50XX MB8842 was clocked 6x too fast (fixed 3599cb6, /2 -> /12); (2) even at the right rate the LLE MB8842<->06XX command/response handshake (chip-select pulse phase, external-IRQ delivery, read-byte count) could not be synchronised, so the score chip returned zeros. Resolved by replacing the LLE with a behavioural HLE 50XX that responds immediately via the proven 06XX read/write dispatch (like the 51XX/53XX HLE): models reset/player/mode/increment tables/multi-byte set-bonus+high-score and returns the 4-byte flags+BCD-score response. Verified: Xevious clears RAM test + 50XX protection, keeps sub/sound running and main IRQ on, and holds a stable attract loop for 3500+ frames (no reboot cycling).

title: atari_system1 asserts IRQ3 on Marble, whose cartridge has no int3 hardware
description:
AtariSystem1Board generates the motion-object scanline interrupt (IRQ3, the
"SLIP" interrupt) for both System 1 games in the tree, and exposes its state at
0x2E0000 bit 7. Only Road Runner's cartridge has that hardware. Marble Madness's
does not.

WHAT THE REFERENCE SAYS. MAME splits the driver in two precisely over this, at
atarisy1.cpp:2686:

  // atarisy1r_state is used because hardware to generate interrupt 3 only
  // exists on LSI Cart 2, 3, 4 & cockpit boards, it is missing on TTL, LSI

atarisy1_state::update_timers is an empty function (atarisy1_v.cpp:407-409), so
the int3 timer is never scheduled for the games that use that class. Every marble
set uses it (atarisy1.cpp:2671-2675). Every roadrunn set uses atarisy1r_state
(atarisy1.cpp:2687-2689), which schedules it.

WHAT WE DO. atari_system1.rs:1107 calls timer_irq_at_scanline unconditionally at
every scanline boundary; timer_irq_at_scanline (:761-784) walks the active
sprite bank's link list for entries flagged 0xFFFF and asserts IRQ3 at the top of
that entry's band. int3_state (:753) reports it at 0x2E0000. There is no
per-cartridge gate, so marble gets an interrupt line its board does not have.

IMPACT IS PROBABLY NIL TODAY AND THAT IS NOT THE POINT. Marble draws correctly,
so either its display list contains no 0xFFFF-flagged entries or the interrupt it
takes is harmless. But the board is asserting an interrupt line that the hardware
it stands in for does not have, and any test that comes to depend on IRQ3 cannot
tell the two games apart.

WHAT TO DO. Gate the timer interrupt on a per-cartridge board flag, the way the
speech option and the slapstic number already are (AtariSystem1Board::new takes
both). Road Runner sets it, Marble does not. Then assert on marble that IRQ3
never fires across a boot: that check can fail today if Marble's display list
does contain a timer entry, and either outcome is worth knowing.

Surfaced by phosphor-emulator-conformance-rom-programme-hl4t.1, which graded
atari_system1 FULL on the strength of this interrupt: it is the finest
synchronisation primitive on any board surveyed, one scanline wide and placed
wherever the program asks. That grade holds for roadrunner and not for marble,
which is exactly the distinction the board file is currently unable to express.
See docs/designs/conformance-rom-board-survey.md.
close_reason: Gated on a per-cartridge flag: has_scanline_int, off by default, set only by roadrunner via with_scanline_interrupt(). Measured from real ROMs over 1800 frames: marble's display list holds a timer entry in 0 frames, roadrunner's in 1416, so the change is behaviour-preserving today and would have broken Road Runner had the feature been deleted instead of gated. Both new tests were made to fail with the gate removed and again with it inverted. Golden frames for marble and roadrunner unchanged (forced past the #[ignore], which is now phosphor-emulator-gn5w).

comments.author: pjl
comments.text:
Fixed, and the impact question the issue left open is now measured rather than
assumed.

THE CHANGE. AtariSystem1Board gains has_scanline_int, off by default and turned
on by with_scanline_interrupt(), which only roadrunner.rs calls. begin_scanline
now reads

  self.scanline_int = self.has_scanline_int && self.timer_irq_at_scanline(scanline);

Opt-in rather than opt-out because the absence is both the more common case and
the safer default: a board built without the flag behaves like the TTL and LSI
cartridges, which never assert the line. The field is #[save_skip]: it is fixed
at construction, so a load rebuilds it from the factory rather than trusting the
bytes. timer_irq_at_scanline is untouched and still answers what the display
list says, which is a property of the list and not of the cartridge; the gate is
the caller's. int3_state needs no change either: the address decodes on every
cartridge, and where the circuit is absent nothing ever sets the latch, so it
reads a flat zero, which is exactly what MAME's atarisy1_state::int3state_r
returns for the same reason.

WHAT I MEASURED, AND IT ANSWERS "IS THIS ACTUALLY DOING ANYTHING". I booted both
System 1 games from real ROMs for 1800 frames each and counted the frames whose
live motion-object RAM held a timer entry (0xFFFF in word 1) in any of the eight
banks:

  marble      0 / 1800 frames, all eight banks zero
  roadrunner  1416 / 1800 frames, all eight banks

So Marble never supplied the trigger and has never taken a spurious IRQ3. The
board was capable of asserting an interrupt its cartridge does not have, and the
program simply never asked. That makes this change behaviour-preserving today
and a correctness gate for tomorrow, and it is worth saying plainly rather than
leaving as "impact is probably nil".

The Road Runner number is the more useful half. 1416 of 1800 frames carry timer
entries, so Road Runner leans on the SLIP interrupt heavily. Anyone who had
"fixed" this issue by deleting the feature instead of gating it would have
broken Road Runner, and the 384 frames without entries are the boot and EEPROM
self-initialisation the boot_check budget already documents as slow.

The probe was a temporary test under harness/tests and is not committed.

THE CHECKS WERE MADE TO FAIL BOTH WAYS BEFORE BEING TRUSTED. Two tests in
machines/src/atari_system1.rs, both driving the identical display list into both
cartridge configurations:

  the_motion_object_timer_interrupt_is_a_cartridge_option
  the_timer_interrupt_lasts_one_scanline

- Gate deleted (the pre-fix state): the cartridge-option test FAILED on the
  Marble half, as it must.
- Gate inverted: BOTH tests FAILED, the first on the Road Runner half.
That is the pattern that rules out a gate stuck off passing the Marble half for
the wrong reason, and a latched scanline_int passing the Road Runner half for
the wrong reason.

WHAT I DID NOT DO. The one-scanline width and the band formula
256 - (word0>>5) - vsize*8 - 1 are still ours and MAME's, unchecked against a
schematic. This issue was about which cartridges have the circuit, not about
where it fires, and the survey (hl4t.1) records the latter as still open.

A THING FOUND WHILE VERIFYING, AND IT IS NOT SMALL.
golden_frame_test::every_pinned_machine_still_draws_its_frame is #[ignore]d. Its
message says "disabled while the vector renderer is being reworked
(phosphor-emulator-ukgy); re-enable or retire it once its utility has been
reviewed". ukgy closed on 2026-08-25. So the only test in the tree that compares
what a machine draws against a pin has been switched off since then, and a plain
`cargo test -p phosphor-harness --test golden_frame_test` reports 11 passed
without comparing a single frame. I ran it for the two machines I touched by
forcing it (`-- --ignored` with PHOSPHOR_GOLDEN_ONLY): marble and roadrunner
both match their pins, so this change moves no pixels. Filed separately.

FULL VERIFICATION. clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -D warnings
clean (with the two files touched first, so machines was actually re-linted);
cargo test --workspace --all-features green; cargo fmt clean. ROM-gated, run
individually: boot_check 7/7, save_state_rom 7/7, audio_sanity 13/13,
golden_frame 11/11 plus the forced per-machine comparisons above.

title: foodf + gridlee: cocktail flip is addressing-entangled, not a clean framebuffer ROT180
close_reason: Deferred (not converting). foodf and gridlee are landscape (4:3) games with NO screen rotation, only a cocktail 180 flip. Unlike a clean post-render buffer reverse (mario_bros), their flip is baked into scanline/tile ADDRESSING: foodf mirrors source tile coords AND reflects intra-tile pixels (7-px) with a -8 scroll that does not reflect; gridlee reverses VRAM row+nibble order and remaps sprite Y via (271-scanline)+VBEND. Proven algebraically that foodf's flipped output != ROT180(native_unflipped), so a declarative NORMAL/COCKTAIL swap would change pixels. Correct conversion needs ROM-level pixel verification; out of scope for the rotation-standardization pass. All 9 baked-ROTATION machines are migrated.

title: lfsr_noise repeats after 11811 states where the board's shift register does not
description:
Found while rebuilding Donkey Kong's stomp from the board. Simulating both
registers side by side over 400k clocks:

  ours   rising edges 0.2500 per clock, duty 0.500, CYCLE LENGTH 11811
  board  rising edges 0.2494 per clock, duty 0.500, cycle length > 400000

The edge statistics match, which is what the stomp's divider cares about, so
this did not block that work — the rumble's rate came out at 124.7 Hz against
the board's 125.0. But our register is not running a maximal-length sequence.
11811 states at dkong's 4 kHz clock is a 2.95 s repeat.

CAUSE. core/src/device/discrete/node.rs LfsrNoise shifts RIGHT and inserts the
XOR at the top, then outputs bit 0. The board's three LS164s shift LEFT, insert
at bit 0, and the tap numbering is relative to that direction — so the same
'taps (10, 23)' describes a different recurrence in each, and ours is not
primitive. The board also inserts the INVERSE of the XOR and takes its output
from the XOR itself rather than from a register bit; both are ordinary options
on real noise circuits.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND dkong. A caller writing down the tap numbers from a
schematic gets a different polynomial than the schematic describes, silently,
and the failure is a shortened cycle rather than an error. Anything using this
for a sustained noise voice would have an audible repeat.

FIX. Widen LfsrSpec to carry what a real shift register has: direction, whether
the feedback is inverted before insertion, and whether the output is a register
bit or the feedback term. Then dkong's stomp can state the board's register
directly instead of relying on the statistics happening to match.

Check the other lfsr_noise callers when changing the semantics — galaxian's
noise is the one to look at first.
close_reason:
Fixed, and this issue UNDERSOLD it. It said the edge statistics matched so the shortened cycle 'did not block that work'. The mean edge rate does match; the run-length DISTRIBUTION does not, and that is what shapes the spectrum of anything downstream of the register. Correcting it moved Donkey Kong's stomp noticeably:

                    before        now      board
  centroid        134.8 Hz   126.6 Hz   124.9 Hz
  band 0-150        72.4 %     81.5 %     89.5 %
  band 150-400      27.0 %     18.0 %     10.2 %

So a register that produces the right average and the wrong sequence is not interchangeable with the real one, even feeding something as forgiving as a divide-by-eight.

WHAT CHANGED. LfsrSpec now states what 'taps (10, 23)' actually means, because by itself it does not mean a polynomial:
  - shift: LfsrShift::TowardZero | TowardHigh. Toward-high is how a chain of shift registers is wired — data in at bit 0 — so bit n is the bit clocked in n steps ago and tap numbers match a schematic's.
  - invert_feedback: some circuits invert the XOR before it re-enters.
  - output: LfsrOutput::RegisterBit | Feedback. Real noise circuits often tap the XOR gate rather than the register.

Donkey Kong's stomp now states the board's arrangement (toward-high, inverted feedback, output from the XOR, seed 0). The other three callers keep their existing behaviour through LfsrSpec::toward_zero, spelled out at each site rather than inherited silently — asteroids and galaxian chose their taps against the old shift direction and migrating them would run a different polynomial, which needs a reference to verify against. Galaxian's is known bad (…-9e1q), so that is not a today job.

Also relaxed the non-zero seed assertion: all-zeros is a fixed point only when the feedback is NOT inverted. With inversion it is an ordinary state, and it is the one a real register powers up in, so refusing it would force a fictitious seed.
